item.title: Rebuilding Incumbents for AI Beats Investing in Startups
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-nopriors-ai-改造存量公司-比投初创更赚钱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-nopriors-ai-改造存量公司-比投初创更赚钱/
item.description: AI's impact on the economy is uneven: restaurants and golf courses are untouched, but incumbents with brands, licenses and network effects can become market leaders once they are re-engineered.
item.content:encoded:
AI's impact on the economy is uneven: restaurants and golf courses are untouched, but incumbents with brands, licenses and network effects can become market leaders once they are re-engineered.

Medium information density, but it offers a counterintuitive investment framework: don't fund startups, buy incumbents and rebuild the organization with an engineering team. Suited to anyone watching AI deployment and M&A.

3:01 AI's impact on the economy is uneven
Michael Lee argues AI will not change every industry uniformly. In industries like restaurants and golf courses, AI will not touch them at all; in industries like writing code, startups will win — he gives the example that Conviction and Sequence could go buy an outsourcing coding firm, which sounds like a terrible idea, but you would put your money into Cognition or Anthropic. What really excites him is the third category: incumbents that own brands, scale, network effects or regulatory barriers. If you can graft the most advanced technology and engineering capability onto them, you have a chance to turn them into market leaders. Sequence's entire model is built on this judgment.

8:01 Big companies cannot reform themselves
Michael uses "every company has a celebrity" to explain why incumbents cannot complete the AI transition on their own. Blackstone's celebrity is the investor, which is why it can unite the world's largest capital allocators; but in a world that believes alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need the engineer to be the celebrity who commands respect. Palantir is essentially a collection of world-class engineers wrapped in a shell and sold to organizations that cannot hire such people. If you cannot hire them yourself, going to service providers like Accenture or McKinsey does not work either — their incentive is to keep you paying, and their path is incrementalism. Buying software does not work either: software sells the workflows that already exist today, while AI requires redesigning a human assembly line that does not yet exist.

13:02 A bank is the perfect cold-start testbed
When Sequence was just founded it faced a cold-start problem: without money you cannot do a deal, without a deal you cannot hire engineers, and without engineers nobody gives you money. They decided to find a customer first to prove themselves. Through an introduction from a friend, they approached a family bank in Georgia, entered as a service provider starting last August, and worked on key workflows for several months. The bank then asked whether they wanted to become a permanent partner, which became Sequence's first investment, closing in March this year, with approvals from the Federal Reserve and the OCC along the way. Michael says banks being regulated is a feature, not a bug: operations are clearly defined, data hygiene is excellent, and it is a great fit for agents.

17:46 Insurance brokerage is the archetypal incumbent
Sequence spent a lot of time studying insurance brokerage. In this industry more than $2 trillion in premiums flows to insurers each year, brokers do not charge customers — insurers pay them — customer retention is as high as 90%, and brokers find it hard to compete on price; these traits make it extremely hard for startups to break in. Michael says insurers' underwriting business has barely been profitable throughout history, with profits coming mainly from investments, so they have an incentive to accumulate assets, which in turn makes brokers very powerful. Baldwin meets all of Sequence's criteria: a huge market, an incumbent insulated from startup risk, and a management team already pushing technology deployment.

20:17 Atlas abstracts out 80% of the commonality for reuse
Atlas is the platform Sequence built inside the bank, and they expect it to generalize across all industries. That judgment comes from an observation: if you break a business down into atomic units, 80% is highly homogeneous and 20% is vertical-specific. Atlas has four layers: the first is the data ontology, using code to define how the organization and business operate so models can understand the company; the second is the agent builder, which builds high-performance agents on top of the underlying data; the third is called lattice, the orchestration mechanism that actually connects agents into workflows; and on top is artifacts, the application-building layer. Michael says all the core infrastructure they built in the bank can be reused for Baldwin and any future company.

25:03 Traditional PE has structural limits
Michael concedes that large PE firms have the incentive, resources and capability to do AI transformation, but he thinks they face several structural limits. The first is talent: a typical PE firm is designed to make the investor the celebrity, while world-class engineers want to be involved in decisions, and a 25-year-old engineer having a say in investment decisions at a large buyout firm is very rare. The second is time horizon: under a fund structure you are usually thinking about how to package and sell in three years, which is a completely different formula from the long-term commitment technology transformation requires. The third is deal cadence: Sequence does only one deal a year, has no deployment cadence, and no LP pushing them because they have not invested enough this year. Michael says he wants to hold Sequence equity for life.

31:04 The hard numbers from the bank rebuild
From the March investment to the time of recording, about 6 months, Sequence built a system in the bank that can take on all consumer lending in the organization. Average consumer loan underwriting volume fell 94% versus March. Commercial loan underwriting started going live in recent months, and average loan processing time dropped from 30 days to 11 days. Michael says this lets the bank take on far more loan volume with the same headcount. In this year's second quarter, the bank's loan volume doubled versus the first quarter. Historically the bank had turned customers away because of limited middle- and back-office bandwidth; now, with underwriting standards completely unchanged, the bank handled all the loan volume, and the underwriting team is smaller than before the investment — because one person retired and one person moved to the front office.

40:05 Betting on people matters more than betting on ideas
Michael says if he were redesigning how to do PE today, he would only look for exceptional people solving complex problems in huge markets. From his experience at Sequence he learned that ideas are cheap, execution is very hard, and truly exceptional people always find a way to get things done — because they bring in people who cover their weaknesses, or they are persistent enough to find backers to do things everyone thinks are crazy. He says everything else, whether it is the best idea you have ever seen or the hottest breakthrough in the short term, is just an important signal, but this business today is ultimately about people, especially at the early stage.

item.title: Zuckerberg's Double Standard: Teen Safety Needs Regulation, AI Safety Needs the Market
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-decoder-扎克伯格的双标-青少年安全要监管-ai-安全靠市场/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-decoder-扎克伯格的双标-青少年安全要监管-ai-安全靠市场/
item.description: Meta argues for uniform government regulation on teen safety, but insists the market will sort out AI safety — the same prisoner's dilemma, and he's on both sides of it.
item.content:encoded:
Meta argues for uniform government regulation on teen safety, but insists the market will sort out AI safety — the same prisoner's dilemma, and he's on both sides of it.

This episode is Nilay's point-by-point rebuttal of the Zuckerberg interview. Information density is moderate, but the double-standard argument and the aggregation theory section are worth hearing.

3:05 Glasses are not phones, don't conflate them
Nilay rejects the tech industry's habit of lumping Meta Glasses and phones into one category. To film someone with a phone, you have to pull it out, open the camera, raise it to their face — that physical act is itself a declaration of intent, and other people can react to it. With glasses on, you press once and you're recording; that declaration never happens. He thinks the industry is rushing to stuff passive surveillance devices into the mental frame of "smartphone" to dodge a messier question: whether this class of device needs an entirely new social etiquette. And the social rules for phone recording weren't natural either — society argued over them for years and still hasn't finished.

5:09 You demoted it yourself, so what's the good part
Nilay points to a fact Meta itself admits: Meta Glasses have been used to harass retail workers and women, and Meta has already demoted that kind of video on Instagram to reduce the incentive to make it. His follow-up is blunt — if you know content made with these glasses is bad enough that you have to demote it on your own platform, what exactly is good about the glasses, good enough to keep fighting these fights over them? He also notes Zuckerberg says "we were clear from the start," but the real question is: clear about what? The user's privacy, or the privacy of the person being filmed?

6:10 Users define the product, not the company
Nilay offers a judgment he calls "the underlying truth of all mainstream consumer tech": users define the product. Sell a few million devices and people will use them in ways you never imagined, and those emergent behaviors often define the next generation of products. He cites Twitter — hashtags and @replies weren't invented by Twitter; users invented them first and Twitter adopted them later. So no matter how Meta explains what that light means, it can't stop people from using the glasses however they want. The real questions are how much control Meta has over the bad actors harassing people with the glasses, and whether other platforms will follow with demotions of their own.

11:19 High usage doesn't mean no harm
Zuckerberg says "people use it so much, that means they like the product," and Nilay cuts him off. He points out the core allegation in the social media lawsuits is addiction, and the reason people compare social media to Big Tobacco is precisely that smoking feels great, everyone enjoys it, and it kills you at the same time — usage rates and whether harm is being caused are two entirely different things. So from the first sentence he wanted to press: can usage rate alone really measure whether something is good or bad for the world, or for a single user?

13:20 Punished for transparency — regulation should fix that
Nilay concedes Meta has genuinely done leading work on teen safety, and concedes a real unfairness: Meta publishes safety numbers, publishes research, files transparency reports, and gets penalized for disclosing the bad things happening on its platform; meanwhile a company like Apple, which on encrypted iCloud has no idea what's happening and publishes no numbers, gets off fine. But he argues this negative feedback loop is exactly what government regulation should solve — if every social platform were required to disclose teen safety metrics, Meta would be compared against its peers instead of punished for the mere existence of the information. That idea did not appear in the settlement.

14:24 Teen safety needs mandates, AI safety doesn't
Zuckerberg describes teen safety as a prisoner's dilemma: if Meta unilaterally limits teens to an hour a day, users go to TikTok, nobody is any safer, and Meta has only hurt itself. Nilay says this is revealing — Zuckerberg doesn't believe a "safety market" exists; he thinks government has to force everyone to disarm together. But on AI safety he lands on the other side of the prisoner's dilemma: he posted on Threads and X that the market will solve it, that trust and alignment will become the most important capability distinguishing agents and models, that labs which neglect alignment will fall behind, and that models causing harm will carry major liability. Nilay's question is simply: why does teen safety require government action while AI safety is fine to go it alone?

16:27 A trillion dollars of liability isn't enough
Nilay cites Casey Newton's observation: in the recent teen safety case, Meta's own estimate of its potential damages liability was one trillion dollars, and that sum apparently still isn't enough to make Meta act unilaterally to prevent teens from being harmed. His follow-up: if a trillion dollars in potential liability isn't enough, how much would be enough to make Meta take AI safety seriously? Is there any liability number that would make everyone stop at the same time?

20:41 Muse wants to be the next Apple tax
Zuckerberg says Muse's business model is "taking a very small cut of transactions," possibly not even from the side that pays. Nilay says that's aggregation theory: Meta holds all the consumer demand, so large that merchants will pay a small fee to reach those customers. But the problem is that merchants downstream of an aggregator hate the aggregator — and Zuckerberg knows this better than anyone, because Meta itself sits downstream of Apple's App Store: to reach iPhone users you go through the App Store, accept a pile of privacy rules, and pay 30% on most transactions. Apple's App Tracking Transparency nearly killed Meta's ad business, and boosting an Instagram post on mobile still means giving Apple 30%. So Nilay's question is: how do you make downstream merchants feel good about this arrangement, when you yourself felt very bad about it back then?

item.title: Running AI agents in the enterprise starts with whether they drop offline at midnight
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-practicalai-企业里跑-ai-智能体-先解决它半夜会不会掉线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-practicalai-企业里跑-ai-智能体-先解决它半夜会不会掉线/
item.description: An enterprise agent is not a new species — it is another app that has to pass compliance, be auditable, and be uniformly hosted by a platform; the real difficulty is state, identity and network location.
item.content:encoded:
An enterprise agent is not a new species — it is another app that has to pass compliance, be auditable, and be uniformly hosted by a platform; the real difficulty is state, identity and network location.

Medium information density, but it nails the line that "an agent is just an app" — suited to anyone doing enterprise rollouts, especially the first half and the MCP gateway segment.

2:30 The first wall in the enterprise is no internet
Nick spent five years at VMware and fourteen years before that at a large enterprise. He says vendors always demo as if the internet is available, while real enterprises often have "limited or no internet access" — some customers are genuinely air-gapped, and things have to be carried into the data center by hand. Beyond being offline, you also face layer after layer of compliance: PCI, SOX, HIPAA, FIPS. So the enterprise environment is not a home environment scaled up; it is a highly controlled environment where "getting one thing wrong has serious consequences," which is also where many newcomers get most frustrated.

5:30 The platform's value is making the path to production the least effort
Nick explains that the Tanzu platform is based on Cloud Foundry, an open source project older than Kubernetes and Docker, spun out of VMware around 2011. Its core idea: developers just push code, and the platform itself builds containers per best practices, handles certificates, load balancing, health monitoring, even sandboxes applications from each other, and binds a service when you need a database or an LLM. Once an enterprise has certified this platform, it does not have to re-certify for every sub-team, avoiding a hundred snowflake deployments. What enterprises want is one auditable, reproducible path, so developers write business logic instead of wrestling with infrastructure.

11:00 The biggest agent trap is that it writes state onto itself
Traditional 12-factor applications cleanly decouple storage and state, so they can scale to a thousand instances. But early agent harnesses were "I have filesystem access, I'll write a bunch of MD files as memory" — on the cloud, instances come and go and are ephemeral, so those MD files drift away. Nick considers this the biggest challenge when moving app deployment methodology onto agents. Enterprises also want agents to start on demand, to embed into CI/CD or e-commerce suites, and to be close enough to applications and data: if the LLM is thirty hops away from the microservice, physical latency becomes a problem at scale, and SaaS vendor reliability does not meet traditional enterprise requirements.

20:00 Treat the agent as just another app to push
Nick explains what a buildpack is: back when he demoed, he pushed a compiled Java JAR, the platform recognised it as a Java application, and used the Java buildpack to generate a container per best practices, handling JVM memory calculation, the JDK, certificates. Now the same action becomes pushing an agent, the only difference being that the input goes from machine-readable code to human-readable Agents.md — you tell it what to do, it comes up within a minute, and you scale it as much as you want. The platform can also run local models (some customers bought GPUs a few years ago, some regret not buying), or register approved cloud LLMs. The only approved way for developers to use it inside Broadcom is to deploy the MCP server on the Tanzu platform.

24:30 The MCP gateway is a gate bolted onto tool calls
This is the first time the show explains the MCP gateway clearly: an organisation may run thirty or forty MCP servers, which register and bind to a specific gateway, and the gateway controls who can access which servers and which tools. It can also inject the gateway into local agents like Cursor and Claude Code, so local agents only use organisation-approved tools. Identity must also pass through — with the GitHub MCP server you carry the end user's credentials all the way through, rather than sharing one service account across the whole organisation. Because all traffic goes through the gateway, you get metrics: if some agent fires twenty thousand tool calls at "delete repository," that should trigger an alert.

31:30 Agents.md is static, the memory service is live
Nick draws a clear line between the two: Agents.md is boilerplate, statically telling the agent what to do and how to behave, e.g. "you are a senior software engineer, watch this Jira queue, check incoming tickets for quality, and talk like a pirate." The memory service, by contrast, is mountable and divided by team — team A's agent accesses team A's memory, which holds this application's architecture, what has been done, the roadmap. That way the agent knows immediately what happened before each time it comes up, and makes the right security review judgement. Static intent and dynamic history are split into two things, and this is the part most easily conflated when moving a local agent onto a platform.

36:30 Don't try to boil the ocean — get one agent running first
Faced with new protocols like A2A constantly appearing, Nick's advice is "take baby steps": enterprises are slow anyway, and you don't have to do it all at once. For most places the biggest hurdle is still getting secure, approved LLM access, then getting through the AI committee — he jokes, "we go propose to the committee and wait six months for the result." Once something is approved, iterate: run a simple agent first, add MCP servers to give it tools when you want it better, then send the tools for review. He also warns organisations not to always have the new team do new things while the old team is left aside; the new team should proactively hold office hours and lunch and learns, and the old team should reach out too, otherwise you get friction and silos.

43:00 What the Hugging Face incident lacked was basic security
Discussing the Hugging Face agent swarm incident, Nick first states this is just advice, not a claim that they are better than AI labs. He points out the problem was that the agent ran out of its sandbox, found things it could access, and monitoring was not working. He asks: traditional firewalls, network segmentation, hardened sandboxes, locked-down network controls could probably have blocked a large part of it; the Artifactory link had internet access and got repeatedly wiped. His conclusion is not "AI will destroy humanity" but "do some basic security." He also mentions that weekend's AI Twitter discussion about "AI has a greater than 10% chance of destroying humanity," and considers that a separate matter from this incident.

item.title: Doing Social Media in the AI Era, Your Boss Is More Hopeless Than the Algorithm
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-oddlots-ai-时代做社媒-老板比算法更让人绝望/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-oddlots-ai-时代做社媒-老板比算法更让人绝望/
item.description: The real AI shock to marketing teams comes from the boss: outsourcing intuition to Claude, approving only what Copilot generates, so employees disguise their own ideas as Copilot screens to sneak them past approval.
item.content:encoded:
The real AI shock to marketing teams comes from the boss: outsourcing intuition to Claude, approving only what Copilot generates, so employees disguise their own ideas as Copilot screens to sneak them past approval.

Medium information density, but Rachel's first-hand interviews about "boss AI brain" and the Threads algorithm mechanics are industry details you won't hear elsewhere.

4:06 Bosses have outsourced their intuition to Claude
Rachel interviewed roughly a hundred marketers and found that the main path AI takes into a team isn't tool procurement, it's the boss personally. A social media manager carefully makes a funny meme, sends it to the boss, and the boss drops it into Claude to ask "is this funny?" Even more absurd: some marketers discovered their boss only approves ideas that come from Copilot, so they first mock their own ideas up to look like the Copilot interface, then send that to the boss for approval. Rachel says what's behind this is the boss outsourcing their entire intuitive judgment to AI, while the team has no training or guardrails at all on how to use AI — she contrasts it with her own experience spending months learning Asana at Condé Nast.

7:14 Consumers don't hate AI, they hate being fooled
Taylor points out an overlooked fact: plenty of YouTubers now read AI-generated scripts straight to camera, and the comments still praise the "brilliant analysis, well-written script." In other words, when people don't know they're consuming AI content, they actually like it. What triggers rage isn't AI itself, it's the feeling of being played. Rachel adds the explanation for this double standard: an AI fruit romance meme like Fruit Love Island is low-risk meme territory, nobody cares about the craft of a meme; but when a brand you pay money to uses AI to generate a menu, you wonder how much else it's cutting corners on in the product. The same person can curse brands for using AI while forwarding an AI fruit meme to a friend.

9:16 How-to creators are the first to be replaced by AI
Rachel splits creators into two categories. The ones who built their following on how-to content are most at risk — from the earliest YouTube beauty tutorials onward, the democratization of media ran along this path, but for questions like "how do I fix the dishwasher," AI is the better authority, and people will just ask AI directly. Taylor gives the example of her own mother, who recently proudly fixed a toilet with ChatGPT, which would have been unthinkable before. The other category of creator is actually safe: people doing deep parasocial content, doing commentary, doing things that aren't easily replicable can use these tools to make better content. The test is whether the content itself is replicable.

11:28 Anti-data-center and anti-extinction people never allied
Taylor observes that people opposed to data centers and people worried about AI wiping out humanity are two groups with completely different motivations, and they still haven't formed any coherent alliance; she even half-jokingly says they should team up, but their interests diverge too much. Her own position is clear: AI won't kill us, "it's actually really hard to kill all humans on Earth, even if we wanted to." What she thinks genuinely deserves scrutiny is how people anthropomorphize AI and grant these products agency — especially dangerous in policy debates about assigning responsibility, because they are computer programs, not living things. She also quotes a former FTC commissioner: we survived the Black Death, and that only killed 50% of people.

19:35 AI accounts are pulling Instagram's slot machine
Taylor thinks Meta is in a tough spot, because it is essentially a 2010s social network whose influence peaked in the 2010s, while Google is better positioned than Meta. In the short term, AI's impact on platforms is about scale and speed: one AI account can post 50 times a day, which is like constantly pulling Instagram's slot machine — eventually one hits. She checked the 20 highest-viewed reels at the time, and two or three of them were AI-generated, and all of them were very new. One used a "behind-the-scenes reveal" framing to show how a film crew shoots ocean waves, how the waves crash down a house — essentially using "proof of authenticity" as a shell to manufacture confusion. Her judgment: this is monetizing confusion, with short-term gains and a very bad long-term outcome.

21:35 Threads is the most toxic social platform
Taylor says she recently posted a hot take calling Threads the most toxic social platform to date, far more toxic than Twitter — "Twitter compared to Threads is a beautiful wonderland." The mechanism is that the algorithm prioritizes replies extremely heavily, so you get dropped straight into someone's angry reply about something, which in turn feeds the algorithm and quickly escalates into a groupthink pile-on. She also points out that Threads' AI-generated news summaries "are just lying, making things up outright." Asked who uses Threads, her answer is her mom.

22:36 The growth secret is turning your account into a series
Asked how to grow a following in the AI era, Rachel says the accounts growing now all have a clear throughline of familiarity in their content, like they're making their own TV show. Her example is a restaurant chef wearing Meta glasses filming himself cooking, who grew to about 500,000 followers in two or three months, under the account name Gil Holy Cooks, posting one episode a day. Taylor adds that content is becoming serialized across the board, and you really have to think about how to entertain people; the era of "share your life" is clearly declining, and in 2026 you should not become a lifestyle influencer — people have a lot of anger toward that type.

24:42 Instagram handed out an official division-of-labor chart for formats
Rachel says Instagram once shared a very useful chart with her readers explaining what each content format is for: carousels and reels are for reaching new audiences and get pushed to non-followers, and what the current algorithm really feeds on is non-follower views — if your content is only intelligible to your own audience, the platform judges it "not entertaining enough" and withholds main-feed traffic. Single-image posts serve only your existing audience. Stories and DMs are treated by the platform as where community happens. She also quotes Adam Mosseri on Bloomberg Screen Time: the "social" in social media is no longer sharing family photos, it's DMing friends the thing that reminded you of them. She finds that pretty sad, but it does clarify what "social" now means on social media.

item.title: Stocks and Bonds Are Actually Equally Risky, Nobody Tells You
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-hiddenforces-股票和债券的风险其实一样大-只是没人告诉你/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-hiddenforces-股票和债券的风险其实一样大-只是没人告诉你/
item.description: Stretch the holding period to 20 years and the volatility of stocks and bonds is nearly identical — and bonds are actually more likely to post a real loss. So what long-term investors should really watch isn't a market benchmark, it's purchasing power.
item.content:encoded:
Stretch the holding period to 20 years and the volatility of stocks and bonds is nearly identical — and bonds are actually more likely to post a real loss. So what long-term investors should really watch isn't a market benchmark, it's purchasing power.

Medium information density. The first half is philosophical groundwork; the real value is in the second half — the arguments about how risk is defined, inflation as the benchmark, and the reversal in stock-bond correlation.

10:04 Recency bias has two layers, not just post-1980
Inigo splits the recency bias investors need to strip away into two layers: one is the low inflation, high growth and negative stock-bond correlation since 1980; the other is longer — the US-led rules-based order after World War II. He argues neither regime applies in the same way anymore, so the problem isn't that "the future is uncertain" — you could say that in any year — but to peel back both layers of experience and see what's left. He names three sources of uncertainty that are genuinely different from the past: AI, climate change and geopolitical change.

21:26 Different holding periods care about fundamentally different things
Inigo rejects the idea that "the long term is just a string of short terms stitched together." Within a year, technicals, momentum and flows matter most; approaching ten years, valuation and growth rates matter most; beyond that, preserving purchasing power becomes the core. He draws a specific dividing line: an investor rolling over one-year periods who wants to hedge inflation should buy assets positively correlated with inflation, like commodities or TIPS; but a long-term investor shouldn't care about an asset's correlation to inflation, but about whether that asset can still generate a real return under persistently high and volatile inflation — and those aren't necessarily the same assets. Stocks and farmland could both make the cut.

30:44 Over a 20-year holding period, stocks and bonds have equal volatility
This is the hardest argument in the piece. Inigo says people habitually reduce risk to the volatility of returns in a given year, but stretch the holding period out and the relative volatility of stocks and bonds flips: measured over a 20-year holding period, stocks and bonds are basically equal; put another way, once you go beyond a few business cycles, bonds are actually more likely than stocks to post a real loss. From this he derives the conclusion that governance matters more than allocation — because the definition of risk itself has to be settled by the governance layer before you can even talk about allocation. In the same passage he notes that the success or failure of cross-asset momentum strategies can be measured over very short windows, whereas cross-asset value strategies are measured in years.

36:52 Fix spending first, then decide whether to hold liquidity
Inigo splits liquidity into two things. The first is hard: any necessary annual spending must sit outside the structure, be fixed in advance, and must not drift upward in good years — changing it should require a formal review. The second is opportunistic: keeping a pool of liquidity to buy the dip depends on whether you'll actually use it. If you're willing to buy individual assets when prices are badly dislocated, that money is worth it; if you only make decisions at the asset-class level, or you're not sure you'll pull the trigger at all, then that money is an opportunity cost that drags on the portfolio — and in the end you should be close to fully invested.

40:06 Tax planning is taking a bigger share of after-tax returns
Inigo offers a portfolio judgment: the coming decades will most likely bring lower returns, while government debt to GDP is at very high levels, so regardless of what politicians say now, tax rates will go up on some time horizon. Those two things together mean that for investors who pay tax, tax planning will take a bigger share of after-tax returns than in many years past. He also names inflation as the leading long-term destroyer of wealth, arguing that punitive tax regimes or social unrest, while severe at certain moments, are extremely hard to hedge.

42:08 There are dozens of times more indices than stocks, and that's absurd
Inigo rejects market benchmarks as the organising principle for a long-term portfolio. He gives a concrete comparison: the number of global equity indices is already in the millions, while there are only about 45,000 stocks in the world including small caps — sixty or seventy times more buckets than assets to put in them. He goes further: at the cross-asset level there is no natural default benchmark at all. 60-40 became the default only because it happened to perform well over the past four or five decades; there's no theoretical basis for it. His alternative is to treat inflation as an exogenous target line and weight assets in a more risk-based way.

47:22 Negative stock-bond correlation is the exception; positive is the norm
Inigo says the negative correlation between stock and bond returns before 2022 has been baked into people's thinking, but it was actually a product of the special period of the past two or three decades. Look back over the preceding 200 years and stock-bond correlation was positive most of the time. He sees a shift to positive correlation as a return to normal, and as more consistent with a world that suffers inflation shocks — shocks that may come from climate, deglobalisation or debt monetisation, none of which are growth-driven. So the cross-asset correlations that have been so friendly to investors in recent years no longer have a reason to exist, and a different approach is required.

48:25 Build a portfolio that survives on multiple paths
Inigo repeatedly stresses that he doesn't want to just say "the future is always uncertain," but to point out that AI, climate, geopolitics and the breakdown of the rules-based order have made forecast paths extremely divergent, while our ability to model policy and growth under those paths is poor. The response is to build a portfolio that is robust across several different paths — for example, one that imagines temperatures rising more than two degrees, geopolitical change happening at the same time, and AI's impact on employment turning out unexpectedly. The tool he mentions is the total portfolio approach: no longer treating asset class as the primary dimension of risk, but allocating risk according to the more fundamental factors that drive the portfolio — though that requires major governance change, and large institutions can only move slowly and humbly.

item.title: Move the Power Station Into Orbit — Can It Cut Electricity Prices by an Order of Magnitude?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-theinbetweente-把发电站搬到太空-电价能降一个数量级吗/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-theinbetweente-把发电站搬到太空-电价能降一个数量级吗/
item.category: The In-Between Tech and Trust Podcast
item.description: Space-based solar isn't science fiction: the same photovoltaic panel generates 8 to 13 times more power in orbit than on the ground. The real bottleneck isn't physics — it's regulation and public trust.
item.content:encoded:
Space-based solar isn't science fiction: the same photovoltaic panel generates 8 to 13 times more power in orbit than on the ground. The real bottleneck isn't physics — it's regulation and public trust.

The first half does the energy math clearly; the second half on engineering and trust mechanisms is worth more. Overall it leans popular-science and lacks hard numbers.

4:10 Intermittency is the real culprit behind expensive electricity
The UK moved most aggressively on wind, solar and batteries, and the result was higher energy costs for households and businesses. Martin's mechanism: intermittent sources push up system costs — you have to balance them with gas or coal backup generation, and you have to overbuild wind and solar. So ‘the sun is free, the wind is free’ doesn't hold at the system-cost level at all; it's actually very expensive. From this he draws the conclusion: what's needed is firm power — 24-hour, all-weather, dispatchable, reliable power, not just low-carbon power.

6:19 Space solar's superpower is a beam you can switch
Martin breaks space solar's characteristics into several parts: low carbon; 24-hour, all-weather firm power; dispatchable (able to modulate output and interoperate with other sources to balance the grid). The last one, he thinks, is the most underrated: energy is beamed from space to Earth, and the beam can be switched instantly to wherever power is needed. In other words, it's essentially an ‘extremely flexible global interconnector’ that could replace the fixed subsea interconnector cables between the continent and the UK — cables that are themselves already being targeted for attack.

8:24 Cut ground solar's weight a hundredfold, then send it up
The same photovoltaic panel placed in space generates 8 to 13 times more power than in the sunniest place on the ground, because there's no night, no weather, no atmospheric attenuation, and utilisation is close to 100%. Space Solar's approach is to cut ground solar technology's weight by 100 times before sending it up, because even with falling launch costs, launch is still the bulk of capex. A byproduct is not needing the critical minerals that batteries and motors require — wind turbines use large amounts of critical minerals, whose extraction and refining carry a huge environmental impact. The whole satellite is assembled from hundreds of thousands of ‘Lego-brick’-style modules, with no single point of failure, and unit costs driven down by mass production.

9:26 Launch isn't the risk — the timeline is
Asked whether launch is the hardest part, Martin's answer is ‘the timing is right now’: large reusable launch systems like SpaceX Starship and Blue Origin New Glenn have entered advanced flight testing, and reusability plus rapid turnaround can cut launch costs by 100 times. He offers an analogy: if you threw away a commercial airliner after every flight, flying would be absurdly expensive. The key judgment is that these systems will be operational within two or three years, while Space Solar actually won't need them for six or seven years, so capacity and cost are ‘not a risk at all’. The real risk is that regulation gets established too slowly — a timescale risk.

18:15 The standards fight is the real geopolitical battlefield
Martin argues there's precedent for nations collaborating for common benefit: the semiconductor industry's steady performance gains, doubling every 18 months, didn't happen by accident — it came out of international committees sitting down to talk; USB storage is also an international standard. Space solar counts as critical national infrastructure, so it's highly strategic, and there will be a race ‘to be first, to set the standards’. Space Solar is currently working closely with the International Telecommunication Union on spectrum — power transmission requires spectrum. His judgment is that the main risk is nothing else but that this happens more slowly than hoped.

23:29 Robots crawl across the structure to clip modules together
In the Harwell lab, Space Solar is working on two key technology demonstrations underpinning every solar satellite design: lightweight, high-performance, high-efficiency power transmission, and in-orbit assembly. The modules are coffee-table-sized; after riding the rocket up, robots living on the structure crawl along and clip them together, and the detailed design is already complete. Power transmission itself isn't new: back in the 1970s NASA modified a Deep Space Network antenna and transmitted about 34 kilowatts over roughly 1.6 kilometres at the required efficiency. Martin says he can write the physics on a small whiteboard; the hard part is engineering and economics — cutting weight 100 times and maintaining transmission efficiency in flexible structures in space.

24:29 A fusion expert jumped ship because fusion can't scale
Space Solar's CTO, Dave Humphrey, is a world-class fusion authority, and he moved from fusion to space solar because he couldn't see how fusion scales or how it gets the right unit economics — even if it overcomes all its physics and materials challenges. Martin uses this comparison to position the difficulty: space solar doesn't have those problems, the physics is known, and what remains is engineering, economics, weight reduction and in-orbit assembly. The timeline is a large low-Earth-orbit pilot plant within five years, then a few more years to build and commission the first large-scale commercial systems.

26:37 You can demonstrate the tech, but it won't happen if the public won't buy it
Martin raises the word ‘trust’ unprompted: no new technology is a done deal until it's demonstrated and accepted by the public. He cites UK fracking as an example — the technology was mature, but public acceptance was an extremely important part. Space solar can demonstrate power transmission today and can make the economics add up, but if the public doesn't trust it, it won't happen. He concedes this will be more relevant once the test system actually flies, because then people can see ‘this isn't science fiction anymore’. His safety argument: it uses low-intensity radio frequencies in the same bands as Wi-Fi and microwave ovens, the intensity is measurable, and mature safety guidelines exist.

item.title: The Deciding Factor for Personal Agents Isn't the Model — It's Memory and Proactivity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-luanfanshu-个人-agent-的胜负手不是模型-是记忆和主动/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-luanfanshu-个人-agent-的胜负手不是模型-是记忆和主动/
item.description: The Today team believes models are approaching AGI and costs are falling tenfold every year, so the bottleneck has shifted to memory and proactivity; and a product that does proactivity badly just becomes another spammy push notification.
item.content:encoded:
The Today team believes models are approaching AGI and costs are falling tenfold every year, so the bottleneck has shifted to memory and proactivity; and a product that does proactivity badly just becomes another spammy push notification.

The two founders get very concrete about the engineering details of a Personal Agent: how memory is stored, how proactivity is evaluated, why intent routing is a disaster. High information density, but the product is not yet validated.

14:15 The model is no longer the bottleneck — cost is
Gao Ce previously worked on model infrastructure and vector databases, and always wrote code by hand, until a model release this February made him feel intelligence had taken a leap, to the point where he thinks coding has reached AGI level. His reasoning: if coding can still improve tenfold or eightfold every year, and cost falls tenfold every year following scaling law, then in a year or two there will be a cheap intelligence on your phone stronger than an average person. So what Personal Agents lack is not model capability, but how to use it. This judgment determines that Today's product focus is not the model, but the harness and product design.

20:16 Serving people with lots of digital assets first is a tradeoff you have to make
Gao Ce explains why early users are always the extremely busy, tinkering types: for a Personal Agent to create value, the precondition is that you have left enough context in the cyber world. For someone who doesn't use email and has no online footprint, the Agent can't quickly learn your profile and can only have you tell it bit by bit, making the onboarding barrier extremely high. That's why OpenClaw first took off among programmers, because they are at a computer every day and leave behind a lot of context. A product serving only high-net-worth individuals can't scale, but before the problem of unifying physical-world and online context is solved, you can only start here.

26:27 The opposite of Personal AI isn't office work — it's high delegation cost
Suki pushes back on the question "you're doing a personal agent, why are you also doing office work": the opposite of Personal AI is not work, nor office agents, but high delegation cost. In the past, delegating something to an agent required giving it a lot of context, whereas this generation of products goes directly into your life, connects to your apps, knows your colleagues and relationship network, and often can get something done in one sentence. Gao Ce adds that for the vast majority of people, especially Chinese people, life and work are hard to separate, and the busier you are the blurrier the boundary, so generalizing from life to work is easier than the reverse.

29:29 Big companies are good at big blitzes, bad at seeing and persisting
Suki says that as far as she knows, Qwen and Doubao saw the OpenClaw direction mid-year and explored it for a while, then quickly gave up. Her learning is that what big companies are best at is not seeing something and believing in it, but big blitzes and burning resources. Right now this direction has no PMF, and the TAM is very small — even at 15% paid conversion, the user volume is a small market in big-company eyes. Last year DingTalk was 4 billion, Feishu 3 billion, WeCom around 3 billion — together less than 10 billion. So big companies usually wait until the TAM is big enough before investing regardless of cost.

35:33 Raising a bunch of agents is emotional value, not efficiency
Last December Gao Ce himself raised three agents — a design chief, a product chief, and a project chief — and in the end only wanted to chat with the project chief, because the context was all in one place and he didn't need to explain things repeatedly to three roles. He thinks multi-agent may be a false need on the consumer side; many people raising a bunch of crayfish are mostly getting the emotional value of "I have a bunch of underlings working for me," while in actual use it wastes tokens — coordination between different roles also costs your tokens and money. The real value of multi-agent is two brains supervising each other, such as in evo and testing scenarios, but most personal agents' daily use doesn't need it.

44:38 The outbox has higher information density than the inbox
Suki describes a concrete rubric for memory construction: after Town gets email authorization, the naive approach is to scan the inbox and outbox for clues, but the core observation is that the emails you send carry higher information density, because sending is done with intent, and you describe your intent clearly — for example, when you want to collaborate with someone you introduce yourself first. The inbox is other people's intent toward you; the outbox is your intent toward others. Email is a protocol that dates back to the 1960s, with a lot of protocol and side-channel signals behind it, and whether you can capture these signals in the product is the difference in memory quality.

47:38 Proactivity is an open scenario — you can't run AB tests
Gao Ce contrasts work scenarios with proactivity: work scenarios are closed problems, like the benchmark Workbody open-sourced — give it a workspace, finish the task, and you're done, easy to evaluate right or wrong. But proactive is an open scenario, requiring a lot of incremental information from you, with goals that are highly subjective, personalized, and multi-dimensional, related to push frequency, quality, and even your mood that day. In the early stage the product can't run GSP or AB tests to validate proactivity's effectiveness, and it will be very difficult in the future too, so it heavily tests the product lead's understanding of the world and information architecture — it's something engineered and product co-designed.

1:02:50 Stacking an intent model in front is an engineering disaster
Gao Ce on intent recognition: the traditional approach is to stack a small intent model in front, then dispatch to different large models by intent — for example, recognizing a weather question and using a very small model. But the drawback is that intent maintenance gets harder and harder; as the product horizontally expands to all kinds of intents, you may end up stacking thousands of intents, and products with strong generalization like Doubao, Yuanbao, and Workbody are especially hard to maintain. Moreover, once you stack an intent model, the context seen below is fragmented, and how messages are shared across multiple sub-models is a big problem — for engineering it's quite a disaster. Manus published a blog in July 2025 about a context-aware state machine, but didn't go into implementation details.

item.title: AI makes starting a company easier than getting a job, but solo founders have no fallback
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-solofounders-ai-让开公司比找工作容易-但单人创始人没有退路/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-solofounders-ai-让开公司比找工作容易-但单人创始人没有退路/
item.description: Durable hit a million users in three months, but the founder says he took a detour: website generation wasn't the endgame — handing the entire back office of the service industry to AI is. Being a solo founder isn't more freedom; it's carrying every decision alone.
item.content:encoded:
Durable hit a million users in three months, but the founder says he took a detour: website generation wasn't the endgame — handing the entire back office of the service industry to AI is. Being a solo founder isn't more freedom; it's carrying every decision alone.

The first half is founder backstory and fundraising, with average information density; the second half — on product judgment, the death of UI, and the pros and cons of solo founding — is worth listening to.

10:19 3.5 million sign-ups, and over half are brand-new businesses
About 3.5 million people have signed up on Durable to start a business, and more than half of them are net new — not existing businesses coming online, but people starting a company for the first time. These people aren't in the brainstorming phase; they already have an idea and possibly a bit of revenue, and the first thing they do on Durable is build an online presence, do SEO and GEO, get found on ChatGPT and Google, and start running ads and following up with customers. Clift says this showed him a mass of businesses he "could never have dreamed existed," like decorating porches for Halloween, which can do several hundred thousand dollars a year.

24:37 The AI website generator was a detour, not the endgame
Durable's original vision was "Shopify for the service industry," close to a franchise model: the franchisee collects $100,000, Durable takes $10,000, and provides the same leads, website and marketing system. After GPT-2.5 appeared they ran a one-week internal hack week, built an AI website generator, and after launching in 2022 it went viral, going from zero to about a million users in three months and bringing in meaningful revenue. But they spent a year and a half on that product, and Clift now calls it an "interesting distraction" — a good business, but not the market they wanted to be in. Four years later they returned to the original vision: an AI version of a "business in a box" for service business owners.

31:50 Users don't want buttons, they want outcomes
Clift deliberately avoids the UI details in customer feedback: everyone says they want to change this button, add this component, customize that, but what they actually want is a better-looking, better-performing website. Likewise, appointment scheduling can fall into a rabbit hole of time zones and multiple calendars, but what people actually want is "jobs getting booked." His conclusion: building UI is now extremely low-value, first because AI makes UI easy to build, and second because nobody wants to click through a pile of things anymore — if users never log into Durable and just get one text message a day, that's a better experience. The product should be input and output: describe the problem you want solved, and it gets solved.

36:01 You should now deliberately pick harder problems
Clift says that since models will keep getting stronger and will make your product obsolete ("it may already be obsolete, and it'll be obsolete again at least once within six months"), you should deliberately choose harder problems. Durable has millions of people starting new businesses in its hands, and making them succeed is an extremely hard problem, but once solved it corresponds to trillions of dollars in GMV and economic value. He also mentions team size: still only six engineers, but "six engineers are roughly equivalent to sixty agents," so adding features is no longer scary, and the real risk becomes "are you building the right thing for the right customer."

44:24 Solo founding is about shedding responsibility to other people
Clift says he didn't deliberately choose to found solo; rather, his first two partnerships with co-founders both got stuck on the same thing: mismatched runway and risk. He couldn't help calculating the other person's opportunity cost — "how much they could make at Amazon, how much they could make consulting" — and by rational calculation you should never start a software company. More important is the psychological burden: with even one co-founder, he felt he had to keep that person happy and take care of them, which meant carrying that person's whole family's livelihood on his shoulders. Founding solo removed that layer of pressure — "now it's all on me alone" — and he can think only about the business and do creative work more freely, and if he fails it only affects himself.

48:30 Built in Vancouver, funded in San Francisco
Clift's judgment: to win venture-backed, outsized outcomes, you probably still have to be in San Francisco; but Vancouver is a great place to build, and San Francisco is a great place to raise money and get inspired. Every time he goes to San Francisco he thinks "we should work harder, faster, be more ambitious," but that energy also often gets in the way of actually building product and understanding customers, producing that lost founder who is "caffeinated, trying a million things, gripping the handlebars for dear life without knowing what they're doing." His approach: company DNA, ambition and fundraising are Silicon Valley-style, but the customers aren't in Silicon Valley — they're in the middle of America, internationally, and they're solo owners.

54:33 Door-to-door knocking teaches you rejection
In college Clift cleaned windows and gutters, selling door to door. He learned two things: first, desensitization to rejection — nobody yells at you for knocking and offering to help, and they forget you two days or even two minutes later; second, volume. Knock on enough doors and you'll close, and then a block "flips": one house does it, puts up a sign, and the neighbors all follow. He directly analogizes this to fundraising and cold outreach emails: the worst outcome is that they don't read it, and that's probably what will happen. He also says that if building gets easier because of AI, then sales becomes more valuable.

1:03:49 Earning your first dollar yourself is a worldview unlock
Clift thinks one of the most interesting parts of the human experience is "earning money yourself," and not even in a financial sense. The world is designed around employment, and profit flows to business owners; yet earning a dollar yourself is still outside the norm for most people — "I had an idea, and someone paid for it." He says it's like opening a small door, and you become more ambitious, going from twenty or thirty dollars to tens of millions in revenue. He also admits you might try it and find you don't like it, but everyone should try it once, and most people are better at it than they think.

item.title: Good ayis are always on assignment: what a domestic-service consultant really sells isn't information
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-bizthisway-好阿姨永远在户上-家政顾问卖的不是信息/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-bizthisway-好阿姨永远在户上-家政顾问卖的不是信息/
item.description: Domestic work is a supply-led industry: good ayis never reach the open market, and the consultant's hard part isn't closing the deal but the after-sales replacement; employers and ayis are both just passers-through of a wage.
item.content:encoded:
Domestic work is a supply-led industry: good ayis never reach the open market, and the consultant's hard part isn't closing the deal but the after-sales replacement; employers and ayis are both just passers-through of a wage.

A frontline post-00s domestic-service consultant lays out a neglected essential-need industry: matching mechanics, pricing, off-platform deals, boundaries. High information density; the second half is worth more.

18:44 Good ayis are always on assignment
This market has a circulation paradox: an ayi with good reviews never reaches the open market. She works for one family for two or three years, and the moment she leaves she's referred straight into the next household. The ones actually circulating on the market are usually the ones nobody could settle on. So the industry's core contradiction is a supply problem — where good ayis come from and how they get discovered. A domestic-service company is essentially a human resources company: it has to recruit, train and re-match.

19:37 Every woman in this trade has a story
The ayi profile clusters in third- and fourth-tier cities and even poor villages, aged 30 to 45, many divorced or single. Live-in sisters spend little time with their own families and give their time to another household. Two traits stand out in why they choose this work: they like children, and they want to earn — not to sit comfortably in the village farming and drinking tea, but to pack up everything they own, buy a green-skin train ticket and squeeze their way to Shanghai.

26:00 This time you're the boss
There has to be a sense of boundaries and tact between ayi and employer — not just for the ayi, but for the employer too. Some people spoil the ayi past the line, but everyone takes a mile when given an inch. More delicate still: a live-in ayi is together with the family 24 hours a day, and may know more about the household's private life than blood relatives do — the pressure is heavy. Some mothers are doing widowed-style parenting, with the father absent, and it's the ayi who keeps the mother company longer; the two become teammates.

37:24 Employer and ayi are both passers-through of a wage
For the employer it's like being a passers-through of a wage, and for the ayi it's the same: the monthly WeChat transfer comes in, and immediately two children's tuition goes out, then the household living expenses go out — transferred away just like that. Many yuesao and yuer sao earn the most important, even the only, income in their family, which is why their role as wife inside the family structure is a strong one. That also explains why employers care about the ayi's family background — you're not hiring a company employee, and her stability is directly tied to her family situation.

41:09 How ten pages of job requirements don't scare the ayi off
The longest yuesao job requirement I've seen ran a full ten pages, yet the price was only the market average. The employer thinks that if every minute of every day is spelled out, the ayi will execute like a robot — but people are emotional. The consultant doesn't forward it directly; she first calls to lay the groundwork by voice: asking about luggage, giving directions, telling her the client says just arrive at this time, then explaining that company rules require the employer to list requirements, and that she can come to the consultant with any question. That way the ayi feels she's been handed a guidebook, not interrogated.

49:47 Closing the deal isn't hard; replacing someone is the test
Yuesao bookings are advance orders, while yuer sao jobs are mostly urgent — an ayi can only enter the market after leaving her previous household, so demand is pressing. Many employers assume that whoever is available urgently must be bad; in fact it's often the booked one who's the fake. Closing isn't hard for a consultant: as long as the employer has a need and a budget, someone can always be found. The genuinely hard part is long-term after-sales — the interview can be thrilling, and afterwards there's a real chance of the thrill going flat; replacing someone is what truly tests a consultant's level.

56:17 The hardest case requires reading the family's core relationship
The hardest case: a single mother who is a female executive, wanting a daytime child-development companion, but also expecting this person to do housework to a cleaner's standard — while the companion's hourly rate is twice a cleaner's. The consultant dealt with the assistant, and the core need was also shaped by the executive mother. The compromise was cleaners for cleaning and companions for companionship, but the mother still had to be won over. The person finally found was the polar opposite of the original spec — originally under 35 with a bilingual-kindergarten early-education background; in the end, a sister close to 50 with an education background and live-in experience.

1:03:36 Yuesao start at 15,000; yuer sao are judged by age
In first-tier cities a yuesao's 26-day contract price is generally 15,000 to 16,000 or more; for one with two or three years' experience who has genuinely cared for a newborn, it's basically 15,000 to 20,000. Shanghai rates for yuer sao: beginners from 7,000, experienced hands judged on age, skills and work history, basically 8,000-plus; stack on English, bilingual, early education or driving and it's 10,000-plus. Prices have risen in recent years partly because more highly educated people are entering the trade, and partly because supply still falls short of demand.

item.title: After the 10,000-worker factory vanished, he had 20 years of workers' daily life on film
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-cn907a40-万人工厂消失后-他用-20-年拍下打工者的日常/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-cn907a40-万人工厂消失后-他用-20-年拍下打工者的日常/
item.description: Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on its ordinary days — meals, punch-ins, English class. When the giant factory finally disappeared, almost no one else had kept this archive.
item.content:encoded:
Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on its ordinary days — meals, punch-ins, English class. When the giant factory finally disappeared, almost no one else had kept this archive.

Not industry analysis: a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography of himself and his generation. The back half, on ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’, is the most valuable part.

2:09 The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value not matter
After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process to make manufacturing more stable and the people more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean: anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. The machines had not yet replaced them, but a person's value already barely mattered. This was the underlying motive for his later picking up a camera and aiming it at his co-workers: inside a system built to erase individual difference, to record specific people.

6:11 Riding the green-skin train felt like riding into a bandit's den
In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The car was already full at the Wuchang origin station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed a window with a brick and shoved people onto the train like livestock. More than thirty hours without sitting, without drinking water; after getting off, his belly was badly swollen. At Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold like a piglet’ — first they took twenty-odd yuan and said it was for Dongguan, then on the expressway they demanded another ten for the toll, and if you refused someone came up and slapped you, and in the end you were dumped in the middle of nowhere to change vehicles. He says he used the phrase for years before he understood what it meant last year.

11:48 He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
In 1995 jobs were hard to find, and men far harder than women: factory notices said outright they only hired women aged 18 to 25. He saw a hiring sign by National Highway 107, and the security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out; by 20 some were dropping, by 40 only eight or ten were left, by 50-something only he was. The captain said you're bragging, go ahead, and he did 102. Then he was told to spar; the other man did a split, he turned sideways, caught the leg and flipped him. That was how he got his first job: gate security at a hotel, 450 yuan a month.

17:16 An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
In 2002 he agonised for a long time before buying his own camera: his wage was only around 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and she said if you like it, buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was still 48 each, plus 5 for developing and another ten or twenty for prints — a huge drain on him in that era. At first he shot factory events, visiting guests, employee tug-of-war, assuming that photography was just a technical problem of getting things sharp. Later, reading Chinese photography magazines, he found there was so much learning in photography and he had no standard to measure by, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook, whose first lesson is the three criteria of a good photograph.

24:00 The model-contest photos passed ten million clicks, then he was told to delete them
In 2007 the factory started holding a model contest: workers in swimsuits, evening gowns and uniforms on stage, plus pole dancing. In 2008 he changed position, went behind the stage backdrop and shot downward — models in front, a dense black mass of audience behind — and sent the files to Tencent in time; they went up on the portal and drew tens of millions of clicks in a morning. But online comments said this was picking a mistress for the boss and a lover for the plant manager; the framing was distorted, the boss came under enormous pressure, and he was told to delete them. Tencent said they could only hide them, other sites' viral reposting could not be stopped, and in the end he was served a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

25:23 The photo of the woman worker looking up — he had not planned to use it
On 5 January 2011, as a senior supervisor, he went into the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. Clean-room work allowed four minutes' rest after two hours; the changing area was hung with unused clean-room suits, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He took one or two frames, and the man heard the sound and looked up at him. He says the advice he was given when learning photography was that ‘a photo where the subject looks at the lens is not a good photo’, so he long avoided using it. Later Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organised the Off-Pix award; he submitted it and it was unexpectedly made the lead image. Looking at it seriously afterwards, he conceded it has its own pull — different viewers will have different inner responses, so a photographer should interpret his own photos as little as possible.

31:26 One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his years of service were zeroed
Looking for work in 1995, Hubei people were not wanted, Henan people were not wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. Factories' records were separate then, with no networked computer system, and social security did not have to be paid, so that set of papers was lent to many people and entered many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system would not accept it — same ID number, same name, same household registration address — and the employer decided you were dishonest and zeroed your years of service. He says this will not do: our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those years of service are real. When even present-day life is insecure, it is impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years away.

36:30 Density: he shot for 20 years before seeing it everywhere
In 2019 he built a photo series around the density of migrant working life, which won an excellence award and the Alpa prize at the third Yingjishi Image Awards. A high-angle shot of a workers' assembly, heads packed with almost no gaps; a collective dormitory hung with clothes, from a distance airtight; workshop switches, key cabinets, lockers for bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures producing a visual density. He says at first it was unconscious: shooting every day on his phone, shooting security training, shooting any co-worker he happened to see on the road, accumulating day by day, on and off for nearly 20 years. When there were so many eras in so many factories, he had not observed in that way; then one morning he found it so frightening that even a switch looked spectacular.

item.title: Companies That Treat Service as a Cost Center Are Giving Away Their Moat
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-twist-把服务当成本中心的公司-正在把护城河让出去/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-twist-把服务当成本中心的公司-正在把护城河让出去/
item.description: Products get replaced by better products, brands by stronger brands; the only durable competitive advantage is hospitality — the continuous, generous investment in relationships.
item.content:encoded:
Products get replaced by better products, brands by stronger brands; the only durable competitive advantage is hospitality — the continuous, generous investment in relationships.

This is an interview with Will Guidara about Unreasonable Hospitality. No AI or fundraising substance, but it nails "service as moat" — worth listening to as an operating philosophy.

4:05 Product moats get filled in sooner or later
Guidara's argument: most companies are looking for their moat, and the traditional answer is to build the best product, the strongest brand. But he thinks those only work to a point, because time has repeatedly shown that sooner or later someone builds a better product, a stronger brand — the other side may be better capitalized, more creative, have new ideas, or simply be better than you. So he argues the only competitive advantage that exists long term comes from hospitality, from continuously and generously investing in relationships. This isn't to say making a good product doesn't matter; it's that you shouldn't reserve your best effort for the product alone — invest it in how people feel, too.

7:09 The front line has information and no power; leadership has power and no information
Guidara quotes retired Navy captain David Marquet: in most organizations, leadership has all the power and no information, while the front line has all the information and no power. His inference: you cannot deliver unreasonable hospitality without empowering the front line, because only the people on the front line know the guest well enough to know what would make this particular service "unreasonable." In his book he covers feedback methods, the daily 30-minute meeting, how to celebrate and create traditions the team looks forward to — but he says the greatest unreasonable hospitality you can give a colleague is to genuinely give them agency.

17:16 Hospitality can be systematized, not just a flash of inspiration
One-off gestures like the hot dog or the first dance are hard to scale — they need someone to come up with them on the spot, and forcing them looks contrived. But Guidara says these are exactly what proves hospitality can be systematized: do pattern recognition, find the moments that recur, then write "how we respond when this moment happens" into the process. Back in the day, for example, guests often had to feed the parking meter — so the rule became: every time it comes up, go top up the meter for the guest. His key observation: once hospitality is written into the system, it actually makes the team want to be hospitable even more — because every time you see the look on a guest's face when they're taken care of, that feeling is addictive.

24:18 A crying baby on a plane is a hundred-dollar bill nobody picks up
Guidara gives an example he calls "criminal": flying across the US with a one-year-old is excruciating, and it happens every single day, yet no airline has ever done anything about it — never handed earplugs to the surrounding passengers, never offered help to the parent trying to soothe the baby, and there's never any milk when you ask. He says this is an opportunity sitting right there in pattern recognition, a "hundred-dollar bill on the ground you don't pick up." Jason then adds the mechanism: you need top leadership to give a budget — say $250 a month per flight attendant to spend at their discretion to do something for a guest — so employees fall in love with their jobs and guests become loyal customers.

26:20 Hospitality shouldn't be an "extra" — it should be standard
Guidara says the top of the organization not only has to give a budget for people to do more than expected, it also has to create a culture where this is no longer treated as "more than expected" but as normal. His analogy: when you buy a car, everyone assumes it comes with tires — nobody thinks of that as an extra service; phones no longer come with a charging brick, and that was someone deciding that step went too far. So why can't an airline decide "this flight just includes these things"? His conclusion: if you run a company, hospitality should be in the table stakes, not an option.

34:24 Refund a bag of dog food when the pet dies, win a customer for life
Guidara tells the Chewy example: dog food is an auto-subscription, and after a dog dies, the owner's first thought usually isn't to cancel — they only remember when the next bag arrives, which is cruel. When you call Chewy to cancel and return the bag, the response is always the same: we can't take the food back, but we'll refund you, just donate it. Then within a day or two, flowers arrive at that home. Guidara's inference: this person will get another dog, and where they buy dog food goes without saying — and they'll never consider anywhere else. He calls this "pattern recognition, recurring moments, systematizing kindness."

53:31 Killing tipping requires a business strong enough to absorb it
Guidara eliminated tipping at Eleven Madison Park. He says it was the most successful no-tipping implementation, but after he sold the restaurant it was reinstated, because the restaurant wasn't performing as well as before. His judgment: eliminating tipping requires you to run the business extremely well, otherwise it backfires. Two preconditions must hold — first, demand has to be high enough that guests don't mind higher prices covering the absence of tipping, because the public will still compare your chicken to other restaurants' chicken without factoring in the tip they'd pay elsewhere; second, you have to stay consistently full, because you're underwriting the team's tips, and one slow night means you eat the loss directly. His approach wasn't a service charge — he built service directly into the fixed tasting-menu price.

1:03:36 Commuter rail hides a minute of grace
Guidara shares a discovery he recently wrote up in his newsletter: commuter rail systems like Metro-North and Amtrak have a built-in "minute of grace" — the timetable says 11:45 departure, but it always actually leaves at 11:46, precisely to leave time for the person sprinting through the doors at the last second. He says he used to think sliding through the doors just in time was luck every time; once he knew it was deliberate design, he started looking for places to add a "minute of grace" in his own work with other companies. He treats it as a takeaway operating principle: where can you add a little more grace?

item.title: Zelensky: The Middle East War Is Draining Ukraine's Air Defense Missiles
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-wsjournal-泽连斯基-中东战争正在抽走乌克兰的防空导弹/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-wsjournal-泽连斯基-中东战争正在抽走乌克兰的防空导弹/
item.description: The US makes only 60 to 65 missiles a month, and 803 were fired on the first day of the Middle East war. Zelensky says what Putin wants is a long war, because running down resources hurts Ukraine.
item.content:encoded:
The US makes only 60 to 65 missiles a month, and 803 were fired on the first day of the Middle East war. Zelensky says what Putin wants is a long war, because running down resources hurts Ukraine.

Medium information density, but Zelensky gives several concrete numbers and judgments, more substantive than a press release. The second half, about his personal life and family, can be fast-forwarded.

0:02 The Middle East war directly drains Ukraine's air defense missiles
Zelensky says the Middle East war's impact on Ukraine is direct: a global fuel shortage and, more importantly, air defense missile supply being squeezed. He states plainly that "there will be a reduced number of missiles for our defense." He is already looking for alternatives, because Ukraine ran short of anti-missile missiles this past winter, and the next winter is still coming. He also says America's diplomatic focus is now on the Middle East, and the trilateral talks keep getting postponed for one reason only: the Iran war.

4:04 What Putin wants is exactly a long war
Zelensky's judgment is that for Putin, a long war in Iran is a plus. The reason is not just energy prices, but that it consumes America's reserves and the production capacity of air defense missile makers. When the US needs extra resources it turns to Europe, and Europe as an ally gives them. The result is that resources do not flow to Ukraine. Zelensky says Putin needs to weaken Ukraine, and the Middle East is one of the ways to do that.

5:05 What the US makes in a month, the Middle East burns in a day
Zelensky gives a set of concrete numbers: the US produces 60 to 65 missiles a month, roughly 700 to 800 a year. The first day of the Middle East war used 803. He says Middle Eastern countries used PAC-3 to intercept drones early in the war, because PAC-3 can hit any aerial target. The question now is when the Middle East's stockpile runs out.
