His conclusion: Ukraine will certainly face a missile shortage.

6:07 What Ukraine wants is production licenses, not sympathy
Zelensky's demands of Western leaders are specific: unity first, speed second. He says the war made Ukraine number one in military technology, not because it is smarter, but because it has underground manufacturers. What he wants is for European friends to give Ukraine's industrial sector the maximum licenses, rights and opportunities so Ukraine can produce the weapons it lacks itself. He says this is Ukraine's first interest.

9:12 Trump wants to end the war but does not want to pick a side
Zelensky says he believes Trump genuinely wants to end the war, because Trump promised voters and wants to finish it fast. But Trump's strategy is to keep close dialogue with Putin, not to provoke him, while not fully siding with Ukraine. Zelensky says Trump positions himself as a mediator, not on either side. Ukraine wants Trump on Ukraine's side, because the more countries stand with Ukraine, the more pressure on Russia. But America has its own strategy.

12:27 Putin is not ready to sign any agreement, only to dictate an ultimatum
Zelensky says Putin is not prepared to sign any agreement; what he wants is for Ukraine to sign an ultimatum. Putin understands that giving up the Donbas means splitting Ukrainian society, and a split society can be exploited. Zelensky says Putin's goal is division, because a divided country is a weak country that can be occupied further. He says Ukraine is ready to compromise, especially if the US is involved, but the US has not demanded major compromises from Russia.

14:30 The Russian regime should be treated as fairly as Iran
Zelensky says the West must be fair toward different regimes. If there is a certain attitude toward Maduro or the Iranian regime, the same attitude should apply to the Russian regime, because they are no different on human rights, freedom or nuclear threats. He says the first step should be a diplomatic solution, but in a tough way that gives Putin the same terms as other regimes. He states plainly that toppling the regime is step two; step one is diplomacy.

20:36 If Ukraine joins NATO, the war is over
Zelensky reiterates that he is willing to give up his position if it buys NATO membership. He says if NATO recognizes Ukraine's army as one of Europe's strongest, he is willing to consider his work done. He says if Ukraine were in NATO, the war would be over. He also says he does not think there is a big problem in the relationship between Trump and Starmer, and that history is stronger than the emotions of two or three people.

item.title: America's Wealthiest Aren't CEOs — They Own Car Washes and HVAC Companies
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-mastersinbiz-美国最富的一群人-不是ceo而是开洗车店和暖通公司的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-mastersinbiz-美国最富的一群人-不是ceo而是开洗车店和暖通公司的/
item.description: Three million private business owners in the US hold net worths above $5 million, and their combined wealth is more than ten times that of the Forbes 400 — they run car washes, HVAC companies, and auto dealerships, and they got rich by owning, not by earning a salary.
item.content:encoded:
Three million private business owners in the US hold net worths above $5 million, and their combined wealth is more than ten times that of the Forbes 400 — they run car washes, HVAC companies, and auto dealerships, and they got rich by owning, not by earning a salary.

The data comes from IRS and Treasury tax records, which are more granular than Federal Reserve surveys. The core conclusion: to reach the top 0.1%, you get there by owning a business, not by earning a high salary.

1:03 The IRS pulled them in to study taxes and they accidentally built a wealth database
The two authors had just finished graduate school when they were recruited by the Treasury Department and the Office of Tax Analysis to solve a tax policy puzzle: pass-through businesses don't pay taxes themselves, so you have to link the business back to its individual owner to calculate the tax burden. The project accidentally produced a panel database that tracks every business along with its owners and employees — far richer than the Fed's Survey of Consumer Finances, which is large in scale but nowhere near as granular as tax records.

3:08 Wealth isn't in Silicon Valley or Wall Street — the whole map lights up
The authors assumed wealth was concentrated in tech and finance, and the data overturned that bias. When they plotted the "everywhere millionaire" on a map, the entire country lit up. These wealthy people are spread across a large number of unglamorous industries — auto dealerships, HVAC, dental practices, restaurants, distribution, sanitation. It isn't just the Forbes 400 getting richer; it's millions of people getting richer.

4:08 Three million private business owners hold ten times the wealth of the Forbes 400
The authors counted roughly 3 million "everywhere millionaires" — private business owners with a net worth of at least $5 million. Their combined wealth exceeds the Forbes 400 total by more than ten times. That number changes the inequality narrative: what drives inequality statistics isn't a few hundred billionaires but millions of unknown business owners.

8:10 The higher the income, the smaller the wage share and the larger the business-income share
Break open the top 10% of earners: people at the 90th percentile rely mainly on wages. But the further up you go, the curves cross — by the top 0.1%, most income comes from business income. The authors say the main typical way to get rich in America is to own something, not to earn a wage. This is both a tax advantage (owning is taxed more lightly than earning a wage) and the actual path of wealth accumulation.

10:15 The 1986 tax reform turned pass-through from a disadvantage into an advantage
The 1986 tax reform (Reagan as president, Democrats controlling Congress, a bipartisan effort) lowered the individual income tax rate below the corporate rate for the first time. Before that, pass-through status was unattractive because of the tax disadvantage; afterward, being a pass-through became cheaper. Later, the Bush tax cuts lowered individual rates further, and the 2017 tax reform added a 20% deduction for certain pass-through categories. The result: more than half of business income is pass-through income, nearly half of employment is at pass-through businesses, and almost all small businesses are pass-throughs.

13:18 Half of the top 1%'s income growth came from pass-through
The authors ran a counterfactual: if you held fixed the importance of pass-through business income as it stood in 1985 (before the 1986 tax reform) and let it evolve as it was, roughly half of the top 1%'s income growth would disappear. Looking at wealth growth, from 1989 to the latest SCF data, two-thirds of the top 0.1%'s wealth growth came from private businesses. This shows that pass-through is, in accounting terms, absolutely central to the growth of wealth and top-end income.

14:20 Entrepreneurship pays only about 10% more on average, but failure isn't the end
Using data tracking roughly 10 million entrepreneurship events since 2000, the authors found that founders' average income is about 10% higher than that of similar workers who didn't start a business — and that's before counting unrealized capital gains from selling the business, and the average already includes a large number of failures. About 20% of founders are serial entrepreneurs — it's the second or third venture that actually earns them yacht money. After a failure you can return to the labor market or start again and fix what went wrong last time.

19:27 Every congressional district has a millionaire business owner
The authors say "every congressional district has an everywhere millionaire." Unlike Silicon Valley and Wall Street, which are concentrated in specific geographic areas, almost every district has a car dealer. These business owners employ many people, pay a lot of sales tax, and are prominent in their local communities, which gives them outsized influence — their approval ratings are higher than those of the military, the Supreme Court, and Congress. About a quarter of members of Congress are private business owners; if you count law firm partners, that share can reach 40% to 50%. At the state and local level, because the positions are part-time and low-paid, business owners make up an even larger share — especially mayors.

item.title: AI can now build a virus; the defense side is still stuck on sequence alignment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-latentspace-ai-能造出病毒了-防御方还停在序列比对/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-latentspace-ai-能造出病毒了-防御方还停在序列比对/
item.description: The models that generate pathogenic sequences and the models that judge whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models, so the teams doing design are best positioned to do defense — but the defense side is far behind, with a baseline that is still sequence matching.
item.content:encoded:
The models that generate pathogenic sequences and the models that judge whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models, so the teams doing design are best positioned to do defense — but the defense side is far behind, with a baseline that is still sequence matching.

High information density; the middle and later sections on the four-layer structure of biodefense, the DNA synthesis pipeline, and "you can't patch a human" are the most valuable.

0:00 The teams doing design are best positioned to do defense
The dual mission Eric set for Radical Numerics is not a PR gesture but a technical judgment: the models that can generate pathogenic sequences and the models that can judge whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models. So the teams doing design are naturally best positioned to do defense, rather than outsourcing defense to a different group. He acknowledges there is an arms-race dynamic here, and that the defenders have always been far behind; what the company wants to do is pull the defenders up to the same level.

8:12 AI built the first genome from scratch
Evo's work generating a CRISPR-Cas system made it into Science, and Eric later gave a TED Talk. More important is what scientists showed last year: using a generative DNA model to generate the first genome from scratch. Humans had previously only been able to copy and paste fragments of known function, and had never built from scratch at the genome level. What Evo generated was a functional bacteriophage, that is, a virus. Eric says this is a turning point for the scientific community and the company — it means being able to build complete organisms that do not exist in nature, and it also implies the corresponding potential harm.

12:16 Omni's breakthrough came from alignment, not pretraining
Evo demonstrated the potential of pretraining, but on human genetics it still lost to specialized DNA models, and the community questioned why one would use a large model at all. Omni's difference lies in mid-training and post-training: presenting tasks in the question-and-answer form scientists actually want, for example, given a wild-type and a mutant sequence, help me find the causal variant. Eric says this kind of form does not emerge naturally from pretraining. The results surprised them — Omni was not just competitive across many tasks the way Evo was, it began pushing the frontier in every subfield, especially variant effect prediction.

23:50 Most real disease variants are in non-coding regions
Traditional bioinformatics tools and statistical methods mainly focus on coding regions, and coding regions make up only about 1.5% to 2% of the genome. Eric says many, perhaps most, diseases actually fall in non-coding regulatory regions, where variants are harder to judge as pathogenic or not. This is exactly where Omni is strong: it can distinguish pathogenic mutations in non-coding regions, especially long-range ones. This is precisely what geneticists who have long been unable to use traditional tools want.

45:44 The biology experiment itself is doing the filtering
The mechanism of the SOLEX experiment is worth remembering: generate a large number of random sequences, turn them into aptamer switches, and read them out at high throughput with NGS — the more binding, the more reads, the higher the fitness; then mutate the winning sequences again and iterate. This experiment explored on the order of 10 to the 11th power sequences in parallel. The key is that "the biology of the experiment is actually doing the filtering" — the wet lab does the filtering, and the model reproduces that process in silico. This paradigm can be generalized to any biological experiment of "progressive refinement," as long as you can capture the intermediate states.

58:15 Stanford scientists said generating DNA was a stupid idea
Eric spent six months at Stanford on the idea of Evo "generating DNA," and almost every scientist he talked to thought it was a stupid idea. The objections were specific: humans themselves do not understand the rules of DNA, so why expect AI to learn them; you cannot even judge whether the generation is correct, so how do you give the model feedback; DNA has too many repetitive sequences, too noisy a distribution, no real rules, all junk. He admits he was just stubborn, felt "it just feels right," but at the time could not say what the use case was. The first time he trained Evo he had no idea whether it would work.

1:12:48 The four pillars of biodefense
They break biodefense into four layers: detection and surveillance (detecting pathogen sequences from environmental samples such as airport nasal swabs and wastewater systems), attribution (judging whether the source is natural, foreign, or engineered by some country's lab), countermeasures (making antivirals or antibacterials), and deterrence (at the government level). They focus on the first three. The core criticism is this: the existing biodefense community relies mainly on sequence matching — aligning sequences against databases of known pathogens. This cannot stop two things: new things that are not in the database, and designs that are deliberately obfuscated, that do not match in sequence space but have the same function.

1:25:15 You can't patch a human
The host points out the key difference between biosecurity and cybersecurity: in cybersecurity, a sufficiently strong model can in principle find every vulnerability and patch it, and as long as people keep updating they are safe; but the genome is fixed, "you can't patch a human," so the defense surface is harder. Conversely there are two buffers: the intensity of motivation to launch an attack may be much lower, and the threshold from printing arbitrary DNA to building a successful virus — especially one that does not first kill the designer — is actually quite high.

item.title: Whose Homes Did His Roads Tear Down: Robert Moses's New York Legacy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-stuffmissed-他修的路拆了谁的房-罗伯特-摩西的纽约遗产/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-stuffmissed-他修的路拆了谁的房-罗伯特-摩西的纽约遗产/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Moses used federal Title I money to demolish 26 blocks, pushing the poor from one slum to another, yet claimed 98% of relocatees were better housed — his legacy remains unresolved to this day.
item.content:encoded:
Moses used federal Title I money to demolish 26 blocks, pushing the poor from one slum to another, yet claimed 98% of relocatees were better housed — his legacy remains unresolved to this day.

This episode has medium information density, but the second half — on how power operates, media manipulation, and the machinery of urban renewal — is worth hearing; the first half can be fast-forwarded.

2:03 The more power, the less explanation required
After LaGuardia retired in 1946, William O'Dwyer appointed Moses as New York City Construction Coordinator, a position that gave him jurisdiction over every public construction project in the city and a direct line to Washington. By 1959, critics pointed out that he simultaneously held multiple government positions and his power was unchecked: consultant fees undisclosed, staff salaries undisclosed, trust meetings held behind closed doors, and land could be seized at will. Reporter Bob Baum noted that private companies could do these things, but as part of a government entity, the public had a right to know. Moses was therefore often called the "Construction Czar" or "Urban Planning Czar."

3:07 Roads first, and whole neighborhoods paid the price
In 1948, Moses began building the Cross Bronx Expressway, a seven-mile road cutting through the already heavily developed Bronx. Dozens of apartment buildings were demolished, hundreds of families displaced, and many streets severed into dead ends. This community fragmentation was later cited as one reason for rising local crime rates. Those affected were mostly the least resourced, predominantly non-white communities. In a 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, Moses wrote that arterial improvements were "not merely a strip of pavement laid in a gasoline ditch, but a real improvement of the entire area," and he genuinely believed he was making the best choices for New York, but his methods were often ruthless.

7:12 26 brochures, one campaign of visual persuasion
In 1949 Congress passed the American Housing Act Title I, providing $1 billion in loans and $100 million in annual grants for slum clearance. Moses realized New York could get a large share of federal money, so in the 1950s he had his team produce 26 brochures, each targeting a neighborhood he thought needed redevelopment. The brochures contained problem descriptions, photographs, and statistics, and were sent to the New York City Board of Estimate, the City Planning Commission, the Title I federal administrator, and the Housing and Home Finance Agency. In 2014, researcher Temis Kronopoulos analyzed the photographs and found: vacant lots were shown 22 times, the most common image of urban decay; 20 photos showed back-alley garbage and clotheslines; almost no people appeared in the photos. Kronopoulos wrote: "In this context, slum clearance was also a tool of social engineering."

10:18 Media praise first, scandal exposed later
On June 29, 1959, New York Times reporter Wayne Phillips began publishing a four-part series exposing Moses's problems in Title I slum clearance projects: associations with people he shouldn't have been involved with, unregulated funds, and information not shared. But as early as June 14, columns by George Sokolski began appearing in newspapers nationwide, syndicated by King Features Syndicate, with titles like "Robert Moses Is a Selfless Man" and nearly identical content, praising him for "constantly building and beautifying, his work never touched by corruption." These articles appeared two weeks before the New York Times critical series. Looking back, Sokolski seems to have been asked to preemptively cover for the coming scandal.

13:22 Mayor's ban and a public tantrum
After the scandal broke, Mayor Wagner did two things: first, he investigated Louis Pokras's role in a Harlem slum clearance project, and because Pokras had organized crime connections, Wagner publicly stated he would never allow him to sponsor any New York development project; second, he banned the city from working with Moses's favored architect Melvin E. Kessler, whose earlier Upper West Side redevelopment involved developer Manhattan Town Incorporated taking Title I funds but building no buildings and demolishing none, just collecting rents while the buildings rotted. Moses publicly responded that the mayor's "devastating charges and misstatements" scared off venture capital, and said "Title I is a dead duck." Other officials said Title I would continue and praised Moses. In media reports, Moses looked like he was throwing a public tantrum.

15:26 "Moses Must Go": an open letter
In December 1959, the Metropolitan Housing Council began distributing flyers in New York addressed to Mayor Robert Wagner. At the top in bold letters: "For New York's development, Moses must go." The flyer listed ongoing problems with slum clearance projects: tenants sold along with the land; indecent relocation practices continuing; luxury housing built at the people's expense while those who needed housing most were pushed from one slum to another; and as former rent administrator Charles Abrams pointed out, slum clearance had become "Negro and Puerto Rican removal." The flyer demanded: more low-rent housing, an end to subsidizing luxury housing, and building new housing before demolishing old. It compared the situation to cancer and repeated: "Moses must go."

21:32 Fire Island showdown: Rockefeller accepts the resignation
In 1962, Moses clashed with New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller over a Fire Island road plan. Moses wanted to build a road spanning the entire island, and after a 1962 storm destroyed most houses, he thought his chance had come. But environmental groups and islanders opposed it, and residents proposed an alternative: making Fire Island a national seashore protected area, which gained federal support. Public pressure gave the governor an opportunity to halt the road project and suggest Moses reduce his government posts to focus on the 1964 World's Fair. Moses submitted his resignation; he had threatened resignation before with other governors, but they always refused because many public projects would collapse without him. Rockefeller accepted, triggering a media storm. Moses claimed the governor had demanded he immediately resign as chairman of the State Parks Commission so his brother Lawrence could take over; Rockefeller said a transition had been discussed for over a year.

26:38 World's Fair: 50 million vs. projected 70 million
The 1964 New York World's Fair drew about 50 million visitors, but Moses had projected 70 million. The New York Times reported that only 85% of the grounds were ready at opening, 15 of 139 pavilions were unfinished, and many completed pavilions had no exhibits. Some exhibitors arrived with nowhere to put their displays. A fair spokesman told the media that seeing all the other options would take over a week, and unfinished pavilions would be done before then. Some attractions were completed within weeks of opening; others were abandoned entirely. After the fair, Moses was no longer New York City Construction Coordinator. In September 1966, his wife Mary died after a long illness, and less than a month later Moses remarried Mary Grady, who served as secretary at the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority. In 1968, Rockefeller merged Triborough into another transportation agency, and Moses was removed — his last New York government post.

item.description: Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show it had found a more resource-efficient quantum attack, without publishing the circuit. Yukon turned the problem into an open competition, letting agents build on other people's submissions — and ended up beating Google's result by more than 60%.
item.content:encoded:
Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show it had found a more resource-efficient quantum attack, without publishing the circuit. Yukon turned the problem into an open competition, letting agents build on other people's submissions — and ended up beating Google's result by more than 60%.

High information density: it explains the mechanics of automated research competitions, verifier design, and several real breakthrough cases. Worth a listen for anyone following AI for science, ZK, and open innovation.

4:07 Google gives only the proof, not the circuit
Google published a paper claiming it had found a quantum scheme more resource-efficient than the previous state of the art for breaking the secp256k1 elliptic curve — the basis of Bitcoin's and Ethereum's public-key cryptography. But Google did not publish the scheme; instead it used a zero-knowledge proof to demonstrate that it did in fact possess such a scheme. Soubhik points out the consequence: if you want to prepare for Q-day, you have to know what schemes will appear, how to harden your systems, what the defence mechanisms are; if you don't understand any of that, you are not prepared for Q-day. Not publishing the quantum circuit is the main consequence here.

8:08 The competition isn't everyone for themselves, it's a relay
The way you participate in ecdsa.fail is not to do your work locally and then submit. The platform backend runs the same verifier Google used; through a command-line interface you have your agent read the competition details and other people's submissions, then build directly on top of someone else's scheme. Soubhik says this is how research actually works: you build on each other's experience, not like an Olympic event where everyone submits independently. Anna says she had assumed it was PvP, everyone finishing on their own machine and then submitting to compete; Soubhik confirms it isn't. This multi-user automated research framework produced enormous acceleration, because you don't have to rediscover everything yourself.

11:08 Three breakthroughs: externalising, mining, starting over
Soubhik sees three big breakthroughs. The first was externalising the environment and letting people outside the company take part — one team member who wasn't in the internal testing spent roughly $5,000 on a codex subscription the day before the internal test and made a huge leap the lead engineer couldn't understand. The second was mining French's work, building on it, and surpassing Google's result within two weeks. After that the chart was almost a plateau for two months. The third came in mid-August: Teddy, from Starkware, went back to the starting point of the competition, summarised all the techniques into a knowledge review, and then built from scratch rather than on other people's ideas, ultimately proposing the NSD ping-pong technique, which pushed the scheme from 49% better than Google to 57% better, and it is now past 60%.

27:15 If the question isn't asked right, you can't run a competition
Soubhik says many problems are posed incorrectly — that is, badly formulated. He gives the example: ‘Build me a quantum computer’ — that problem is too big, we don't know what it is. But if you break it down, you find that the problem state of ecdsa.fail is one of its subproblems. You need to split the big problem into a series of well-formulated subtasks, then run automated research on each subtask. Another example is the proximity gap conjecture: EF committed a $1 million prize, but the original statement is binary — you either prove it or you don't — and it's hard to write a verifier for it. Later Alexander Hicks and Gako wrote a simple verifier for one specific instance of the conjecture, and only then did it become the better.codes competition.

39:15 An algebraic geometer broke 64 bits in a few hours
better.codes has two bounds: the lower bound is the soundness bound, the upper bound is the attack bound. The lower bound had been stuck at the Johnson bound for years. On 21 August the competition was stuck at 63.99 bits, and 64 bits is the Johnson bound for this specific instance. Then there was no progress for 6 days; the chart was a straight line. Until 28 August, when the team contacted Bartosz from ECDSA — a Polish mathematician specialising in algebraic geometry, not a cryptographer at all, who had never heard of the problem. Within a few hours of joining he pushed the result from 63.99 to 64.0101 bits, breaking the Johnson bound for the first time. The technique he used was some combination of algebraic geometry, because he was already using his own codex subscription to do algebraic geometry work, and he probably applied algebraic geometry methods to this problem.

41:15 One breakthrough set off a 30-year open problem
After Bartosz broke 64.01 bits, the whole circle blew up, with Ariel Gabizon, Kobi and others discussing it on Twitter. The story didn't end there: a few days later, some cryptographers had a bigger problem in coding theory that had been open for 30 years — proving a certain soundness bound. Within days three papers appeared claiming inspiration from the method used to break the Johnson bound. Soubhik says nobody could have predicted this; this is open innovation and collaborative research, and it still looks very early: people are starting to realise that problems they thought couldn't be solved for a long time can at least be pushed forward, improved.

45:18 Domain experts point the agents the way on GitHub
On the hish tiling problem, Yukon piloted a discussion-format feature. The whole process is in the CLI; you don't even need to think or prompt your agent. While doing research the agent searches for information in the hills, formulates strategy locally, and uploads discussions to a GitHub forum. Other agents read those discussions, and domain experts like Bartosz answer by hand, and the agents then read those answers — so the domain expert is effectively steering the automated research network. Soubhik says this is exactly what they want to achieve: a domain expert should be able to see how far the automated research network has got on his problem statement, then use his best intuition to steer it and leave clues about what to explore.

52:20 Yukon wants to be an AI-native research institution
Soubhik says Yukon's vision is to grow into an AI-based research institution, imitating three features of traditional research institutions: research means building at a higher level on each other's ideas; the originators of ideas must be given credit; and even failed ideas should be recognised, because one success may come out of a thousand failures. What AI changes is that the whole research lifecycle accelerates from months or years to days. They are implementing a partial credit system that lets people give each other credit for ideas, including negative credit — failed ideas also earn credit. They also want a system that helps you break a badly formulated problem into a series of well-formulated subproblems.

item.title: Information Has Never Been More Plentiful, Yet We Choose Not to Know
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-iq2-信息从未如此充裕-我们却选择不知道/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-iq2-信息从未如此充裕-我们却选择不知道/
item.description: Lyse Doucet has reported from war zones for forty years. Her judgment: not knowing isn't because information is scarce, but because we don't want to know. And this Iran war is a war of choice that has made everything worse.
item.content:encoded:
Lyse Doucet has reported from war zones for forty years. Her judgment: not knowing isn't because information is scarce, but because we don't want to know. And this Iran war is a war of choice that has made everything worse.

The first half offers immediate judgments on Iran and Hormuz; the second half is a rare retrospective on whether twenty years of intervention in Afghanistan was worth it. High information density, but requires patience.

3:13 Not knowing is because we don't want to know
Doucet calls this "a really jarring time": information has never been more plentiful, but "If we don't know about something, it's because we don't want to know about something. We choose not to know." She attributes this to being bombarded daily by statements from the US president—yesterday it was "we don't need guardrails for AI," even as some leading AI founders are asking for regulation; today it's rolling back some environmental regulations. She reminds us: a president who says he won't get involved in "forever wars" still ends up leading the country into them.

5:15 This is a war of choice, and it's getting worse
Doucet rarely offers personal judgment: this war puts her under great pressure because it is "a war of choice" rather than "a war of necessity," and "it just seems to have made everything worse in every way." She acknowledges that the US and Israel have inflicted massive damage on Iran's military and navy, and Iran's economy is suffering, but strategically "this is a war where President Trump doesn't know how to end it." Iran has not collapsed; the regime is harder than before; promises to protesters have not been kept, and their lives are worse.

6:16 Market life under 82% inflation
Doucet uses inflation to illustrate Iran's predicament: Brits worry about single-digit inflation, "Oh, 4%, oh my God, it's 5%," while Iran is at 82%. She quotes an Iranian woman: I come to the market every day just to watch prices go up; that's how I pass the time. She then juxtaposes Iran and Ukraine—both are "wars of choice" and miscalculations. Trump thought he could go straight through Iran, Putin thought he could go straight through Ukraine, but they found that people's resistance is both creative and determined.

8:16 Iran has weaponized the Strait of Hormuz
Doucet gives specific mechanisms: the Houthis control the western coast of the Red Sea and the islands in between, claiming not to affect maritime traffic, but the previously de-escalated war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen has reignited; oil prices have risen above $108 a barrel; the Strait of Hormuz is completely deadlocked. Iranians will not let go—they don't just see it as a bargaining chip, but a long-term one. "They've weaponized the Strait of Hormuz." She points out that Trump repeatedly says "I didn't expect them to do this," but anyone who has done war-gaming will tell you that the simulations always quickly lead to Iran controlling Hormuz.

40:12 The 'traditional Afghanistan' denied by exiles
When the Taliban required Afghan women to wear a burqa that leaves only the eyes visible, Afghan women abroad countered that this is not traditional Afghanistan. Doucet points out that the burqa is locally called chadili, with an embroidered mesh; but at the same time, women were also educated at Kabul University. While writing her book, she dug up many old photos and decided she had to tell this history well, so she tracked down a person living in the US—the person's first reaction was "The Intercontinental Hotel, I love that hotel." Their first call lasted four hours; the person drew the hotel's ground floor plan from memory, pointing out which room belonged to the German wife of the mayor of Kabul and which to an Indian.

41:12 Four hours of oral history, six months of silence
The second call lasted three hours, after which the person disappeared for about six months. The reason lay in Afghanistan's political turmoil: the 1973 kingdom was ended by the first coup, and hotel employees were taken away for questioning—"Why do you work for an American hotel? Are you working for the CIA?" In 1978 came the communist coup, people were thrown into prison, and she had to flee. Happy memories thus dredged up sadness and pain. Finally, Doucet called to ask for permission, and the person said: I cannot appear in your book; it's too sad and too painful for me. Doucet's conclusion: a writer can only get up the next day and find someone else to tell the story, and it will never be told as well.

1:03:14 Two trillion dollars bought a generation that knows its rights
Faced with the question "What was it all for?", Doucet admits both sides made mistakes, and this should be a humbling lesson for all NATO allies; there will be a formal review in the future. But she insists it was not in vain: twenty years of international engagement created space for the most educated and connected generation in Afghanistan's history to grow up. She quotes Malala Yousafzai—even reading a book is an act of resistance—and says these girls know their rights, know that Islam gives them the right to education, know that girls around the world go to school while they cannot. "Not enough, but not zero."

1:14:42 The difference between hope and optimism is agency
Doucet says she could never distinguish hope from optimism until she read Gordon Brown's "The Future Starts With Us": optimism is wishful thinking, but hope is different because hope carries agency—you don't just wish, you actually work to bring it about. She says she doesn't have the privilege of "not needing to hope"; the agency she has is to fight for Afghan visas, to listen to stories there, and to tell them as well as possible. And everyone has their own bit of agency: some donate, some help girls with online classes, some teach girls in Africa, some help South Sudan, Nicaragua, and some help disadvantaged areas in the UK itself.

item.title: Russia Won't Invade NATO, but It's Testing Whether NATO Holds Together
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-goodfight-俄罗斯不会入侵北约-但正在测试它会不会散架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-goodfight-俄罗斯不会入侵北约-但正在测试它会不会散架/
item.description: Russia has no capacity for a ground offensive; its real goal is to corrode NATO's political cohesion — using drones, parcel bombs and grey zones to force the US to expose its divisions in a crisis.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has no capacity for a ground offensive; its real goal is to corrode NATO's political cohesion — using drones, parcel bombs and grey zones to force the US to expose its divisions in a crisis.

The first half, on Russian hybrid warfare and NATO cohesion, is dense and high-value; the Middle East section in the second half drifts somewhat, but the detail about Houthis using Claude to improve their missiles is worth hearing.

4:30 No ground-invasion risk, but hybrid escalation is rising
Joshi is explicit: there is no risk of a Russian conventional ground offensive against NATO, this is not the kind of alarm from January 2022. The entire security apparatus of Estonia and Finland exists to spot exactly that kind of movement, and every port, naval base and forest route in western Russia is saturated with intelligence and technical sensors. But another risk is rising: Russia's tolerance for hybrid operations below the Article V threshold is increasing. They have already used drones against Ukrainian cargo planes that might be bound for Ukraine, put explosives in DHL parcels in Leipzig, and sabotaged power plants and railways across Europe. The question is: would they actually fire missiles at Polish facilities? Joshi thinks Russia remains fairly cautious and wants to avoid dragging NATO into a broader conflict, but that debate is unresolved in Europe.

10:15 Poland sounds the alarm loudest; the Baltics say things are fine
The most alarming signal this week came from Poland. Tusk said intelligence indicated Russia might attack Poland and other NATO allies — not a conventional ground attack, but drones and missiles landing on NATO territory that Russia could portray as accidents. But Latvia's leadership, including the defence minister and the president, said there is no reason to panic and no elevated operational risk. Estonia also said it sees no risk of Russia aggressing in that way. Joshi says he has spoken to intelligence officials in multiple countries and sees no reason to worry about a ground offensive. The split itself is information: Poland is raising the alarm, the Baltic states are cooling things down, and Russia is watching who believes whom.

14:20 Russia's real goal is to corrode NATO cohesion
Joshi lays out Russia's political objective: not to conquer NATO territory or occupy Western Europe, but to weaken and break apart NATO's unity. The mechanism works like this: if a drone lands on Polish territory and blows up a warehouse, Russia says it was an accident, and then Trump says ‘I talked to Putin and he assured me it was an accident’ — and that lays the alliance's internal divisions bare. Under the Biden administration, Jake Sullivan would call the Russians and say that if this continues, you are risking us joining the war on Ukraine's side, and we will retaliate. But under a Trump administration, does Russia really believe Trump would step into a crisis the same way? So Russia has an opportunity not only to retaliate against attacks on Russia, but to test NATO's cohesion and its boundaries.

19:40 On Ukraine, Trump criticises in public and supplies intelligence in private
Joshi says Trump's support for Ukraine is quite limited, far below the Biden era. The US has effectively let weapons aid lapse; Ukraine desperately needs Patriot interceptor missiles, but because the US has burned through so much in the Iran war, it has given Ukraine almost no interceptors recently. Diplomatically, the administration leans toward Russia and expects Ukraine to make concessions. But there are two exceptions: first, the new Graham bill, which the president has agreed to, would impose new sanctions on Russian entities and force Trump to levy tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and do not reduce their purchases — in practice China and India, possibly plus Central European countries. Second, Trump is quietly, not publicly, providing intelligence to Ukraine to help it strike Russian energy facilities. That is the strange reversal: Trump criticises Ukraine overall, yet secret assistance is still flowing.

26:10 The Strait of Hormuz is still half-closed
The Trump administration insists this is not a war; Trump calls it an ‘excursion’. But the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed, with oil traffic far below pre-war levels. There is no deal with Iran, no resolution. Iran's nuclear programme has no formal restrictions, and there is no formal commitment to reopen Hormuz. Trump faces the midterms in a month and desperately needs to avoid a sharp escalation of the war that would send oil prices soaring. But politically he cannot make the concessions to Iran that a deal would require, because that would be too humiliating, too obviously equivalent to defeat, and would look catastrophic before an election. So it is a stalemate: Iran has considerable control over the strait, with occasional clashes — the US bombing Iranian coastal missile bases, Iran striking tankers trying to pass through Hormuz.

31:45 Houthis used Claude to improve their ballistic missiles
Joshi tells a striking detail: when Anthropic published its report on harmful uses of Claude, one of the examples was Houthis using Claude to improve their ballistic missile programme. A group widely seen as technologically primitive is using the most advanced AI on Earth to improve the guidance systems of the ballistic missiles they fire at Middle East shipping. Mounk adds that being able — at least until being cut off — to access the most advanced American technology to strike America and America's allies is itself a fascinating story. This connects the Ukraine and Russia discussion to the Houthi discussion: in modern war, defensive capability dominates on the ground, but offensive capability dominates in the air.

38:20 Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield
Joshi offers a unifying framework for why ground defence dominates while air strikes still work: it is all about perception. To hit something, you first need to perceive it — find it on the battlefield, then fire at it. That is much harder than it sounds. Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield; actually firing is secondary. On the Ukrainian front line, this is a sensor-saturated environment: small drones everywhere, thermal cameras spotting movement at night, radar penetrating foliage, satellites targeting the area. Anything that moves gets hit — it is a kill zone. But you cannot perceive everywhere equally easily. Drones can see ten kilometres behind the battlefield, but fifty kilometres back, satellite coverage is patchy. It is like the fog of war in a real-time strategy game — you send units out and the fog lifts, but where you have not been remains fog. That is why Iran can still launch ballistic missiles, and why Houthis can fire from the mountains of Yemen into the Red Sea.

item.title: The young are useful to society as heretics, not as good citizens
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-a16z-年轻人对社会的用处是当异端-不是当好公民/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-a16z-年轻人对社会的用处是当异端-不是当好公民/
item.description: Universities train young people to be good citizens, but what society actually needs is for them to question what everyone takes for granted; in the AI era every student can build their own projects — all they lack is permission.
item.content:encoded:
Universities train young people to be good citizens, but what society actually needs is for them to question what everyone takes for granted; in the AI era every student can build their own projects — all they lack is permission.

Medium information density, but Amjad's path from chess to training models to building new Replit products is very concrete, and useful for judging whether young people should start companies now.

4:07 The young are useful as heretics
Amjad uses the sci-fi novel The City and the Stars as an analogy: in that city governed by an AGI, everyone is repeatedly reborn from compressed memories, until the machine breaks down and a genuinely new person is born, who immediately starts asking ‘what is outside the walls’. Amjad says the young are useful precisely for asking that kind of question, for being heretics. But today's universities do the exact opposite — they tell you ‘we have already figured everything out, just learn our way’, and train you into a good citizen: marry, have kids, buy a house, buy a car. The problem is that world no longer exists; you can perform brilliantly in college and still end up unemployed with a pile of debt.

5:11 Silicon Valley is itself a monoculture
Amjad says every society has blind spots, and Silicon Valley has plenty — it is a monoculture with a fixed way of thinking, so many ideas simply will not grow out of Silicon Valley. Even the most radical culture is, at bottom, a monoculture. So you need young people to experiment, to attempt what is considered impossible, and occasionally someone breaks through: impossible yesterday, suddenly possible today because the technology changed. What universities should do is gather clear-minded, first-principles thinkers and encourage them to question what is held to be beyond doubt.

15:33 Raising money at 18 is an overused option
Gagan says young people today face a deeply unfair binary: either go to a four-year university and be governed by attendance, homework, exams and grades, or tomorrow someone hands you $50,000 to start a company. He thinks the investor path should be used far less, and only a very small number of teenagers should raise money. Most people at 17 or 18 know they want to enter the business world, but being able to explore and learn for two years without pressure is precious. He argues for a middle ground: two years to explore freely, with Silicon Valley actively sending information and resources your way, and more support if you have a good idea.

17:35 Starting too early is premature optimization
Amjad borrows a phrase from programming, ‘premature optimization is the root of all evil’: a lot of founding is premature optimization. He sees many kids now inside a circle where friends are raising big rounds and some have become unicorns, so the motive becomes a negative one like envy, and then they pre-commit to an idea they are not even interested in, optimizing early for a path they have not yet reached. He says the real question is what your curiosity is driving you toward; once you find the idea you are willing to spend ten years, a lifetime on, it has enormous gravity and you cannot escape it — he himself actively did not want to start a company, but the thing blew up into one on its own. He also says VCs now go to Stanford and give students a million dollars with no idea yet, so they have a cap table before they have even started, which is a bit like the music industry signing young artists.

20:43 From chess all the way to training models
Amjad says he has always oscillated between ‘wanting to build things’ and ‘wanting to read and explore widely’, the two feeding each other in a recursive process. He gives his recent obsession with chess as an example: he started playing very late, does not know why he was interested, then started writing programs to solve chess and training models, and found that LLMs are terrible at chess and hallucinate moves that do not exist. To understand why, he — who had never trained a model — spent a lot of time studying how to train one. From this he realized AI can now do machine learning itself, just as in 2024 Replit's agent suddenly learned to write code and coding changed completely afterward; machine learning may be at that same moment — he calls it vibe research or auto research. He is now building products at Replit to let anyone become a machine learning researcher, or let someone with data fine-tune a model to solve a specific problem.

23:46 Companies will become self-driving organizations
Amjad thinks the shape of companies will change. Silicon Valley has tried many experiments to remake companies — Holacracy, Medium tried it, GitHub tried a no-manager system, all failed spectacularly — but he thinks that was a technology problem: now you can let agents act as the connective tissue inside an organization, turn bureaucratic processes into invisible things machines do in the background, give people genuine autonomy to work on what interests them most, and let AI judge your impact. He says he has already changed how management works at Replit, calls it a ‘self-driving company’, and that ultimately the company will run itself. He admits he does not have a fully formed idea, but is quite sure everything will change, and much faster than you think; if you do not natively understand this stuff, the transition will be hard.

28:51 Trust makes money arrive six weeks faster
Gagan says he volunteers in local politics in his spare time, and the biggest takeaway is understanding how valuable trust is. He gives a concrete comparison: in a nonprofit, after a donor verbally commits $50,000 to you, the probability that the money actually lands in your account is only about 20% to 50%; in Silicon Valley, that probability is about 75% to 100%. The difference is that if you are certain the money is coming, you can confidently push forward, and by the time the check actually arrives you have already advanced six weeks, which makes the check worth even more. Conversely, without trust you change your approach out of fear the donor will be unhappy, drift from your mission, and are left with only anxiety and stress. He thinks this can be transplanted into schools: trust students to do what they want to do.

32:01 Without grades there is no fulcrum to push against
Asked how to handle disruptive students — for example Zuckerberg, who nearly got expelled for FaceMash — Gagan says there must of course be red lines; sexual harassment, publicly humiliating others and the like need rules, and you need to build trust and a positive-sum atmosphere. But he says one core principle of the academy sidesteps the problem entirely: with no grades and no exams, the resistance students have to push against is already much smaller. So if you want to build FaceMash, go build it, and he is willing to defend that right even if he personally finds the idea weird and does not like it. He thinks that as long as you create an environment of trust and keep students from developing an anti-authority mindset, you unlock a great deal of creativity and opportunity. Amjad adds that this drive to test boundaries can be channeled in healthy directions: kids who learn to program and hack on Roblox, rather than being sent to prison, could be put in a sandbox, have their talent discovered, and be steered into cybersecurity jobs or even government.

item.title: Jensen Huang: Saying There's a 10% Chance AI Destroys Humanity Is Irresponsible
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-ezra-黄仁勋-说-ai-有-10-概率毁灭人类是不负责任的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-ezra-黄仁勋-说-ai-有-10-概率毁灭人类是不负责任的/
item.description: He concedes AI will change every job, but treats the risk of losing control as a solvable engineering problem: if a lab truly believed it was losing control, the right answer is not to ship the product, not to buy the most compute while asking to be slowed down.
item.content:encoded:
He concedes AI will change every job, but treats the risk of losing control as a solvable engineering problem: if a lab truly believed it was losing control, the right answer is not to ship the product, not to buy the most compute while asking to be slowed down.

Huang rarely engages the AI doomer case head-on; here he gives concrete positions on alignment, evaluation and the compute split, and concedes the cycle will eventually turn. The unit economics in the back half are worth more than the front half.

6:28 Reading scans got automated, and there are more radiologists
Huang uses radiology as his core case: over the past decade computer vision reached superhuman levels, AI has permeated every radiology application, and it can detect any abnormality and any disease. But reading scans is a task a radiologist does, not the purpose of the job — the purpose is to diagnose disease and help patients. Once reading is automated, doctors can handle more cases, hospital revenue rises, and they need more radiologists, not fewer. From this he draws the distinction between the purpose of a job and the tasks of a job.

9:32 For jobs like customer service, the task is the job
Huang concedes AI will change every job and automate a great many tasks, and he names one category that gets replaced wholesale: when the job and the task are one and the same, as with phone customer service, the job itself is the task. But he offers counter-evidence too: AI only became genuinely useful in the past six months, after 15 years of getting it to run at all, and in those six months $500 billion of venture capital went into AI-native companies.

22:01 Data from 26,000 Chinese students: homework faster, exams worse
Ezra cites a study from China: 26,000 students in grades 7 through 12, with staggered AI adoption. The result was an 18% rise in homework scores and a 30% drop in time to completion, but within six months monthly exam scores fell 20% and high-stakes entrance exam scores fell 18% to 24%, with the full penalty showing up about two years later. Huang's response: he agrees completely with that last part, just as nobody does long division anymore and the multiplication table is being forgotten, but he doesn't think it matters — ‘we'll discover new skills, they just may not be those.’

35:28 Cheating isn't malice, it's the cheapest path in compute
Huang breaks down the Hugging Face agent attack: software given an objective function optimizes toward the objective, that's just what the algorithm does. If you tell software to score perfectly on this test, the most obvious move is to go find the answers; if it can't do that at all, the second most obvious move is to figure out who the smartest kid in class is and copy off him. Only the third approach is to decompose the problem, go learn the material, and grind it out — and that consumes the most compute and the most energy, so unless you align it and tell it that's how it must solve the problem, the software takes the most obvious path.

40:48 A company with agency can't say it needs to be saved
Ezra relays what the labs say publicly: they face a hybrid problem of engineering, alignment and operational excellence, they're being pushed too fast by competition with each other and with China, they feel they're losing control of what they're building, and they want outside help to slow down. Huang rejects the frame: these are companies with agency, CEOs with agency, and they're using that agency to say ‘we need help.’ His analogy: if a car company believed it was about to ship an unsafe product, it has the ability, the power and the responsibility not to ship it — and it already has the incentive not to ship it.

59:49 Hinton's prediction has no scientific basis
Ezra brings up Jeffrey Hinton saying a 10% chance of societal destruction is not unreasonable, and Huang answers directly: I'd tell Jeff that saying these things is irresponsible, that his predictions have consistently been wrong, that the 10% figure is not grounded in science and not grounded in research — ‘just because it comes from a scientist doesn't make it science.’ He then brings up the old score: the advice that nobody should go into radiology, the claim that deep learning would surpass radiologists within five years, which didn't happen; and if that scares young people out of college because they think they won't find work, that's harmful.

1:17:30 The R&D split has to flip from 80/20
Huang gives a concrete split: at NVIDIA roughly 10% to 20% of people do design and 80% do verification, whereas most labs today, understandably, put 80% into capability and 20% into safety, verification and evaluation. He says that ratio will flip, and that's the transition he means. He asks labs not to send him anything unevaluated: don't send NVIDIA any product that hasn't been evaluated with a human in the loop. His position is that safety, alignment, evaluation, guardrails, sandboxes, containment, monitoring, telemetry and external AI monitoring are all AI technologies and should be accelerated to the maximum.

1:24:48 The books on a one-gigawatt AI factory
Huang gives the unit economics of the new computing era: building a one-gigawatt data center, a one-gigawatt AI factory, costs $50 billion, and it can be rented out for $40 to $50 billion a year. He describes the shift from retrieval based computing — retrieving files, hence the name data center — to generative computing, with compute per user rising sharply; and since agents are also using generative AI, it isn't just a billion people using computers, it's hundreds of billions of agents plus people, and the compute required could rise a billionfold.

item.title: The UK's productivity crisis was a statistical error: 0.7% became 1.3%
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-moreorless-英国生产率危机是统计错误-0-7-被改成-1-3/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-moreorless-英国生产率危机是统计错误-0-7-被改成-1-3/
item.description: Fifteen years of Britain being cast as the worst-performing developed economy on productivity may have been an ONS miscalculation of hours worked — holidaymakers counted as working 40 hours inflated the denominator and pushed productivity down.
item.content:encoded:
Fifteen years of Britain being cast as the worst-performing developed economy on productivity may have been an ONS miscalculation of hours worked — holidaymakers counted as working 40 hours inflated the denominator and pushed productivity down.

Medium information density, but the UK productivity revision alone is enough to change how you judge the "British disease"; the other three segments are routine fact-checks you can take or leave.

1:05 The UK productivity crisis was calculated into existence
After the financial crisis, UK productivity growth was estimated at 0.7% a year, the worst among advanced economies, and it became the raw material for fifteen years of the "productivity puzzle". After the ONS changed how it measures hours worked, that figure became 1.3%, nearly double. Output and GDP did not change; only the denominator did: Britons actually work far fewer hours than previously thought. Chris Giles says pre-crisis growth was 2%, and 2% means productivity doubles roughly every 35 years, while 0.7% means a century to double; 1.3% falls in between. Britain is no longer an international outlier, but growth is still below its pre-crisis level.

4:16 You cannot trust asking people how many hours they work
The old method simply asked respondents how many hours they worked in a week and took the answer at face value. The problem came at follow-up: if no one answered the door in August, the ONS carried over the 40 hours that person had reported three months earlier and plugged in a 40 — when that person was probably on holiday and had not worked a single hour. The OECD recommended back in 2018 that countries stop doing this; the UK took eight years to change. Giles says that over those eight years people wrote a batch of "UK productivity crisis" articles that no longer hold up. He admits this is infuriating, but the change is in the right direction.

11:38 One in ten Irish people becoming clergy is a myth
The book says that in the 1960s one in every ten Irish children became a nun, priest or Christian Brother. The 1961 census shows 18,854 Catholic clergy and nuns, 2,125 Christian Brothers and other religious brothers, and 4,842 seminarians — 25,821 in total, or 1/104 of the population. The 1951 ratio was 1/127. The original source is research by Mary Daly, who looked only at students sitting the leaving certificate exam in 1966, when fewer than 20% of the school-age population took that exam — about 12,000 people, roughly one in ten of whom entered religious life. That qualifier was lost in retelling and became "all children". The author has said subsequent editions will be corrected.

14:41 Grid queue numbers are inflated by applications
Between November 2024 and June 2025, cumulative electricity demand in the UK grid connection queue jumped from about 41 GW to 125 GW, tripling in six months, with data centres accounting for 73 GW. But queuing is cheap, like booking a table at a popular restaurant months ahead; many projects will never actually be built or will shrink. Ofgem estimates that if all this data centre demand materialised, the cost would be close to £700bn, nearly a quarter of UK annual GDP. A 2025 government report projected 6 GW would be needed by 2030, while another queue analysis reckons about 20 GW has serious financial backing behind it. Johnny Gowdy of Regen says nobody knows how much will ultimately be built.

17:45 The data centre emissions comparison counts only direct emissions
Foxglove's analysis claims two planned data centres at full load would emit more carbon than ExxonMobil's UK operations. That comparison counts only ExxonMobil's own operational emissions, excluding the petrol and diesel it sells — which is the main source of emissions, something an ordinary reader may not spot. Foxglove also assumes the data centres run at 100% power year-round, while a scholar studying AI's carbon footprint uses 65%. More important is the power source: the planning documents for these two projects say that initially, because they cannot connect to the grid, they will use on-site gas generation. The UK grid as a whole is about half renewable and only 30% gas, so these data centres amount to stimulating demand for higher-carbon generation.

23:00 Vinyl's physical limits actually got weaker
The 1950s story goes: the closer a record gets to the centre, the lower the linear speed, and the less bass and brightness a groove can hold, so you put the quiet song at the end of a side. Mitchell Sterling's database has 2,284 albums and 27,000 songs spanning 1953 to the present. Measured by relative loudness, before 1982 closing tracks averaged about 0.65 dB quieter than the tracks before them; after 1982, when cassette sales overtook vinyl in the US and the constraint disappeared, the gap widened to about 1.5 dB. In the streaming era after 2010, the gap is still twice what it was in the vinyl era. In other words, the less the physical constraint mattered, the quieter closing tracks became.

26:02 The quiet ending went from constraint to artistic device
Sterling defines a quiet, acoustic closing track as a "typical quiet acoustic farewell". In the 1950s more than 60% of albums ended with a quiet, acoustic song; as recordings overall got louder, that absolute share slid all the way down to under one-sixth in the 1980s; by the 2000s and 2010s it had climbed back to about one-third. Sterling's analogy is the save icon on a floppy disk: the constraint is long gone, the habit remains. He also found in streaming data that an album's final track averages longer, more acoustic and sadder — but that is an average, and hip-hop, heavy metal and electronic music are full of loud exceptions.

item.title: US Debt Tops $40 Trillion: Even the Doves Are Calling Themselves Hawks Now
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-planetmoney-美国债务破-40-万亿-连鸽派都改口当鹰派了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-planetmoney-美国债务破-40-万亿-连鸽派都改口当鹰派了/
item.description: The 2010 paper that said growth halves once debt passes 90% of GDP was used by politicians as a red line for over a decade; now even the dove economists who once argued for spending boldly have switched to calling themselves hawks, but nobody can say where that line is.
item.content:encoded:
The 2010 paper that said growth halves once debt passes 90% of GDP was used by politicians as a red line for over a decade; now even the dove economists who once argued for spending boldly have switched to calling themselves hawks, but nobody can say where that line is.

Medium information density, but the second half's reversal of positions and the interest-rate data are worth it. For understanding how the US debt debate evolved from 2010 to today, this episode is a clear recap.

2:05 The real fuse on the debt snowball is interest
The textbook worry isn't the debt itself, but that interest costs feed on themselves: pay more interest, the deficit grows; a bigger deficit pushes debt higher; next period's interest is even bigger, and compounding makes it worse and worse. The other path is investors losing their appetite for Treasuries, forcing the government to keep raising rates to attract buyers, and the snowball rolls faster. Neither of these terrible outcomes happened after the financial crisis, and in hindsight the people who argued the government should spend more were on the right side of history — Karen Dynan even thinks it should have spent more at the time, and the recession could have been shorter.

8:21 The 90% line was read into the paper
The 2010 six-page paper by Reinhart and Rogoff, “Growth in a Time of Debt”, looked at decades of debt data across 20 advanced economies and concluded that when debt reaches 90% of GDP, growth is only half its normal level. But what the paper actually did was sort countries into four buckets — low, medium, high and very high — with the very high bucket containing countries whose debt was far above 90%, and technically it said that this bucket, on average, was associated with lower growth over long stretches. Politicians and the media read it as a red line: ‘cross 90% and the economy crashes.’ The paper never said that.

11:28 An Excel error detonated the austerity fight
The argument the paper sparked raged across blogs and newspapers, with calls for austerity and belt-tightening on one side and don't-kill-the-recovery, you-can't-stop-spending-now on the other. Later, more debt-friendly economists published a piece pointing out a major error in the Excel spreadsheet Reinhart and Rogoff had used, and the paper's final sentence said that since their finding was wrong, Europe's and America's own austerity agendas should be reassessed. Correcting the error weakened the claim everyone had seized on, but didn't overturn it — the updated paper still showed high debt generally associated with slower growth, just not as steeply.

13:41 Low growth can also cause high debt
High debt being correlated with low growth doesn't mean high debt causes low growth. Andrea Presbitero points out the causality may run the other way: when the economy underperforms, policymakers want to stimulate it, which means public consumption and public investment, and one way to do that is to borrow — borrowing pushes debt up, so you see low growth and high debt in the data at the same time. He and his coauthors ultimately reached the same conclusion as most people: based on the empirical evidence, there's no definitive answer, and causality may run both ways. On top of that, the tipping point for debt varies by country — it could be 90%, it could be 45%, it could be 100% — and depends on who the creditors are, whether they're domestic or foreign investors, and whether the debt is short- or long-term.

17:50 Rates at zero shelved the whole issue
What makes high debt destructive isn't the debt itself, but the interest you pay on it. After the financial crisis, global rates fell to near zero and stayed there for years, so plenty of macroeconomists figured maybe there was no need to worry much about debt at all, and attention drifted away from the topic. Then the world changed twice: the pandemic and the spending that followed pushed debt higher, and more importantly, rates rose again. Today the cost of holding a lot of debt, for the US and other countries, is far higher than five or six years ago, and the question that had been shelved is relevant again.

19:57 Rogoff says 91% and you're damned is a misreading
Ken Rogoff is still annoyed about how the paper was interpreted. He says 90% was just their highest bucket, they never said that at 91% you suddenly go to hell — that's like a 55 mph speed limit, and if you drive 56 you'll crash the next minute. He thinks that reading was used and distorted polemically. But he also stresses you can't conclude from that that there's no threshold and any level of debt is fine — that's crazy too. His basic intuition hasn't changed: constantly levering up is playing with fire, and the US trajectory needs adjusting — not just debt, but also Social Security and Medicare.

25:22 The dove who argued for spending has flipped
Two years on, debt has grown by more than $4 trillion, the big tax cuts Congress passed in 2025 cut revenue further, and interest alone costs over $1 trillion a year, a record. Karen Dynan, who once thought the spending was worth the risk, now says ‘I'm a debt hawk now,’ because changes in financial markets, especially the rate on Treasury borrowing, make her think this is trickier than she thought two years ago. She describes it as walking on ice and comforting yourself that it ‘hasn't cracked yet.’ Last week the 10-year Treasury rate hit its highest level since before the Great Recession, and the CBO projects debt will exceed 120% of GDP by 2036, higher than at any point in US history including World War II.

28:32 Rogoff puts the odds of a big problem above half
Rogoff thinks the biggest misconception is believing rates will stay low forever, and that if they're high for a while, it's just a nightmare that will pass. He says he thinks the probability of something very serious happening is greater than 50% — not the end of the world, a debt crisis isn't the end of the world either, but something very significant will happen, and we're not prepared. He also says we need to reflect on how wrong everyone was and for how long, because that belief hasn't gone away — how mainstream opinion leaders thought back then is basically how they still think now. As for the red line, neither economist can draw it, but both agree the fix is spending cuts, tax increases, or both — and that looks impossible to move.

item.title: AI Debt Is Crowding Out Treasuries, and the US Economy Is Actually in Deflation
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-betteroffline-ai-债务正在和美元抢钱-美国经济其实在通缩/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-betteroffline-ai-债务正在和美元抢钱-美国经济其实在通缩/
item.description: AI capex has grown large enough to push into the Treasury market and distort global trade and inflation data; strip out the AI-related portion and the US economy is mildly deflationary, while the Fed is hiking for the wrong reasons.
item.content:encoded:
AI capex has grown large enough to push into the Treasury market and distort global trade and inflation data; strip out the AI-related portion and the US economy is mildly deflationary, while the Fed is hiking for the wrong reasons.

Paul Kedrosky strings AI capex into a single causal chain running through Treasuries, trade and inflation, and the back half on an Anthropic IPO and OpenAI's valuation is especially dense.

1:06 AI capex can now move Treasury yields
Over the past 12 to 18 months, AI capex has consistently accounted for 30% to 70% of US GDP growth. More anomalous is that it has started to seep into the Treasury market: AI-related debt issuance is approaching $1 trillion, and debt's share of AI financing has risen from 15% to 20% a year ago to over 60%, making it the single largest block in both the investment-grade and high-yield markets. The result is that yield-sensitive investors would rather hold hyperscaler debt than Treasuries at the same duration, pushing the 10-year yield up. Kedrosky stresses this is not the market losing faith in America's ability to pay — the US can print money and will not default — it is competition at the margin.

6:10 More than half of global trade growth is AI
The WTO had forecast that global goods trade would fall noticeably because of US tariff policy; instead it grew about 4.5%, close to double the forecast. Digging into the data to find out why, the WTO found that over the past three quarters about 19% of global goods trade was AI-related, and close to 55% of global trade growth was AI-related — mostly NVIDIA GPUs. Kedrosky's conclusion: AI capex is masking the real effect of Trump's tariffs, because it is so large it drowns out every other signal.

8:12 Both sources of US inflation trace back to AI
US inflation is still above 3%, yet consumers are more stretched and more indebted than they have been in a long time. Break inflation apart and the two biggest pieces are: first, AI capex pushing up energy prices, which pushes up construction costs, materials and a range of services; second, the energy shock from the Iran war. Kedrosky counts the latter as AI-related too — he argues the Trump administration was emboldened by the success of the operation it ran in Venezuela using Anthropic, turned war into an app, and Iran is next. So both preconditions for inflation sit on top of AI.

19:30 Strip out AI and the US is in deflation
If you remove AI-capex-related inflation and the energy inflation from the AI-emboldened Iran war from the US economy, Kedrosky calculates the US is actually running about 0.25% deflation. That means the Fed is hiking for the wrong reasons — it thinks it is suppressing demand-side inflation, when the actual inflation is exogenous. This resembles the path into the 1929 crash: high rates plus a weak consumer are the classic precursor to a long balance sheet recession. He cites Richard Koo's work on Japan's lost decade and argues all the conditions are now in place.

22:35 Balance sheet recession: a decade of deleveraging, no spending, no hiring
The hyperscalers will not go bankrupt, but they will spend a decade cleaning up their balance sheets — going from the least indebted companies in the market to the most indebted. A balance sheet recession is when firms, regardless of the level of rates, focus on deleveraging and getting debt off the books. The consequence: no investment in growth, no hiring, while simultaneously looking for ways to use AI to cut headcount. Companies like CoreWeave face a different problem — rolling over debt over the next five years may force them into some form of insolvency. Kedrosky says this will be the most underrated macro event of the next five years.

29:47 The system is screaming: data center financing costs are rising on their own
The 10-year yield has risen about 100 basis points over the past few months, directly raising the financing cost of new data centers. But it goes further: when the system is under stress, the spread between issuance yields and the 10-year widens from 100 basis points to 150 or even 200. So every time you see rates rise, you should translate it as "data centers just got a lot worse at proving their future cash flows." Kedrosky judges that on financing costs alone, this breaks within 6 to 12 months — the most stressed end of the market is demanding an 11% to 12% return, and that is impossible to deliver.

37:58 Data centers need to earn 7%, but nobody can make the math work
The investment-grade market currently demands a median return of about 7.2% from data centers, and the junk market demands 10%. But Kedrosky stresses this is the threshold to attract creditors, not the threshold to get your capital back — that is a separate question, and he thinks the capital never comes back. He coined the term EBBT — earnings before bad things — where you cut out everything that costs money and of course the cash flow looks great, but that assumes hyperscalers stop burning money on frontier models, and nobody is doing that. If you only do industrial-grade inference, then it is fundamentally an energy problem: China adds roughly 3x the new energy capacity the US does each year, and is already ahead.

41:01 Anthropic's IPO slipped from October to November, and employees are borrowing millions to exercise
What Kedrosky has heard is that Anthropic originally planned to IPO on October 1, and it has now reportedly slipped to November. His general rule: even in a good market, at least half the companies that say they will list by year-end do not list that year. Internally there is panic about what an IPO this year would look like. More concretely, the employees: many have already exercised their options, and if the IPO does not happen they face the IRS's AMT, generating tax bills in the millions — he knows quite a few people who have borrowed millions of dollars for this. He also mentions a supplier close to the company saying Anthropic's Q3 came in below expectations, but stresses this is rumor, and consistent with the backdrop of customer concentration and the ebbing of token maxing.

item.title: Silicon Valley Makes Too Much Money, and That's Why California's Government Has No Incentive to Get Better
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.description: California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax payments are so generous that the government doesn't need to survive on results. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.
item.content:encoded:
California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax payments are so generous that the government doesn't need to survive on results. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.

What's worth listening for is two causal chains you can check: how Sacramento's bill assembly line has piled up 420,000 regulations, and how Silicon Valley's tax revenue lets the government skip improving.

5:04 The rules aren't written, they're piled up every year
Hilton gives the consequence of one-party rule a countable form: Sacramento passed 1,118 bills last year, and when he printed them out, the stack was twice his height. ‘No one is reading this’ — do you think Gavin Newsom reads them all before signing? The result is that California has accumulated more than 420,000 regulations, and he promises to cut that below 200,000 within his first term. Who are the bills written for?
