He says for the narrow interest groups that control the process: unions, plaintiff's lawyers, and the people who donate to politicians — which is why California is the highest litigation-risk place in the country, and why starting a company there carries a 90% chance of ending up in court. Structurally, over those 16 years Democrats took all eight statewide elected offices, a two-thirds majority in the state legislature, every major county and city, and a 6-to-1 state Supreme Court.

13:08 The key is that 26% of undecided voters
What he offers isn't a ‘Republicans flip it’ story but an arithmetic problem: his internal poll at the start of the race was 33% firmly for him, 41% firmly for Becerra, 26% undecided. Those 26% are the key — mostly Democratic voters but not die-hards, overwhelmingly non-college-educated working people who are financially maxed out, and whose top concern is the cost of living. So the platform is all priceable line items: cancel high-speed rail, cut the government payroll by 10%, stop funding the nonprofits that make homelessness worse, and you get ‘the first $150,000 free of state income tax’; gas goes from $6 toward $3, because the low carbon fuel standard and cap and invest add roughly 150 dollars to the price of gas, and cap and invest money is flowing to high-speed rail; cap the vehicle registration fee at 73 dollars by abolishing the DMV. The polling gap has narrowed from 30 points on primary night to 8 points recently.

19:14 Silicon Valley's money removes the pressure to perform
This is the most counterintuitive stretch of the whole piece. One host cites Peter Thiel's observation from years ago: Silicon Valley is to California what a resource curse is to a petro-state — it generates so much wealth and tax revenue that the place doesn't need a good government, and that is also why one-party rule has held. Hilton adds the evidence: before the primary, Becerra was asked on CNN what policies he would change given homelessness, the highest poverty rate, the highest unemployment rate and a terrible cost of living, and his answer was that this is the world's fourth-largest economy, people still love coming to Disneyland and the beaches, so things must be heading in the right direction. Hilton's rebuttal is that the fourth-largest economy figure includes the size of the government itself — which doubled in a decade — while net private-sector job creation in California since the pandemic is essentially zero.

23:19 What worked was the content, not the AI
Spencer Pratt is running for mayor of Los Angeles as an independent and got a flood of free media off a batch of AI-generated videos. He breaks down the mechanism himself: what actually worked was what the videos said — he went on every platform and just told the truth as he knew it, and then creative people across the country started throwing ideas into this ‘machine’. ‘I don't think what worked was the AI, it was just one piece of a much bigger puzzle.’ He thinks there's evidence for this: most of the people who voted for him are Democrats. He also claims that if Los Angeles's 200,000 registered Republicans had actually turned out to vote, he would have won.

27:21 Taxpayers are paying for needles handed out in the park
Hilton and Spencer together describe MacArthur Park: last Tuesday at 10:30 in the morning, sunny in downtown Los Angeles, and in every direction people are smoking crack, injecting drugs, hunched over from fentanyl. The reason is that four nonprofits show up every day to hand out crack pipes, needles and drug supplies, and the money comes from taxpayers. Spencer adds the follow-up: one of the needle distributors was found to be selling drugs at the same time. Hilton stresses that this isn't a case of no one being in charge — Los Angeles has a new DA cracking down on drugs and crime, and there are federal prosecutors going after gangs and cartels — but the scene in the park is the same every Tuesday.

29:22 Do the right thing and you're punished; do the wrong thing and you're rewarded
A Latino couple in South Los Angeles ran a shoe store for 14 years. The shop was spotless, and they paid every tax, license, electricity bill and permit, each year more expensive than the last. They asked Hilton to step outside and look two blocks down the sidewalk: it was entirely vendors selling shoes, clothing and T-shirts who pay no tax, no electricity, no rent, no license. That is why the couple is closing. When did it start? In the last six or seven years — in 2018 Sacramento passed a bill legalizing street vending statewide, and neither the city nor the county has the power to regulate it. His conclusion: here, doing the right thing is punished and doing the wrong thing is rewarded, and the whole situation is upside down. Spencer adds the numbers: 50,000 food vendors, a permit costs just 21 dollars, yet the city council allocated 500,000 dollars to buy them carts, while the unrepaired Palisades reservoir cover would cost only 200,000 dollars.

42:32 Ballot collection is legal, so it can't be audited
Spencer's claim is that it isn't fake ballots, it's ballot harvesting, which California law allows. The mechanism has three steps: a witness signature can be a smiley face or an X; the same witness can witness 43,000 ballots, and there is no verification allowed; and once ballots reach the counting center they are separated from their envelopes, the signatures stay on the envelopes, and the chain of custody is broken — so even if you know who these people are, you can't audit it, and a recount just recounts the same ballots. The other side's rebuttal: voter fraud is a felony and is prosecuted regularly; after Trump lost last time he filed 60 such lawsuits and lost all of them. Asked directly whether he believes he lost because of fraud, Spencer's answer is ‘without evidence I'd say no’, and he lists the 200,000 registered Republicans who didn't vote as one of the reasons.

47:35 The empty reservoir and the reconstruction lawsuit
Spencer's house, his parents' house and his neighbors' houses all burned. Reconstruction is stuck on two things. First, that empty reservoir is still empty — even the one across from his house, the one he was sure would never burn, is empty, and Palisades is now supplied by a hose run all the way from Tanga through regrown dry brush. Second, they are pursuing a mass tort suit with 10,000 victims, naming Gavin Newsom's state parks department, the city and the city's water and power department as defendants. His chain of allegations: on New Year's Eve there was an 8-acre fire in Pacific Palisades, state parks should have monitored it per the manual but didn't, letting embers smolder into the known wind event of January 6–7; firefighter whistleblowers told him there were visibly smoldering coals on the hillside, and state parks employees produced photos in testimony showing the hillside smoking.

item.title: Individual productivity triples, but company delivery only goes from 20 days to 17
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.description: AI armed everyone, but the organisation didn't get faster — because the weakest plank in the barrel isn't a person, it's the process. The real dividing line is whether you can rework the process and the organisation, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
item.content:encoded:
AI armed everyone, but the organisation didn't get faster — because the weakest plank in the barrel isn't a person, it's the process. The real dividing line is whether you can rework the process and the organisation, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.

A frontline CEO explains the nuts and bolts of building his own CEO AI, cancelling the weekly meeting, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and the numbers are concrete, and the decision-hub section in the back half is the most valuable part.

16:07 Individual productivity triples, delivery only gets three days faster
NetEase ran the numbers last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design doc to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled-to-quintupled their personal efficiency, some tenfold. But for a feature of the same scope, the whole process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of the 20 planks, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product-manager planks shoot up fast, but some planks aren't people at all — they're process, and they haven't improved one bit. So landing AI means clearing three hurdles: awareness, getting it into individuals' short-range tasks, and reworking process and organisation — the third is the hardest.

20:11 Cancel the weekly meeting: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. A weekly meeting usually serves three purposes: syncing information, spotting problems and opportunities, and making decisions. It used to run 2.5 hours a week, but the time spent on that meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepares materials layer by layer, and the information sync itself isn't even done well, because nobody listens attentively the whole time and may miss the one sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agree on what information is needed, everyone fills in a template and stores it in the knowledge base, and AI scans and consolidates it into a focused, interactive HTML report you can leave comments and follow-up questions on; an AI agent produces a first pass of problems and opportunities, which human brains confirm and supplement; solving problems and making decisions move to dedicated meetings.

28:20 SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, it just changes form — AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may really die, while genuinely good SaaS that has already entered a company's critical processes will only get better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. In the past humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future a mass of agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, review APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs — call volumes far exceeding the number and actions of humans, a massive increase, and the more it's called the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that the Service itself is critical enough inside the company.

32:21 Distil your top salesperson into a skill and hand it to everyone
Two things give bosses headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is so strong that if they leave, what then. There used to be no answer; now you can distil or extract a good salesperson's moves, scripts and behaviour into a skill. Two uses: distribute it to other salespeople to use directly; and have AI turn the elite salesperson into a teacher who trains ordinary salespeople. What training should distil isn't the salesperson, it's the customer — take the customer interaction data the salesperson has touched, calls, WeChat, email, and have AI simulate all kinds of customers to train salespeople. Online sales is fully digital and on record; for offline sales, recommend or even require a recording card — after a visit, while memory is fresh, record two or three minutes of voice notes, because salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is there to manage them) but don't mind a recording card, since it's also useful for their own customer review.

44:31 Fewer middle managers, strong individuals return to the front line with agent legions
Ruan Liang judges that middle management will shrink, though not necessarily by being eliminated — rather by going to the front line, and the front line can also carry a pile of agents. Middle managers performing management duties will become fewer and fewer, while elite people with formidable skills will become more and more numerous. He gives his engineering team as an example: socialised division of labour used to slice software development ever finer — frontend, backend, algorithm, test engineers; in the last half year it has visibly swung back to full-stack, everyone becoming a full-end engineer. The future organisation looks more and more like a distributed-peak structure: countless engineering peaks are very strong, one mother peak commands some of them, and countless agents fight a battle. He imagines a future interview negotiation: the candidate says I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, the summary of all my past experience and skills, and the premium the company has to pay might be some kind of OPC.

50:35 The AI value formula: quality times time saved
Ruan Liang offers a formula referencing a paper: AI's value = the quality with which AI completes the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit of time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at eight out of ten, AI also makes it at eight out of ten, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit of time and you can compute the ROI. Prioritise four kinds of work for AI: things worth spending time on, high frequency, unavoidable, and where different people produce roughly the same result. Once computed, you can immediately decide whether to use AI for it. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Cloud, GPT) to prove the thing can be done, freeze the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheap ones can too.

59:40 Crushing leads in token consumption, crushing leads in output too
NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work into points with work value. By the AI era they found one kind of person whose token consumption is astonishing, and whose work output and work value are also astonishing, forming a statistical regularity: people with a crushing lead in token consumption are most likely building themselves a system, saving their own working time and increasing their thinking time, so their work quality and work results also lead by a crushing margin. Many bosses worry about waste from AI abuse; Ruan Liang's hot take is that genuinely excellent or elite people don't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through the statistics they found elite colleagues don't waste. He also says small companies embrace AI more thoroughly, because there are fewer organisational relationships, the boss uses it first, the hierarchy is shallow and the chain is short.

1:11:50 The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base, and what really matters is the historical decision processes and the basis for decisions. This year NetEase is preserving decisions that have happened historically and bringing them into the knowledge base; the two kinds of knowledge are combined to train an agent or skill, and then the original several hundred cases are fed back in for the agent to judge, with accuracy above 90%. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater gave researchers and analysts an agent it built itself, precipitating decision processes and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater does better is making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a person adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment enters the next round of reinforcement, keeping pace with the times, essentially human-machine collaborative self-evolution.

item.title: Mooncakes sell for only two months a year, yet they've become a 28.2 billion yuan business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.description: Being tied to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps mooncakes' selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from the gifting occasion and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.
item.content:encoded:
Being tied to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps mooncakes' selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from the gifting occasion and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.

Worth listening for food industry practitioners and anyone wanting to understand the holiday consumption business, but information density is low — much of the runtime is spent on explaining regional styles and flavors, with the business mechanics concentrated in the middle and later sections.

6:06 Zongzi can be sold year-round, mooncakes cannot
Zongzi is tied to Dragon Boat Festival, but once vacuum-sealed for long shelf life it can be sold all year round — Wufangzhai even opened restaurants to put zongzi into everyday settings. Mooncakes' problem is not that the craft can't achieve long shelf life, but that it is defined as a ‘traditional festival pastry mainly eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival’, and the national standard GB19855 writes the season directly into the definition. So of two festival foods, zongzi can decouple from its festival through shelf life and channels, while mooncakes cannot.

12:12 The national standard draws hard lines on fillings
Lotus seed paste mooncakes must contain no less than 60% lotus seeds, fruit mooncakes must contain no less than 25% fruit products, and five-kernel mooncakes must use the five kernels: walnut, almond, olive kernel, melon seed, and sesame. The purpose of these lines is to push up ingredient costs and prevent cheap candied winter melon, red-and-green shredded garnish, and inferior nuts from being used as filler. For consumers, reading the order of the ingredient list is enough to judge how much of the good stuff is actually in there.

26:30 Why custard lava mooncakes are made so small
Custard lava mooncakes are small not out of stinginess but because of structure. The outside is flaky pastry, the middle is a custard layer, and the innermost is the lava layer, with the custard layer acting as a moisture barrier. Production requires two rounds of baking to keep the lava semi-solid, and the lava's melting point has to be engineered — solid during transport, turning into flowing liquid only after a few seconds in the microwave. If heated too much, the lava gets absorbed by the pastry and it reverts to an ordinary custard mooncake.

37:34 ‘Everything can be a mooncake’ has five preconditions
Not everything can be stuffed into a mooncake. First is water content — hot-and-sour soup mooncakes are impossible because there's too much water to contain. Second is safety — meat, egg, and dairy are also favored by microorganisms, so processing temperatures and sterilization processes must be tested repeatedly. Third is particle size — too large and the pastry can't wrap it, too fine and you can't taste it. Fourth is flavor retention after high-temperature baking — some aromas simply disappear once baked. Fifth is whether the cost can be handled. So long-term stable flavors are ones confirmed by generation after generation.

44:40 Choosing an OEM isn't a matter of bigger is better
When big brands look for OEMs to make their branded mooncakes, there's a common misconception: you must pick the best OEM in the country. But a top-tier OEM's production scale actually doesn't match yours. Indicators you can screen on include registered capital, tax payment records, number of employees with social insurance contributions, and accumulated days of safe production. Also, the nine major regional styles correspond to different factories — you can't ask Guangzhou Restaurant to produce Shanxi egg-skin mooncakes; they simply don't have that capability or production line.

48:44 Flexible production lines can take orders of a few hundred boxes
Mooncake production is semi-automated and semi-manual — machines can handle wrapping and forming, but brushing egg wash, pressing patterns, and stamping require human hands, which actually makes it favorable for OEM and customization. Flexible factories can go as small as a few hundred boxes, and can do thousands or tens of thousands of boxes too. If a company has only 50 employees, it can use the factory's existing mooncakes directly and only needs to design the box. This small-batch, fast-response capability is the core of why mooncakes can support a corporate customization business.

51:47 The 28.2 billion yuan scale is held up by gifting
In 2025 China's mooncake output was 518,000 tons and sales scale was 28.2 billion RMB, both down from the previous year. At 80 grams each that's about 6.4 billion pieces; at 100 grams, about 5.18 billion pieces — across a population of 1.4 billion, an average of three to four per person. For comparison, Dragon Boat Festival zongzi annual sales are about 10 to 11 billion, and instant noodles about 68 to 120 billion. That mooncakes can do 28.2 billion selling only two months a year comes down to their gifting attribute — brands prepare large volumes of PR gifts at the two annual nodes of Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival, and zongzi's gifting attribute is far weaker than mooncakes'.

58:55 499 yuan is a number forced out by the regulatory line
In 2022 the National Development and Reform Commission and three other departments jointly issued an announcement placing boxed mooncakes priced above 500 yuan per unit under key supervision. So the highest price on the market is 499. The calculation logic: a box of mooncakes costs about 70 yuan per box, and adding channel commissions and allocated expenses, it's impossible to exceed 500. Back when the economy was good there were sky-high mooncakes with very expensive tea or liquor inside, even wooden gift boxes, with both cost and price very high.

item.title: AI for Science Is Stuck on the Last 0.001 Points, Not on Compute
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.description: ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to judge ‘you got this paper wrong’.
item.content:encoded:
ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to judge ‘you got this paper wrong’.

High information density, but it takes a little patience: the first half covers ERA's mechanics, the second half covers contrails, wildfires and quantum computing, all first-hand detail.

9:24 ERA's input is a chat, its output is a scored notebook
ERA's product form isn't having people write config files — you just start talking. Because mapping a scientific problem onto a scorable task is itself non-obvious, Michael Brenner wrote a dedicated agent to conversationally help you define which score to optimize. When the conversation ends, a Python notebook is generated underneath, containing a function that produces a score, and then the system starts mutating that notebook in a ‘clever way’, continually proposing new code to push the score higher.

10:24 It doesn't always pick the best candidate
ERA runs Monte Carlo Tree Search internally, holding hundreds or thousands of notebook candidates at once in a tree-shaped pool. Selection uses the upper confidence bound from reinforcement learning: estimate the 95th percentile outcome of a mutation and pick the one with the highest optimistic upper bound. So it doesn't always greedily pick the currently best-performing notebook; sometimes it picks the fifth best, in order to explore more efficiently. It has also tried combining the ideas of two candidates to generate a third.

18:38 Evolutionary coding was stuck for decades because random mutation is useless
Platt says evolutionary coding has been attempted since the 1970s — mutating Lisp code and the like — but it never took off, because random mutation in code space is basically worthless: just like DNA, the vast majority of mutations are harmful. ERA works because the inner loop is itself an AI that knows which direction to try, effectively giving it a meaningful gradient underneath. The price is that it also overfits, and it also goes off the rails in ‘genie wish’ fashion.

22:44 Predictive models and descriptive models are two different things
John Platt splits scientific modeling into two kinds: a predictive model only seeks the lowest error rate on some dataset; a descriptive model is what science actually wants — it contains some description of reality inside it, so it can extrapolate. His example is Newton: an apple falling can be fitted, but gravity isn't about apples, and if you take a model that only fits apples and ask it about planets, it has no planetary data and knows nothing. He admits the line is blurry, because the scientist themself also constrains the model with a pile of known facts and intuitions.

31:59 This is a power tool, and it will cut your fingers off
Faced with multiple hypothesis testing and overfitting, Platt's answer isn't a new method but a harsher old one: because ERA is a power tool, you have to be stricter than before, with a holdout buried so deep you never look at it yourself. He states plainly that no system yet discovers entirely new physics or entirely new science, and that scientists are still responsible for judging whether a conclusion is descriptive.

39:18 AI is stuck on the last 0.001 points
Ira pushed the score very close, but it didn't close the gap on the last 30 places or so, because nobody goes and scrapes off that final 0.001 points. This exposes the system's real structure: the inner layer is a machine running for hours to produce candidates, and the outer layer is a human making judgments like ‘you got this paper wrong’. Platt compares it to a graduate student who never sleeps and is extremely eager — you tell it a direction, it goes and tries, but when it gets stuck a human has to change the approach.

48:08 The counterfactual model stalled the team for two years
To judge which contrail to avoid, you need to know how much warming it actually causes, and that's a counterfactual problem: you can't enter the universe where the contrail doesn't exist. The team produced a counterfactual model that worked for outgoing longwave radiation, but they could never build one for the part that reflects sunlight, and it stalled them for two years. They even self-tested with a dataset where contrails were artificially injected, and their own attempts couldn't pass their own test. In the end ERA found a simple model that searches over all confounders, passed the test, and cracked the problem.

1:24:27 A wildfire is best put out before it's room-sized
Google has a crisis resilience effort, and one project in it is called Firesat: a wildfire is extremely easy to extinguish when it's only as big as ‘this room’, and once it reaches an acre it's far harder, while the growth from room size to an acre may be exponential. The plan is a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation using mid-wave IR (which corresponds to blackbody radiation, exactly the temperature of fire) for detection; roughly 50 to 80 satellites could cover the globe, spot a fire about 5 meters square, and raise an alarm within 15 to 20 minutes. The partner is the nonprofit Earth Fire Alliance, the satellites are built by Muon Space, and one prototype has already launched.

item.title: Trump Invites Xi to a Show. What Did the US Get in Return?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.description: This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US is trading symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.
item.content:encoded:
This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US is trading symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.

The first half covers the summit and US-China relations; the middle and later sections on China after Xi and fifty years since Mao's death are denser with information and worth listening to.

6:06 This visit has no substantive agenda at all
Gewirtz's judgment is that this state visit has ‘there is not a very deep substantive agenda at all’. Trump invited Xi mainly because he wants to put on a show, wants the pomp and the cameras, and incidentally to push issues like the Iran war out of the news. For Beijing, this actually makes them less nervous — because if it were a more confrontational meeting, they would be more anxious. But Gewirtz flags two things: Trump himself is extremely unpredictable, and Beijing has internalized this; and Beijing, watching the chaos in Washington, sees the US president himself often in a position they would never want Xi to be in — going to the wrong place, being photographed in unflattering images, being pressed by reporters. So the real question is not whether someone deliberately sets a trap, but whether things slip into the scenario they most want to avoid.

9:25 Symbolism for substance: where is the trade
Gewirtz characterizes this visit as ‘we are in a space of symbolism and optics’. He says that in US-China relations, trading symbolism for substance is itself a reasonable play: give Beijing the pomp and cameras it craves, and get back something concretely useful to Americans and US interests. That was the model for US relations with the Soviets during the Cold War and after — the US gave symbolism, legitimacy, and that handshake photo, and got a step back from the other side on Third World countries or nuclear issues. But the problem this time is that the Trump administration does not even seem to have tried to design a set of ‘deliverables’. Gewirtz says ‘it doesn't even seem like they're trying’. So what to watch is not where things go wrong, but ‘where is the trade happening’.

11:37 The direction of concessions has been completely flipped
Gewirtz points to a counterintuitive dynamic: concessions the US might once have given China are now flipped into ‘gifts’ China gives the US. Pomp and cameras were what Beijing wanted, but in Washington they are treated as Xi's visit being a concession to the US. The same flip happens on advanced semiconductors: the US used to not sell these things, and opening up products like the H200 would have been a huge concession; now if Beijing agrees to buy, many in Washington would see it as Beijing conceding to Trump. Gewirtz says this flip keeps recurring, and the reason it matters is not to score points for the administration, but that it reflects what happens when the power gap in superpower competition narrows — small differences, interpersonal dynamics, can cause much larger displacements in the overall strategic picture.

12:39 US-China relations are also K-shaped, held up by the upper leg
Gewirtz uses the ‘K-shaped’ idea for US-China relations: one upward leg is the leader-level channel — dense exchanges of visits, friendship, cameras; one downward leg is the competitive reality and the actions certain parts of both governments keep taking. The system is currently held up by the upward leg, but it is very fragile. He stresses this metaphor is not just a parallel analogy: saying ‘truce’ or ‘detente’ sounds too static, like a state already reached, but US-China relations are actually quite dynamic, quite unstable, moving in two directions at once. He applies the same K-shaped logic to China's economy — manufacturing and AI are flying, real estate and consumer demand are struggling, the upward leg is pulling the whole system forward, and the question is whether the system can hold as the K widens.

22:03 The bipartisan consensus on China policy has shattered
Gewirtz argues that Trump changed the tone of America's China discussion in the 2016 election, becoming the symbol and standard-bearer of that turn; but now, after helping create that turn, he has helped destroy or transform it. He cites David Feith's article in the Reagan Institute on ‘a new cold war in an age of doubt’ — that great rethink on China was not as great as many assumed. Gewirtz's conclusion: if the political dynamics are more complicated than imagined and the bipartisan consensus some people talk about does not exist, then this is a moment of ‘incredible fluidity’. He says he has no confidence in the direction of either Democratic or Republican China policy in the medium term, and Beijing has no confidence either.

31:24 Chinese officials cannot talk about risks they have no solution for
Gewirtz offers a different read on how the US should interpret Chen Yixin's article. On the surface, Americans are panicking about existential risk and China is panicking about regime security, and that is correct. But he says: heads of US AI model companies can talk at length about risks they have no solution for, and they all do; China's minister of state security cannot. In China, when you point out a risk in public, you are simultaneously saying ‘we the Communist Party see it, we will handle it, we have a solution’. So the real question is: should we take what we can see from Beijing as the whole, or acknowledge there is more in the system we cannot see. He gives an example from 25 years ago — when Americans predicted the internet would cause regime change in China, Clinton said it was like nailing Jell-O to the wall, and Beijing did nail the Jell-O to the wall, namely the Great Firewall.

35:37 Beijing has not decided how to regulate open models
Gewirtz says that around Xi's speech and Chen Yixin's article, the outside world has been through several cycles of excitement and interpretation, but Beijing has still not given the single most important thing: how they plan to regulate open-weight models spreading globally — models that carry both risk and strategic benefit for Beijing. He calls this ‘the trillion dollar question’. Both speeches can be read as pointing in some direction, but the decision has not been made. His guess is that this is because Beijing itself has not decided, because things are changing too fast and the trade-offs are too large. He contrasts with the Trump administration: it did not make a decision until Mythos came out, and then made another when Fable came out.

41:55 What to prepare for is not China's decline, but Xi's decline
Gewirtz says that a few years ago the ‘peak China’ debate asked whether to start preparing for China's decline, and now most people think China's economy is at least temporarily on a relatively sustainable path. But he thinks the real question is not that, but ‘do we need to prepare for Xi Jinping's decline’ — because people die, and modern Chinese history tells us that leaders in power for a long time change with age, certain obsessions become more prominent, behavior changes. By ‘prepare’ he does not mean the departure itself, but acknowledging uncertainty: the outside world has long treated Xi's tenure as fairly predictable, because since taking power in 2012 and 2013 he laid out a set of goals and largely pursued them. But he stresses the change could well be worse for the US — ‘That doesn't mean he's going to mellow’.

item.title: Canada Wants Into the EU: This Is a Permanent Breakup With America, Not a Wait for Trump to Leave
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-wsjournal-加拿大想加入欧盟-这是对美国的永久分手-不是等特朗普下台/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-wsjournal-加拿大想加入欧盟-这是对美国的永久分手-不是等特朗普下台/
item.description: Canada wants to be the EU's first "associate member," but the EU has no such status. It's a generational pivot toward Europe and away from the US — and Europe's economy grows at half America's rate.
item.content:encoded:
Canada wants to be the EU's first "associate member," but the EU has no such status. It's a generational pivot toward Europe and away from the US — and Europe's economy grows at half America's rate.

Medium information density, but the nonexistent "associate member" status, Carney's European network and book club, and the EU's Brexit-driven red line are three judgments you won't hear elsewhere.

0:00 Canada wants to be the EU's first associate member, but the status doesn't exist
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Canada is negotiating to become an associate member of the EU. But the show says it plainly: the EU has no such thing as an "associate member" — you're either a member, paying into the budget, accepting free movement of people and seamless truck crossings, or you're not. All 27 current members are in Europe, sharing borders, regulations, and mostly the euro. So what Canada gets will be a status invented for it, with details still being negotiated. What Carney wants isn't another buyer but a group of "like-minded" countries to build, together, the institutions and technological capabilities that America's "wrecking ball" can't reach.

3:01 Canada once saw itself as Europeans living in North America
This isn't a new idea; it's a return to an old identity. In the first half of the 20th century, some Canadians genuinely saw themselves as "Europeans living in North America" — today's oldest Canadians were born British subjects, and Canada didn't open an embassy in Washington until the 1920s. On the eve of World War II, Canada's trade with Britain still exceeded its trade with the US. After the war America became the center of gravity of the West, the auto industry integrated in the 1960s, NAFTA took effect in 1994, and Canadian elites switched from going to Oxford and Cambridge to going to Harvard and Yale. Trump's tensions reopened a forgotten historical question: where do Canadians belong in the world?

6:13 The 51st state isn't a trade negotiation, it's a sovereignty question
When Trump returned for his second term, he didn't just want to renegotiate a trade deal; he questioned the territorial integrity of allies like Canada and Denmark, and said publicly he wanted Canada to become the 51st state. The show's judgment: if it were just renegotiating trade, you could negotiate; once it touches sovereignty, it hits something deeply emotional, sensitive, electorally meaningful and bound up with a country's self-image. One Canadian official, after reading every Trump biography he could find, concluded that the 51st state talk was "price discovery" — throwing out an outrageous idea to test the reaction. Whatever the intent, the effect was real: Carney went from trailing by 25 points in the polls to winning, overnight.

8:17 Carney defined the trade war as "we've been attacked"
Carney had two signature moments after taking office. One was the Davos speech, landing right in the middle of the Greenland crisis, with Trump due to speak the next day; Carney went first and delivered the clearest anti-Trumpist manifesto yet: Canadians' old comfortable assumption that "geography and alliances automatically bring prosperity and security" no longer holds. The second came after the US imposed tariffs — instead of backing down he escalated, hitting back with tariffs of his own, and still wouldn't budge after the final round of trade talks collapsed. Asked at a press conference why it felt like war was about to start today, his answer was "because we've been attacked." The show says a technocrat and centrist taking escalatory action is counterintuitive, and that is exactly what made him seen as the leader of the Western allies' anti-Trump movement — for better or worse.

11:22 Carney's European network matters more than his policies
A prime minister of a North American country has an unusually large number of European friends: a doctorate in economics from Oxford, the first foreigner to run the Bank of England. Macron was a banker, German Chancellor Merz worked at BlackRock, Finnish President Stubb also came from finance, and Carney knows them all. In Ottawa he also has a book club whose members are political heavyweights and industry leaders, with a Fight Club-style rule — "the first rule of book club is you don't talk about book club." Most of them were educated at Oxford or Cambridge, are familiar with Europe, and remain in touch with the prime minister, feeding him exactly the kind of ideas about how to bring Canada closer to Europe. The show says interviewees were far more secretive about the book club than about Canada's plan to join the EU.

14:27 The talks aren't just trade — they're data cables and Erasmus
What the two sides are discussing goes far beyond tariffs: laying data cables connecting Europe and Canada; jointly building data centers, cloud storage and satellite networks placed beyond the reach of American tech giants; building new pipelines in Canada to send natural gas to the East Coast and on to Europe; using icebreakers to open Arctic shipping routes for fertilizer. They also plan to entwine Canadian and EU research institutions to create a network of academic and scientific output that can rival the American system. Canada is even pushing to join the EU's Erasmus student exchange program — the show says this is a big deal in Europe, and has led to a lot of marriages. If a generation of Canadians goes to school in Paris, Spain and Italy, and a generation of Italians comes to Ottawa, Montreal and Vancouver, then what's being discussed isn't just economics but social ties deeper than the flow of natural gas and minerals.

17:45 The EU's red line: no one can think you can quit the club and keep the perks
For Europe, Canada is a "shiny new toy": it has raw materials, critical minerals and energy Europe has long coveted, its values are similar, and Carney speaking French and English and making his first trip to Paris and London rather than Washington means a lot to Europeans. But the risks are just as clear. The EU is haunted by Brexit, and its long-standing red line is that "no one can ever be allowed to think they can leave this club and keep enjoying the benefits" — if big countries start quitting and demanding a Canada-style deal, that would be fatal for the EU. So the puzzle Carney has to solve is: get Canada a large share of trade and connectivity benefits without creating a precedent that lets a country like Italy say, "we don't like these regulations, let's quit and become a Canada-style member — no rules but all the benefits."

19:54 The real pain hasn't arrived yet; the White House bets geography decides fate
There are concerns inside Canada: joining an associate membership with an undefined status means how much sovereignty do you give up, which regulations do you accept, what happens to immigration — conservative voters and mainstream newspaper columnists are all asking. But the bigger fear is the cost of decoupling from the US, because so far it's only a war of words and the real pain hasn't hit the Canadian economy: two-thirds of exports depend on the US, and that's a lot of people's businesses and jobs. The White House's judgment is that geography is destiny, Canada is right there, decades of economic ties are real, and in the end they will pull Canada back to the table — flirting with Europe can't change economic reality. You can't force Canadian businesses to do business in Europe when a few miles (kilometers, in Canada) across the border sits an attractive market.

item.title: Ranking Psychology's Classic Experiments: Many Conclusions Don't Survive Replication
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-verybad-心理学经典实验排等级-很多结论撑不过复现/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-verybad-心理学经典实验排等级-很多结论撑不过复现/
item.description: Milgram's shock experiment still replicates, which is itself absurd; and the Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 subjects total, so even if they got it right, they got it right by accident.
item.content:encoded:
Milgram's shock experiment still replicates, which is itself absurd; and the Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 subjects total, so even if they got it right, they got it right by accident.

Two philosophers plus a psychologist rank classic studies from D to S, and along the way settle accounts with the replication crisis, Zimbardo's fraudulent original notes, and small samples.

10:08 Milgram still replicating is itself absurd
Milgram recruited New Haven workers into a Yale basement, got them to believe they were shocking another person, with voltage labeled up to 300 volts and marked dangerous; the person being "shocked" was actually a trained actor, and about 65% of them pressed all the way to the end. He ran a large number of variants, manipulating whether the experimenter wore a white coat, the distance to the person being shocked, and which university's name was on the door. The study directly rewrote psychology's ethics review system; today this kind of experiment can't be done. Dave says that a social psychology study from the 50s or 60s that still replicates is itself "[ __ ] banana," which is why it goes in S tier — he's using replication as the bar, not fame.

29:20 The Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 people
Darley and Batson had seminary students go to the other side of campus to deliver the parable of the Good Samaritan, with a visibly injured, groaning person asking for help placed along the way; the manipulated variable was the time pressure they were under. It turned out time pressure predicted whether they stopped to help better than what topic they were going to speak on. But Dave points out that the whole experiment had only 40 subjects total, and once split into groups the samples were tiny. He lumps this kind of study together with the phone booth coin-drop experiment as a common disease of 60s and 70s social psychology: severely underpowered, "even if they were right, they were right by accident." Paul says it's great as material for making people reflect on human nature, but as a scientific finding he doesn't trust it, and gives it D tier.

48:38 On the cloth mother, mothers already knew
Harlow separated infant monkeys from their mothers and built two surrogate mothers: a wire frame with a bottle attached, and a soft, huggable cloth mother that provided no milk. Except when they had to nurse, the infants stayed on the cloth mother the rest of the time. This refuted the behaviorist explanation that infants love their mothers because the mother provides food, and supported the role of contact comfort. The episode clarifies that Harlow did not shock the monkeys; what's hard to watch is the footage of frightened infants lunging at the cloth mother and clinging on for dear life. He also called the isolation device the "pit of despair" and the restraint device the "rape rack" in published articles, and the reaction on the show was "he's just a psychopath." Tamler argues for the lowest score, not because of cruelty, but because these studies didn't show anything any mother could have told you by intuition after being asked one question.

1:10:52 The prison experiment's author was coaching guards to abuse
Original notes and recordings dug up on the Stanford prison experiment show that Zimbardo himself was coaching the people randomly assigned to be guards to engage in abusive behavior. If the intended story of the study is "put people in this role and they spontaneously become sadists," then on the available evidence that conclusion is highly suspect — he didn't report how much he pushed them. David thinks this is close to scientific fraud, groups it with "dog torturers," and no longer teaches it. But David also cautions: across the Milgram and Asch series, people differ — some said "screw you, I'm not doing it" at the lowest shock level. Tamler adds that when he interviewed Zimbardo, Zimbardo talked about Milgram, saying Milgram didn't do psychological screening and some of the people who showed up might have been sociopaths, while Zimbardo claimed he did screen, using that to prove these were normal people.

1:15:59 Even adults fail the false belief task
The false belief task comes from Premack and Woodruff's paper "Does the Chimpanzee Have a Theory of Mind"; Dennett proposed this design in a commentary: Sally puts a toy in a box and leaves, Anne moves it to a basket, and you ask where Sally will look for it when she returns. Children before age three or four say the place where the toy actually is, and around age five they start getting it right; this shift from failure to success is one of the most robust findings in all of developmental psychology. But Paul and Susan Birch tested adults and found adults find it hard too — there's an immediate intuition pointing at "where the thing actually is" that has to be inhibited; he demos it live in his intro course and about a third of students get it wrong. What bothers Tamler is that once the paradigm got hot, the whole field shifted from that interesting question to the methodology itself, and the test became the construct.

1:24:06 To deny the methods are all broken, you have to accept ESP
Daryl Bem published a paper in a top social psychology journal in 2011 claiming to have found precognition: subjects first rated their preference for unfamiliar Chinese characters, and only afterward were shown emotional images as primes, and it turned out that characters later positively primed had been rated higher beforehand. He made all materials and data public, and Paul thinks he genuinely believed the result. Bem's defense is a dilemma: if you say my study isn't a good study, then almost no study in social psychology is a good study — so either admit your methods are reliable and accept ESP, or admit the methods are unreliable. Paul says he was furious at the time: this would overturn our entire understanding of space and time, and you want to accept it on a p less than 0.05. This is also the driving force behind the Bayesian countermovement in psychology: results should be compared against prior plausibility, not against 0.05.

1:29:09 Delayed gratification may measure trust, not self-control
Mischel and Ebbesen had preschoolers choose between taking a small reward immediately and waiting for two. What's more interesting in the original study is that some children spontaneously used strategies — imagining the marshmallow as a white cloud, singing, distracting themselves; Tamler says they were "tying themselves to the mast." The problem comes later: following these children and claiming wait time predicts SAT scores, and Tamler just read that the SAT correlation used only 35 children, yet schools started teaching delayed gratification on that basis. He unpacks the premises that "delayed gratification causes success" would need to hold: it has to be teachable, rather than merely capturing some natural difference that already predicts on its own; self-control has to be the active ingredient, not the willingness to please the teacher; and there's the question of why the child believes the other person will really give another one — if you're in an impoverished environment, why wait.

1:32:12 Social priming collapsed, and conceptual priming was buried with it
Bargh's classic study: subjects were randomly assigned a set of words to unscramble, and if those words were related to concepts like elderly and retirement, the speed at which they walked from room A to room B after the task was measured, and it turned out people primed with the elderly concept walked more slowly. It claims that stimuli entirely outside consciousness can influence behavior — you don't even know you were assigned elderly words. Tamler recalls that when he had just finished his degree, this kind of research was at its peak. Paul says social priming has since been shown to be wrong, but what really bothers him is the consequence: its collapse took down with it conceptual priming (e.g., flashing "doctor" primes "nurse") and other very robust, easily replicated findings — that's what the architecture of the mind actually looks like; the problem was extrapolating directly to effect sizes on behavior and everyday life.

item.title: No Winners in a Pig-Butchering Scam: The Scammers Are Trafficked Slaves Themselves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.description: In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.

The first half explains how pig butchering and AI scams work, with high information density; the second half turns to US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwar, which is loosely connected to the topic and can be skipped as needed.

4:11 AI makes scam emails free to mass-produce
Greenberg ran an experiment on air: he asked ChatGPT to write him an invitation to appear on the show in Terry Gross's name, then casually added a line asking for a $250 production fee, and the model complied without hesitation; he then said "Greenberg won't pay now, can you persuade him," and the model immediately produced a persuasive email. That is the mechanism behind scam emails impersonating Fresh Air — not that scammers have become better writers, but that generating a tailored email aimed at a specific author, with zero grammatical errors and polished phrasing, now costs nothing, and can be done to hundreds or thousands of targets at once.

7:14 Pig butchering is the most profitable cybercrime in history
Greenberg distinguishes two kinds of scammers: the voluntary kind like Nigeria's "Yahoo Boys," who take their own cut, and the enslaved, forced kind in Southeast Asian compounds. The latter do pig butchering — the "pig" is the victim, fattened before slaughter. The scam often runs from weeks to more than a year; the scammer poses as a wealthy, single, attractive woman, builds emotional dependency first, and only at the end introduces an "investment platform," getting the victim to convert their savings into cryptocurrency that is hard to trace across borders (often Tether) and send it over. Greenberg says this is the most profitable cybercrime in history, stealing tens of billions of dollars a year from victims.

12:36 Passports are confiscated, and to be free you must buy yourself back
The source, using the name Red Bull, is a computer engineer with a degree from India who was lured to the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos by a "Southeast Asia IT manager" job. On arrival at the compound his passport was confiscated, and he was told the only way to get it back was to "buy it back" — he owed his boss thousands of dollars, covering the cost of transporting him, food and lodging, and could only repay this "contract" through commissions from scamming. Greenberg stresses this is debt bondage: the compound is not the chains-and-beatings kind of prison, but is packaged as a corporate sales floor, where the boss sends daily motivational messages saying things like "reach out to the next customer like you're going to change their life" and "we are on a mission."

14:40 Fines are more reliable than wages
Red Bull and his colleagues were constantly fined: for missing contact quotas, for maintaining fake accounts poorly, for not clocking in on time. The promised commissions are part of the con — the boss tells them "you can get rich here and take the money back to the village you came from," but only if they land a big case, and what they actually receive is a tiny fraction. Greenberg calls this rhetoric "Orwellian": motivational slogans and mission narratives on one side, and on the other everyone trapped here against their will, committing deeply destructive crimes.

15:45 Video calls run on a dedicated face-swap model
Red Bull said everyone in the compound was trained to use ChatGPT and the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek to come up with new topics, polish their language, never run out of graceful phrasing, even write little motivational poems, and find just the right goodnight line. More critical is video: the boss required them to discourage victims from video calls as much as possible and stall with excuses; when stalling failed, the compound had a dedicated room and a model who handled video all day, using face-swap software to change the model's face into the photo originally sent to the victim. Greenberg says this kind of software is not perfect, but by the video-call stage the victim wants so badly to believe it is real that they overlook the flaws.

18:54 The next step is fully autonomous AI pig butchering
Greenberg judges that AI is currently just a tool for human scammers, but the next step — already beginning to appear — is fully autonomous AI scams. He cites a case from an Anthropic report the previous week: a Chinese group built 20 dating apps populated entirely by AI, where victims must keep paying to continue the conversation, and "most" of the other side are actually fully autonomous large models. He also mentions a study showing that in most parts of the scam process, AI is better than a real person at building relationships — more responsive, more invested, more attentive — and that is exactly what the scam is doing for the vast majority of the time before it reaches the endgame of asking for money.

23:08 Thirty people, three months, only $2.2 million
Greenberg gives a concrete scale: Red Bull's group of about 30 people earned only about $2.2 million in total over the three months that Red Bull recorded and leaked to Wired. This shows pig butchering is a game of probability — a single group's output is limited, but Laos alone has dozens of such compounds, and Cambodia and Myanmar have more, and together they add up to the billions of dollars a year. Greenberg also notes that Red Bull himself was a "very inefficient scammer," so he was penniless, eating only the compound canteen's rice and vegetables that tasted of strange chemicals, constantly sick, and disgusted by what he was doing.

24:12 Forging a police letter to escape, then beaten when it was seen through
Red Bull's escape attempt was to forge a letter from the police in his home region of India, saying he was under investigation and had to return home to deal with it, or the boss would be in trouble too. Greenberg advised him not to do it, but he went ahead, and the forgery was immediately seen through. The boss locked him in a room, beat him, kicked him, denied him food, interrogated him, and even gave him a glass of water with white powder dissolved in it and forced him to drink it — Greenberg guesses it was some kind of stimulant, making him talk more while his skin broke out in hives. They never found out he was in contact with a journalist; Greenberg says if they had, he would certainly have been killed.

item.title: Entropy Doesn't Mean Getting Messier: Oil and Water Layering, Frost Flowers, and Other Spontaneous Order
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-intotheimpossi-熵增不等于变乱-油水分层-霜花结晶都是自发的秩序/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-intotheimpossi-熵增不等于变乱-油水分层-霜花结晶都是自发的秩序/
item.category: Into the Impossible With Brian Keating
item.description: The second law of thermodynamics is usually told as "things get messier," but oil separating from water, beach sorting, and frost on a window are all spontaneous order. Carlo Rovelli says low entropy may not be in the universe but in how we look at it.
item.content:encoded:
The second law of thermodynamics is usually told as "things get messier," but oil separating from water, beach sorting, and frost on a window are all spontaneous order. Carlo Rovelli says low entropy may not be in the universe but in how we look at it.

This episode is medium-to-high in information density. The first half, on entropy and time, is the most valuable; the second half, on AI and free will, is more speculative. The ad segment can be skipped.

2:03 Oil separating from water isn't anti-entropy — it's entropy producing order
Rovelli uses a set of everyday images to dismantle the popular claim that "entropy = disorder": water and vinegar mix into a uniform blend, but water and oil separate into layers; on a beach, fine sand and pebbles sort themselves apart; frost on a window grows regular structures on its own. He says that under a properly defined notion of "order," a great many things in nature become spontaneously ordered if you just leave them alone. This doesn't overturn the second law; it says popular science draws the correspondence between "order" and "entropy" too crudely. He points out in particular that the complexity of biology and the structure of the Earth's surface are often misread as "anti-entropy," when in fact entropy growth itself is constantly producing order.

7:12 Low entropy may not be in the universe but in your coarse graining
Rovelli proposes a hypothesis he has put into a paper himself but isn't sure is right or wrong: low entropy means "special," but what is special is not the state of the universe — it's coarse graining itself. Coarse graining is a perspective: looking at only some variables and not all the details. If the hypothesis holds, the universe can be in a completely arbitrary state, yet from our perspective, which sees only some variables, it appears low-entropy in the direction we call "the past." This turns the "initial low-entropy boundary condition" from a fact about the universe into a question about how an observer slices up information.

12:16 You can be in two places at once, just not to yourself
Rovelli pushes quantum superposition onto people: if quantum mechanics is universal, Brian can be in a superposition of Los Angeles and San Francisco, and Carlo can measure that interference. But to Brian himself, quantum mechanics never tells you that you're in a superposition — you look around and see either San Diego or Los Angeles. So "where you are" is two different things for you and for me. He compares this to Galileo's discovery that velocity is relative: saying "velocity is zero" actually omits "relative to the Earth." What quantum mechanics says is that all properties must be understood relative to something.

19:34 Galileo got the tides wrong using his own relativity principle
Rovelli uses Galileo's tidal model to show that "having an idea" and "pushing the idea to the end" are two different things. Galileo thought the combination of the Earth's revolution around the Sun and its rotation stirred the seas and produced the tides. But Rovelli points out that revolution is, to first order, uniform straight-line motion, and rotation alone can't produce an effect either, so the tides can't come from this — what actually explains the tides is Newton. Galileo himself violated precisely the relativity principle he had discovered. Rovelli says Einstein was the same: after writing general relativity in 1915, he later wrote a paper denying gravitational waves (and corrected it after a referee sent it back), and insisted the Schwarzschild singularity was the end of the world — an error he never corrected until he died.

31:06 Without dissipation you can't record anything
Rovelli says that already in classical mechanics he found a fact that made him "see a light": if you want to model a measuring device with classical mechanics — a barometer, say, or a device that records whether a ball is on the left or the right — you can't, unless you introduce dissipation. A ball dropped into a box will bounce back up; it has to dissipate to stop and leave a record. So measurement is essentially a statistical process that requires dissipation, and this was already true before quantum mechanics — it isn't peculiar to quantum mechanics. This directly answers the puzzle of "unitary evolution is reversible, so where does irreversibility come from": recording itself requires that something be thrown away.

33:45 A chess program deliberates, and so do you
Rovelli uses his chess computer to take apart free will: the computer is deterministic, and given its internal state and the opponent's move, its output is necessarily predetermined. But why does it still spend time enumerating all possible moves and evaluating them one by one? Because the only way to reach that result is to go through this evaluation process, and that process is called deliberation. He says it's foolish to say it isn't deliberating, because deliberation is exactly this. Brian is the same: without going through this complex process, he wouldn't make the decision to start a project or choose a career. So-called freedom is not violating the laws of nature; it is precisely the fact of "having gone through deliberation."

40:56 In principle yes, not now, and within two years he doubts it
Asked whether a machine could have Einstein's "happiest thought" (the equivalence principle in free fall), Rovelli answers in three layers: in principle yes, he doesn't think humans are so special as to be unreproducible; not now; and within two years he's skeptical, though he has no hard evidence that it's impossible. He mentions that last week he had Claude do something his PhD student hadn't finished in a month, and Claude finished it in half an hour, so the capability is beyond doubt. But he says Claude didn't invent the equivalence principle, and doing that within two years he finds hard. At the same time he states plainly that there is a lot of hype in AI.

56:45 Ten years and unlimited funding, he'd build a roomful of Josephson junctions
Asked what he would do with "ten years and unlimited funding," Rovelli's answer is not a telescope or a collider but a large room full of Josephson junctions, plus an engineering team. The reason: loop quantum gravity predicts particles of Planck mass, possibly dark matter candidates, with a mass roughly equal to a small piece of hair or a flea egg. He says we already know the direction, mass, and interaction strength of dark matter clouds — only extremely feeble Newtonian gravity, but Josephson junctions could catch it with simple physics. He thinks it's technically feasible within ten years; what's missing is only the money.

item.title: Supersonic Passenger Flight Stalled for Fifty Years — the Engine, Not Aerodynamics, Was the Blocker
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.description: Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to data centers to generate power first.
item.content:encoded:
Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to data centers to generate power first.

A founder's first-person account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building his own engine and pivoting into data-center power generation, with specific numbers and regulatory detail, high information density.

5:12 Bend the sonic boom and the ban disappears
Boom's solution to the sonic boom is not to make the aircraft quiet, but to use the atmosphere's own refractive capacity to redirect the boom back up into the sky. Blake calls this boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff: the boom is still generated at the aircraft as usual, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. This works below Mach 1.3 — that is, 50% faster than today. So you can't go full speed over land, but a 9 a.m. departure from New York landing in San Francisco at 9:30 still holds. Over the ocean no one is listening, so full speed is fine. Push the logic to its limit and you get the line: if there's no sonic boom at all, there's nothing to argue about.

5:12 From executive order to act of Congress, unanimous
The U.S. ban on supersonic flight over land, in place since 1973, ended on June 6 last year. But Blake knew an executive order can in theory be overturned by the next person, so he turned to pushing Congress. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He put the significance plainly: supersonic isn't a partisan issue, which is the only way to get that kind of vote. For a hardware company that has to span multiple administrations on a timeline measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to law turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

6:12 Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, Boom split publicly with Rolls-Royce, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch, and not just design it — even the hardest parts, like turbine blades, they make themselves. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing have to be done together, and if you want to reindustrialize America you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed to run at high temperature, full power, for long durations at Mach 1.7, once you take off the front fan and bolt a generator on the back, is a power generation device.

8:13 The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
Boom's engine's first application isn't in the sky, it's on the ground. Take off the fan, swap in a generator at the back, put it in a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation — and because the engine core was designed to run at high temperature, it needs no water. Blake specifically calls out that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, the target is multiple gigawatts a year, and more than 10 gigawatts added to the grid over the next five years. The financial significance of this path: before the supersonic airliner gets its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell — and it's selling to the buyer who currently has the most money.

10:14 Run on the ground first, then fly
Boom putting the engine to work in ground power generation first has an engineering side effect: it will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run for enormous numbers of hours on the ground before ever being installed and flown. Blake admits many hard problems remain and success isn't guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over the ocean, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — normally an aviation engine's validation comes from accumulating flight hours, and Boom has moved validation to the ground and to data-center scenarios, effectively having another market pay the test costs for the aviation business.

10:38 Transatlantic round trip, breakeven fare $3,500
The numbers Blake gives: a Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, actual ticket price probably higher, and every extra dollar is United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom wants all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he says explicitly that ‘fast matters more than predictable’, can't give a firm date, and only promises to deliver at the earliest time physically possible — from the outside that looks like around 2030. There's a tradeoff worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it's unpredictable, trading certainty for speed.

13:15 Data-center demand is so large they'll auction it
Asked whether the data-center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and says there are tens of gigawatts of demand in his inbox. The first engine fires up next month, and then they plan to auction off all the capacity. Asked whether he's talked to Elon, whether it's for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this segment is that it gives an anomalous supply-demand signal: for a power product that isn't in mass production yet, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing mechanism has shifted from a quote to an auction.

16:19 Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Office Thursday
Blake recaps the speed of this regulatory push: Monday, break the sound barrier, post it, Elon reposts, fly to Washington that night to start the legalization lobbying, and by the time he lands there's already a White House invitation; Tuesday, into the West Wing; Thursday, the aircraft model goes into the Oval Office — and it's still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he thinks is slow, though he admits another administration would be slower. His assessment of this administration: ‘I like that it moves fast’. This is the most concrete policy-operations sample in the whole episode: how a technical milestone gets converted directly into political attention.

item.title: Why rebranding a charity is more dangerous than rebranding a company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.description: Mercy Corps changed its name to Prosper Global not because its strategy changed, but because the old name no longer fit what it was already doing — yet in conflict zones, a name change can put staff more at risk.
item.content:encoded:
Mercy Corps changed its name to Prosper Global not because its strategy changed, but because the old name no longer fit what it was already doing — yet in conflict zones, a name change can put staff more at risk.

Medium information density. The first half covers the disaster situation and the rebranding logic; the second half, on the erosion of international humanitarian law and AI's entry into aid, is more valuable.

4:21 The name change isn't a strategy change; the old name no longer fits the new business
Jada says an organization's identity grows up like a person's. The name Mercy Corps described the starting point of aid — rushing in to save people, handing out food, casting itself as the ‘benevolent giver’. But when she now talks to potential donors about cash assistance, seed insurance, using blockchain for identity management, they say flat out ‘that has nothing to do with your name’. The name change isn't a change of mission; mission and values are the source of continuity, the name isn't. Prosper Global wants to shorten the conversation and put values up front: we believe everyone has the capacity to prosper, not just survive.

6:31 Rebranding in a conflict zone puts safety on the line
Prosper Global operates in more than 30 countries, many of them remote sub-offices, often in conflict zones. Communities recognize Mercy Corps' colors and know who to look for. The name change means a phased rollout, one country at a time, with locals judging the timing and context. Jada puts it bluntly: they don't rate armed guards, they don't carry weapons, and their ability to work rests entirely on the trust of the communities they serve. So this isn't an ordinary corporate logo swap; in the short term it may put frontline staff more at risk. Interestingly, 90% of staff live in the communities they serve, and many program staff were the first to understand the name change — they don't want to be treated as ‘charity cases’.

8:37 Syria is the best example of the rebranding logic
Jada drove from Aleppo to Damascus and saw rubble the whole way. Syria has just emerged from 14 years of civil war and is one of the few countries in the world where the population is returning rather than leaving, with millions going home at the same time. But many still live in camps, and the communities they return to have no working water systems and destroyed houses. She tells of a woman named Ola: her husband was injured in the war, she didn't work before the war, and her community wasn't used to women doing certain things, so she was forced to take over the farming and start cultivating. Prosper Global helped her with drip irrigation and repairing the local water system; along the way she learned to ride a motorcycle and brought along another group of women. Jada says Syria may be one of the world's rare good-news stories, but it's been forgotten.

10:44 Oil in Hormuz determines whether African farmers plant at all
Prosper Global published a report called From Hormuz to Hunger, tracking how conflict in the Strait of Hormuz ripples into six fragile countries: Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Myanmar, Lebanon. The mechanism is this: these countries depend on Hormuz for basic fuel, and higher fuel prices hit fertilizer supply directly. When Jada was in Sudan, farmers had only a two-to-three-week window to get seeds in the ground, and fuel costs had already risen 60%. When farmers can't figure out what to plant or what inputs they can afford, some decide to abandon the land. This isn't just a problem for now; it cripples next season's food supply too. At the same time, aid agencies themselves are paying higher oil prices, so the same money serves fewer people.

12:47 Ukraine's grain silos are being bombed on purpose
Prosper Global just launched a grain storage project with the UN and the Ukrainian Red Cross. Jada says Ukraine actually had a good harvest this year, but Russia is increasingly targeting civilian and economic infrastructure, especially using drones against grain silos and storage facilities. The logic is straightforward: even with a good harvest, if silos and storage are bombed out, or roads and ports are bombed so grain can't move, that season's income is gone. This is a deliberate attack on that kind of infrastructure. What they do includes providing sleeveless bag storage for grain, helping farmers clear mines, and helping those who lost machinery rebuild or find alternatives. Ukraine was once the breadbasket for many countries; it needs that grain to feed itself and its own economy.

14:47 Prevention is seven times cheaper than disaster response, but no one wants to pay for it
Jada says there's a tendency in the current relationship with the US government to do only life-saving aid, which is actually the least efficient approach.
