Her number: doing prevention, trying to avert a crisis, is about seven times cheaper than intervening afterward. She also mentions they had been ready to rename as Prosper Global before the Trump administration took office, but held off to see how things would go — the funding had already vanished and the whole sector was in a tough spot. Instead they doubled down on helping Americans understand the nature of humanitarian need, what aid looks like today, and correcting a lot of misinformation. She says the key to a leadership moment is intentionality: what are you letting go of, and what are you continuing to build on?

19:59 After USAID evaporated, the sector has to rebuild an architecture
Jada acknowledges they have to do more with less money, but stresses this isn't just about saving money — it's about rebuilding an architecture in a sense. USAID's offices and missions around the world used to carry a huge amount of coordination and information sharing, and now all of that is gone. So the question isn't just ‘can AI help’; it's that the sector's entire coordination layer has been pulled out. She says AI can't physically deliver supplies for you, and it has limits in knowledge, but it's useful at the program level: accessing best practices, more precisely targeting what a community needs, anticipating certain needs. They haven't found that ‘magic solution’ yet, but they're talking to AI companies, hoping to build something together that truly changes humanitarian aid.

23:02 International humanitarian law is eroding, starting with Ukraine
Jada says the checks and balances of international humanitarian law are being tested and violated, and that this is a broader trend. She believes the first case seen as a deliberate pattern was Russia's invasion of Ukraine — attacks on ports, bridges and other civilian infrastructure traditionally off-limits soon appeared. Then the pattern spread to the way war is waged in Sudan, and they believe violations of international law are also occurring in Gaza. She notes it took the deaths and destruction of millions after World War II to bring these rules into being: no collective punishment, people must be able to go to school, have hospital networks, civilians shouldn't pay the price. Now these rules are being violated everywhere. She says even the phrase ‘international humanitarian law’ sounds like Greek to many people.

item.title: In the AI Era, the Most Valuable Thing Isn't Intelligence — It's the Audit Trail
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.description: Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever lays pipe into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.
item.content:encoded:
Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever lays pipe into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.

Worth hearing for vertical AI founders, investment banking/PE practitioners, and enterprise software investors. The first half's product history is middling in information density; the back half on pricing, auditability, and sales mechanics is worth more.

2:03 Model companies are refineries; vertical companies are chemical plants
Gabe reasons from Dario's line: if tomorrow a whole data center full of geniuses appeared at the door of Goldman, Millennium, Citadel, these institutions would still take a long time to figure out how to change the way they work and how to wire it into their systems. So he thinks the biggest challenge for every great investor over the next five years is not getting access to intelligence, but wiring AI into the investment lifecycle. This also explains why he isn't worried about Anthropic and OpenAI: finance is a collection of niches, each with different data, definitions, and regulatory requirements, and for Anthropic to stop and pick up this coin would be pulling over on the road from $100 billion in revenue to $1 trillion.

4:04 Applied AI companies have a first-mover disadvantage
Gabe says companies that did applied AI early were actually at a disadvantage: you think you know where the world is going, you build the product for that end state, but the models aren't there yet, and users try it and just say ‘this is garbage.’ Rogo went through this phase itself. His judgment is that if your read on the end state is right and you keep building toward it, the moment the models catch up is the magic moment. He ties Rogo's product eras directly to model eras: 01 Pro was the first version reliable enough to at least serve as a search tool; by Opus 4.5, and from late 2025 into early 2026, the models can basically do anything a junior investment or banking professional does, provided you give the right instructions and context.

6:06 The MD annotating on an iPad is the real last mile
Gabe gives an example as concrete as it gets: the typical workflow of an investment banking MD is to email deck comments to an analyst, and Rogo lets that MD email the comments to an AI analyst, get the revised draft back in 20 minutes instead of two days, automatically notify the junior analysts on the deal, and show a full audit trail of every small change. He points out the key: this finance professional hasn't logged into a computer in ten years, but he has an iPad, and he knows how to annotate on an iPad. That kind of product detail for a specific end user can only come from someone with a spidey sense for the job.

16:57 The harness matters more than the model itself
Gabe compares Claude Code and Claude Cowork with ChatGPT: the models are actually similar, but Claude's harness and presentation are far better, letting the model exercise more long-horizon capability, and so usage and expansion took off. He extends the analogy to the brain: humans have high agency not just because of raw memory, IQ, and knowledge, but because there are a bunch of microservices in the head — how to store knowledge, how to retrieve it, how to trigger it, and emotion is one way of triggering a microservice. A great investor's judgment comes from seeing something in the market that triggers the memory of some event, leading to a creative decision. Those microservices are what vertical companies have to build.

23:43 Skip from per-seat pricing straight to outcome pricing
Rogo today is classic enterprise software: priced per seat, because buyers are used to comparing it to Bloomberg, FactSet, Capital IQ, PitchBook, and every deal signed needs an AE plus a solutions architect to shake hands and explain the integration. Gabe says Anthropic can sell to them easily, with spend rising exponentially and no human involvement, because it's a token-consumption model; but many industries can't ride the token-consumption wave, and Rogo is one of them, so it has to build its GTM machine at five times the speed. His pricing judgment is that every company goes through two pricing revolutions: first to usage based, then to outcome based. He'd rather skip tokens and usage and ask the customer directly: how much do you charge per good investment idea? Per quarterly LP report? Per investment banking CIM?

31:19 Auditability matters more than accuracy
Gabe says accuracy is of course still super important, but auditability matters more than accuracy, and the two are often conflated. The logic: if the answer is wrong and you don't know how to check it or see where it came from, then whether it's accurate or not you can't use it, because you don't trust it. Conversely, if it's right most of the time, and even when it's wrong you can clearly see the assumptions and the data sources, it's still actionable and still saves time. As tools move from copilot to autopilot — not just retrieving information but having agency, actually making investment decisions or sending emails — you have to be able to look back at why it decided the way it did, because you need to debug it, just as when an individual investor makes a bad decision you check whether the data input was wrong or someone lied to him. In regulated capital markets, a decision you can't explain simply doesn't pass.

34:48 The company brain is called Shrek, and every conversation is recorded
Every conversation inside Rogo is recorded, and new hires are told on day one ‘you are always being recorded,’ and that content is filtered into the company brain, named Shrek because the engineers thought that was funny. There's a dashboard showing the ‘swamp’ of what everyone is working on, connected to the company's various systems, with a very clear sense of company goals, values, what needs to be delivered to customers, and the north star metric, so it can shape every answer and deliverable. It's both passive and active: you can go in and ask ‘how do I pitch the value proposition and savings of model routing to a large institution,’ and it pulls the information out; it also proactively reminds you, ‘Patrick, I see you're meeting this private credit firm on Thursday, here's what you should know, the use cases that will resonate, and the ROI metrics companies you've worked with before want to hear.’ Gabe says this is the core problem of enablement: suck information in, and give it out when people need it.

42:18 What it's like to be rejected by 40 investors in a row
Gabe says the hardest low point was the A round: at the time there were no star investors on the cap table, David Tisch introduced him to 40 investors, he met Sequoia, Kleiner, Benchmark and others, and all 40 passed. And not the send-a-deck-no-interest kind — it was ‘interesting, meet Gabe,’ ‘like Gabe, chat for an hour,’ ‘come to IC,’ ‘let's grab a meal,’ ‘come back over the weekend’ — and then ‘we've decided not to invest.’ He says that phase had nothing to do with anything except you, like being dumped by 40 girlfriends, each time you fell in love and each time the other person said it wasn't for you. In the end Thrive didn't invest either; Keith Rabois came about a month after everyone had passed, and Gabe asked Keith back: if this isn't a contrarian bet, why do all your friends say it's a bad idea and none of them believe in me? He sums up the three reasons investors passed: underestimating the finance TAM, the product genuinely being bad at the time, and not having enough data points to believe he could chew glass and ship the next version.

item.title: The Rocky Statue Is Not Art, Yet Philadelphia Cannot Tear It Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.description: A bronze made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — and what finally saved it was not artistic merit but that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.
item.content:encoded:
A bronze made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — and what finally saved it was not artistic merit but that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.

Thirty minutes that carries one complete narrative line: class, artistic authority, race and monument politics, dense with detail and almost no filler.

4:09 Bronze instead of foam is what decided its fate
In Rocky III there is a scene: a fictional mayor stands on the museum steps and dedicates a statue to Philadelphia. The production could have had the art department build a prop out of painted plastic and foam and toss it in a dumpster after shooting. Stallone didn't do that — he paid $53,000 to have the artist A. Thomas Schaumburg cast the statue in bronze. Laura Holzman says that choice was crucial: the material wasn't something you throw away after filming, it was an art material. Stallone went to high school in Philadelphia, called Rocky a ‘euphemism’ for the city, and then offered to donate the 1,800-pound statue to Philadelphia to stand permanently at the top of the steps. It is precisely because it was bronze and not foam that the next fifty years of fighting were even possible.

10:25 The root of the opposition was Philadelphia wanting to be Athens
The museum leadership opposed it most fiercely, and their reasons were far bigger than aesthetics. Philadelphia's glory days had long faded by the early 20th century, and by the 1976 Bicentennial it was the city that could never shake its bad luck: crumbling infrastructure, corrupt local politics. In the 1980s the arts world wanted to remake Philadelphia into a cultural metropolis and restore the title a famous architect had given it — ‘the Athens of the Western world.’ They had bet heavily on the city's most important museum, and they did not think a nine-foot-tall, sharply abdomened boxer could carry Philadelphia toward that dream. The art commission's chairman, F. Eugene Dixon Jr., wrote to colleagues that the statue standing temporarily on the steps was fine, but that placing it permanently in the courtyard — ‘I hope you're joking.’ In the winter of 1980 the commission voted 6 to 2 against permanent placement, and the remaining two votes were for banning it from the steps outright.

12:34 Thousands of signatures are no match for eight people with votes
What brought the statue back to Philadelphia from Los Angeles was a grassroots campaign. A local truck driver, Art Gorman, was one of its biggest champions — Mark Bowden describes him as a straight-shooting Philadelphian from a blue-collar neighborhood, thinking: who are these self-appointed connoisseurs to tell us what we can see on the steps of the art museum? At the end of 1980 he drafted a petition, all in capital letters, knocked on doors for thousands of signatures, and drew a pile of media coverage. The show says it plainly: the story got told as blue-collar Philadelphia versus elite high-culture Philadelphia, a ‘slobs versus snobs’ narrative. But the petition could not change the commission's basic position — the snobs were still the ones voting.

13:34 The prop crew had bolted the statue into the ground with steel rods
Rocky III opened in May 1982, and the art commission allowed the statue back on the steps only for the premiere; once it was over, it had to go. But the production company simply left it there, the city wouldn't pay to move it, and the museum was left to deal with it. Months later the movers finally came and found an obstacle: the statue was bolted to the sidewalk with steel rods driven several feet into the ground — ‘as if the filmmakers intended it to stay there forever.’ In the end the statue was pried loose and hauled five miles away to the Spectrum arena in South Philadelphia, where it stood with other athletes' statues. Most people thought the fight was over, but over the next twenty-five years Stallone repeatedly asked for it to return to the museum, and every time he got the same answer: no.

15:35 One phone call did more than twenty years of aesthetic debate
In 2006 things moved: the mayor was pushing a batch of public-space renovation projects, Stallone was about to release his first Rocky film in 16 years, and the statue was sitting in a warehouse because the city was building a new sports complex. Stallone's friend Jimmy Binns — who had appeared in the sequels and was a well-connected Philadelphia lawyer — called the mayor and asked whether he'd help get the statue back to the museum. Binns recounted the conversation: he asked the mayor, do those museum trustees invite you to their homes for cocktails on Sundays? The mayor laughed and said no. Binns said, then to hell with them. The mayor said, alright, to hell with them. With the mayor behind it, even the Philadelphia Museum of Art started to give ground, and the compromise they worked out was: the statue returns to the museum permanently, but not at the top of the steps — a little off to the side at the bottom. The only remaining obstacle was the art commission, which held the final vote.

19:46 By 2006 the debate was no longer about art
In May 2006 the commission announced it might move the statue, setting off a new round of public discussion. City official Harris Baum argued against it on a local NPR call-in show, on the grounds that the Parkway was to be developed into a cultural district like Paris's, ‘but that is not a work of art.’ The response he got was completely different from the 1980s: listeners didn't want to talk about art. Judy said the statue was an image of the blue-collar spirit; Jack, calling from Lansdale, said ideally he'd want it at the top of the steps, but a bunch of pretentious old guys in wigs would never let that happen, and he called Baum a snob and an insult to the audience. Baum was fighting the battle of twenty years earlier. On September 6, 2006, the art commission voted 6 to 2 in favor, and the minutes read: the majority believed the statue's iconic symbolic meaning had earned it a place in the city's identity. Less than a week later the statue was unveiled, fitted with nighttime lighting, and lifted onto a brand-new granite base.

26:14 The real champion's steps are called the Rocky steps
The 2015 Charleston church shooting, in which nine people died, set off a national reckoning with racist symbols, and the wind reached Philadelphia: the Columbus statue and the statue of former mayor Frank Rizzo — known for violent policing and racist demagogy — became targets. When Monument Lab asked Philadelphians what kind of monuments they wanted to build, some began questioning whether Rocky was appropriate: Philadelphia has a real boxing history, and those boxers were mostly Black, including heavyweight champion Joe Frazier, who beat Muhammad Ali in a fight watched by more than 300 million people. The show points out that the two most famous things in the first Rocky training montage — running up the museum steps and punching raw meat — actually came from Frazier's real training routine. Frazier got a statue in 2015, but many Philadelphians feel the twelve-foot bronze falls far short of a real champion: ‘His image isn't on the tour buses, and the steps he ran up are called the Rocky steps.’

28:21 In the monument reckoning, Rocky became the city's emotional container
After George Floyd was killed in 2020, Philadelphia's largest Black Lives Matter demonstrations set out from the art museum steps every day, with thousands of protesters gathering right beside the Rocky statue. By then it was already a monument, and by rights it should have faced the same scrutiny — a statue of a fictional white movie character that had taken the place of a real Black champion, its days should have been numbered. But no one tore it down; instead they folded it in: someone hung a sign reading ‘no justice, no peace’ on it, early in the pandemic it was given a face mask, later a Ukrainian flag, and when the Eagles' Brandon Graham retired his cleats were hung on it. Paul Farber saw the most contradictory scene: a Black family posing for a photo all raising Black Power fists, and three or four people later, a group of white men in their early twenties raising white power gestures — the two things happening almost simultaneously without conflict.

item.title: Vitamin K Refusal Rates Have Doubled, and Infant Brain Hemorrhage Is Preventable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.description: Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular injection drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates have risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.
item.content:encoded:
Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular injection drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates have risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.

High information density: it covers both the clinical mechanics of newborn hemorrhage and the discovery of vitamin K, plus how a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust. The back half, on who refuses and why communication fails, is the most valuable part.

20:34 Every newborn is born deficient in vitamin K
Vitamin K does not cross the placenta effectively, so even if the mother supplements during pregnancy, the newborn's vitamin K-dependent clotting factors do not rise appreciably. Add an immature gut microbiome, very little self-synthesized K2, and breast milk averaging only about 2.5 micrograms per liter of vitamin K, and a exclusively breastfed infant takes in less than 1 microgram a day for the first six months. The result is that every newborn is at high risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. This is not an outlier phenomenon; it is physiological normality.

22:35 Late bleeding often comes with no warning, straight to brain hemorrhage
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns comes in three types: early, within 24 hours of birth; classic, within the first week; and late, from one week to six months. Late is the most dangerous: about 60% of cases are intracranial hemorrhage, and there is often no warning bleed beforehand, just sudden brain hemorrhage, seizures or unresponsiveness. Mortality ranges from 50% to 60% depending on era and country, with modern figures around 20%. That is why the value of a single preventive shot cannot be measured by ‘the bleeding probability is low.’

25:46 One intramuscular shot pushes the risk to near zero
Since 2003 in the US, and in the vast majority of medical societies and public health agencies worldwide, a single intramuscular vitamin K injection at birth is recommended. It provides a stable supply through the first few months, cutting late bleeding risk from 4 to 7 cases per 100,000 live births (some countries report as high as 80) to about 0.4. Infants who receive no prophylaxis are 81 times more likely to suffer late bleeding than those who do. Oral regimens also reduce risk significantly, but require multiple doses, are affected by absorption and vomiting, are less effective than injection, and no oral formulation is approved by regulators in the US.

44:27 How a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust
In the postwar research climate, informed consent and patient protections had not yet entered the picture, and the logic was ‘vitamin is harmless and possibly beneficial, so give it to all premature infants.’ In the mid-1950s Britain gave some premature infants up to 60 milligrams of synthetic vitamin K, after which jaundice, hemolysis and kernicterus rose, and several infants died. The formulation was withdrawn and the dose dropped back to 1 milligram, but confidence had been shaken: of more than 16,000 infants born in Britain in a single week in 1970, only 20% received vitamin K. This history shows the fallout from a single overdose incident can last decades.

46:31 The 1990s leukemia scare still has not cleared
In the early 1990s two British studies linked intramuscular vitamin K to later leukemia risk, and the reaction was swift and strong: some countries switched to recommending oral dosing and reserved injections for the highest-risk infants, and British injection rates fell from 58% in 1988 to 38% in 1993. But the two studies had small samples and insufficient controls, and a large body of subsequent research and a WHO working group found no association, with IARC also concluding there was no evidence of carcinogenicity. The problem is that bad news travels fast and good news does not, just like MMR and autism: once doubt is planted, the world never fully recovers.

49:35 Refusal rates doubled, and the 81-fold risk is badly underestimated
US refusal rates nearly doubled from 2017 to 2024, rising from 3% to 5.8%, with some hospitals reporting higher. Infants whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a figure that is badly underestimated because the bleeding itself remains rare and communication is inadequate. Research shows most parents, whether they accept or refuse, know vitamin K is related to bleeding, but do not know that this bleeding can cause severe brain injury and a mortality risk above 20%. The information is present, but it is not being effectively conveyed.

50:36 Refusal reasons fall into three buckets, and birth attendants matter enormously
Refusal reasons roughly fall into three categories: distrust of medicine, pursuit of ‘natural birth,’ and preference for alternative medical lifestyles. Some argue that if infants needed more vitamin K, evolution or God would have provided it; others read a recommendation to supplement vitamin K as ‘you are not fit to be a mother.’ Research also finds refusers are more likely to be white, college-educated, over 30, and planning a home or birth-center delivery. The birth attendant's stance is critical: in a New Zealand survey, 100% of doctors thought all infants should receive vitamin K, versus only 55% of midwives, 26% of whom would not give it to their own children; in Canada, infants delivered by midwives are 8 times more likely to have vitamin K refused than those delivered by doctors.

55:46 Doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time
Some parents who lost a child or whose child suffered brain injury because vitamin K was not given are doing something very brave: saying publicly, ‘I made this decision, this is the consequence, do not do what I did.’ Meanwhile, doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time in their careers, and they are raising the alarm in their communities. Some researchers and doctors are pushing to establish a national US registry of vitamin K refusal and administration, because vitamin K deficiency bleeding is not a notifiable disease and cases are likely undercounted. In a post-pandemic era when expertise is treated as a dirty word, these preventable injuries and deaths will keep rising.

item.title: US Strategic Oil Reserve Hits Bottom, and Venezuelan Oil Can't Save It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-indicator-美国战略石油储备见底-委内瑞拉石油救不了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-indicator-美国战略石油储备见底-委内瑞拉石油救不了它/
item.description: The salt-cavern reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and overuse is dissolving the salt walls and destabilizing the cavern structures; Venezuelan oil is a different grade and needs $100 billion in infrastructure spending, so it can't get around the deadlock of congressional appropriations.
item.content:encoded:
The salt-cavern reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and overuse is dissolving the salt walls and destabilizing the cavern structures; Venezuelan oil is a different grade and needs $100 billion in infrastructure spending, so it can't get around the deadlock of congressional appropriations.

Medium information density, but it explains the physical degradation mechanism of the SPR — the part most coverage leaves out. Suited to anyone watching energy security and macro.

0:00 He promised to fill it, and it fell another 30%
In his inaugural address, Trump promised to fill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve ‘to the top’, but since then the reserve has fallen another 30%. The Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, a huge share of the world's oil couldn't get out, and the reserve was used as a price buffer to shield Americans from the global supply shortfall. The problem is that the buffer itself is nearly used up. Trump's new answer is Venezuelan oil, which he called ‘the largest oil deal in our country's history’, saying 65 billion barrels would go to the US. But the question the show pursues is: can Venezuelan oil actually save the SPR? And what does this mean for ordinary people's wallets?

2:03 The reserve isn't tanks, it's salt caverns dissolved out of the ground
After the Arab oil embargo against the US in the early 1970s, the US government realized it needed a standby oil supply, and the SPR was born. About 30 countries around the world hold standby reserves — Japan, Germany and Australia all have them — but the American version is unusual. Siddharth Mishra, a petroleum engineering professor at Texas A&M, says the US government determined that the most efficient way to store millions of barrels of oil wasn't metal tanks but salt caverns. Engineers pump in huge volumes of water to dissolve underground salt layers and create cavities — these aren't traditional caves you can walk into, they're man-made caverns, and a single cylinder is roughly the size of the Empire State Building or larger. Between Texas and Louisiana, 60 such caverns make up the SPR.

4:10 Overuse is dissolving the caverns themselves
The SPR was first tapped in 1991 for Operation Desert Storm, and then for Hurricane Katrina, the 2011 Arab Spring and the 2022 Ukraine war. The 2022 global release saved Americans roughly 17 to 42 cents per gallon. But the reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and it's dropping fast — down 50% over the past six years, with 85% of that attributable to the Ukraine and Iran wars. The risk isn't just about volume: the lower the reserve, the more water has to be injected, and the more room there is for the oil to be contaminated. Refineries don't like contaminated oil, and it's harder to sell; contamination also forms sludge that makes rapid extraction harder — and rapid extraction is the entire point of the SPR's existence. As water keeps being injected, the salt layers dissolve, the cavern structures become unstable, and this engineering marvel that once amazed Mishra is being weakened.

5:13 Filling the reserve still runs through Congress's wallet
Joseph Mikit, an energy security expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, says the US is not in a position to simply buy oil and fill the reserve. Under the normal mechanism, Congress has to agree to buy the oil and bury it underground, and with the deficit as large as it is, that's a hard problem. Previous administrations thought up workarounds: during the Clinton and Bush years there was the royalty-in-kind program — when companies produced oil from federally owned reserves, instead of paying the government in cash they handed over oil directly to go into the SPR. Now the government is looking at more unusual strategies: in April, Energy Secretary Chris Wright proposed drilling for oil underneath military bases, but nothing more was heard; the recent headline plan is Venezuelan oil, with a private company giving the US 20% control of its existing and future oil fields in Venezuela.

6:15 Venezuelan oil isn't the same grade as what's in the SPR
A key detail: Venezuelan oil is a completely different type from the oil in the US SPR, so it has to go through some kind of trading mechanism — sell one grade, buy another. Energy security expert Joseph is optimistic about the Venezuela deal, believing such a trade could work. He says the plan needs a lot of mechanisms to line up, but it adds a source of oil that won't cause large-scale market disruption, and it doesn't require the US to get Congress to agree to spend big on filling the SPR at a time of high oil prices and fiscal imbalance. In other words, any plan that doesn't require Congress to buy oil looks great. But the challenge is that getting oil out of the Venezuelan ground is notoriously hard, and after years of underinvestment and corruption it needs enormous infrastructure spending.

7:19 $100 billion, and no one knows who pays
One Latin American energy expert puts the figure at $100 billion over the next decade to restore Venezuelan production to where it was 20 years ago. And it's unclear who foots the bill — oil companies, the US government, or someone else. Arnab Data, a managing director at Employ America focused on energy markets, flatly calls the Venezuela plan ‘a bit of a pipe dream’. His objection: our own domestic and allied production can already meet demand, so why support Venezuelan production? Rather than putting $100 billion into another country, coordinating between agencies and untangling Venezuela's political chaos, it would be better to put that money into the SPR. His exact words: we don't need to go out looking for oil, there's plenty in the fridge, right here.

8:22 The current oil-lending mechanism is actually working well
Arnab thinks the Trump administration's current strategy is working fine: the Energy Department lends barrels to oil companies, which promise to return them later, at a premium of up to 24%. He sees this as a well-executed way of delivering to the market, while also signaling to the market that there's demand for US barrels. So here's the split: Joseph is optimistic about the Venezuela deal, seeing it as a source of oil that doesn't disrupt the market and doesn't need congressional appropriations; Arnab thinks it's a pipe dream, that the existing lending mechanism is good enough, and that the $100 billion would be better put back into the SPR. The show closes with a reminder: global oil supply keeps falling, another strait is under Houthi control and at risk of closing, and Americans don't know how much longer the SPR can shield them from higher costs.

item.title: Making a Child Perform Isn't Connection, It's Depletion
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.description: Connection isn't getting your child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.
item.content:encoded:
Connection isn't getting your child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.

This episode isn't dense — it's a single topic on a parenting podcast. But if you're currently dealing with relatives pushing your child to perform, or you want to understand what "connection" actually means, it's worth listening to.

1:04 Making a child perform is fast-food connection
A mother writes in that her 17-month-old son can identify shapes and colors, speak sentences, and recognize dinosaurs, but her mother keeps making him "perform" — repeating what he's learned, clapping — and when he won't cooperate she grabs his arm and does it for him, and recently even kicked him in the butt. Janet says this isn't an isolated case: we often assume connecting with infants and toddlers means getting them to react to us, to imitate us. But this is "fast-food connection" — the child may smile because he's getting attention, but no one is truly seen.

4:08 We're performing too
Connection goes both ways: not only do we make the child perform, we ourselves are often performing rather than being ourselves. In her forthcoming book Baby Person, Janet writes that she used to dance, make funny faces, and try every trick to get a reaction out of babies in order to bond with them. These surface methods left her exhausted, and the payoff was tiny and fleeting — "I made her laugh" is just a moment. She says this isn't deep connection, it's all surface.

6:14 Performance connection teaches children to be insincere
Janet lists five reasons connection shouldn't be a performance: one, it isn't real connection; two, it teaches the child insincerity — everything we do with our children teaches them something, and this teaches that "connection requires performing rather than being yourself"; three, it wastes energy and effort, and parents can't afford it; four, it doesn't satisfy, and doesn't move the relationship toward trust; five, it subtly belittles the child — why should a child have to perform to hold our attention and interest?

8:19 Charismatic people are charismatic because they're paying attention to you
Janet quotes something she's always remembered: certain people are charismatic to us not because of how they present themselves or what they put out, but because they are genuinely interested in us and paying attention to us. Children especially need this, because it's harder for them to express themselves proactively and they don't know what to say to connect. They need us to tune in to their subtleties: what they're interested in, what their expressions are saying, who they are.

9:19 Even a parenting expert couldn't connect with her grandchild
Janet read a book by a well-known psychologist regarded as a parenting expert, in which the author, now a grandparent, said she simply couldn't connect with a toddler grandchild and felt the child had no chemistry with her. Janet's immediate judgment: this grandparent was trying too hard — wanting to initiate games, wanting the child to cooperate, she was "operating" rather than connecting. Her method works for every child from infancy on: observe, listen, receive, pay attention.

10:21 Comment on what you see, don't fake interest
The concrete approach: treat the child as a person with depth, talent, interests, and a real point of view worth knowing. Then comment on what you see — "You're looking over there, did you hear a dog?" "You seem really interested in those blocks, I see you're lining them up." Not faking interest, but genuinely becoming interested. Children can tell the difference between "good job" and "wow, that took a while, I saw you thinking about which one goes on top, and the round one rolled down."

12:31 Children can put a grandparent's behavior in context
How do you let go of the fear that "this is bad for the child"? Janet says children are more aware than we think. They know "this is my grandparent, this isn't how my parents treat me, this is just how this person is." So it won't affect how they feel about themselves. Parents have enormous influence, but grandparents are different — even with frequent contact, the child can put it in the context of "my relationship with that person."

14:34 Narrate instead of correcting
Janet advises this mother not to try to teach her mother or correct her, but to connect, reflect, and trust them to handle the relationship themselves. Concretely: if her son does what the grandmother asks, let it go; if he doesn't and the grandmother kicks him, don't say to the grandmother "you shouldn't do that," but say to her son "Grandma really likes it when you do what she asks, she's really into this" — without sarcasm, just stating what's happening. This is called sportscasting, and it helps both the child and the grandmother understand what's going on.

item.title: The Pentagon doesn't lack models — it lacks the chain that puts intelligence on the president's desk
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.description: The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft — it was procurement reform, the intelligence analysis institutions, and the chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it. APIs alone are not enough.
item.content:encoded:
The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft — it was procurement reform, the intelligence analysis institutions, and the chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it. APIs alone are not enough.

The first half uses the U-2 analogy to lay out clearly where the government's AI integration bottleneck is; the second half's judgments on procurement incentives, token economics and cybersecurity are worth more, but overall it's a loose interview chat with medium information density.

2:02 The U-2's miracle wasn't the plane, it was the procurement and analysis chain
Garrett says the U-2 story is usually told as a technology breakthrough, but what really mattered was three things: procurement reform that let government and industry work together that way, intelligence analysis being institutionalized (NPIC, which later became NGA), and getting judgment in front of the president and other decision-makers. That, he says, is the ‘miraculous’ part of the story. Today's AI problem is the exact inverse: the technology comes from the commercial world and moves too fast, already far beyond the government's ability to integrate it into systems, workflows and decision processes — so ‘APIs alone are not enough’.

9:06 AI is moving fastest in warfighting, slowest in business systems
Garrett says the Pentagon and other departments have made visible progress in warfighting spaces like CJADC2: using AI to build situational awareness across the battlefield, identify targets, and get intelligence quickly to decision-makers at the front. But core business systems — logistics, personnel, finance — have seen the least progress. His personal view is that systems should no longer be split into ‘mission systems’ and ‘business systems’, because supporting the front line requires clean, well-organized data usable at the tempo of operations, and those business systems were never built for that tempo.

10:06 One policy rule blocks the data of twenty thousand logistics troops
He gives a concrete example: some business systems' rules say status only needs to be updated once a week. That's policy — someone wrote it down. But decision-makers now want that data daily, which means going to roughly ten or twenty thousand Army supply sergeants and saying ‘you have to enter it daily, not weekly’. That's ‘a big boat to turn around’, and there has to be clear value in it. Worse, the systems the government gave them were bad to begin with — making it hard to enter data while also demanding a big reduction in data latency.

14:10 Government has no market competition as a forcing function
The host points out that companies that don't do AI get eliminated, but the Air Force or the national security system won't be ‘competed out’ — that kind of forcing function comes along once or twice a century. Garrett agrees, but says we underestimate our own ability to manufacture mechanisms. He argues for using personnel policy and leadership as carrot and stick: reward people who take risks and take weird career paths, and let those who don't move fast enough face career stagnation or removal. He says it sounds ‘crude’, but that's the mechanism you have to follow.

19:18 Second-mover advantage: watch others burn money and hit the pits first
Garrett says this time it's the reverse of the U-2: the technology happens in the commercial sector first and then enters government, so government has a second-mover advantage and can see what's working. He cites the lesson of token economics: do you open it up like Uber and let everyone burn tokens without limit, blowing the budget in a quarter, or do you understand token economics first and then deploy to employees? Also, as the federal government, if it gets this right it can act as a supersized buyer and negotiate volume pricing.

23:20 To put GPUs at the front, first clear the policy on signing and accountability
Garrett says if you put these tools in soldiers' hands, you'll be shocked at how innovative and clever they are at using them for their actual jobs, and that may mean pushing compute to the edge and putting GPUs in service members' hands. But the obstacle is policy: a logistics officer signs for $500,000 worth of chips — who's responsible if a chip breaks? He says you have to clear the policy and just say ‘we're taking that risk’, and if it means some GPUs get broken and money is lost, that's worth it, because capability reaches the edge.

29:26 Intelligence analysis is more tractable than modeling decisions
Garrett thinks using AI to model strategic decisions is very hard, because it needs good data, and the decision process is deliberately opaque — you can't get all the private notes, emails and situation-room audio and video. But intelligence analysis is a more tractable project: the intelligence process is structured and rigorous, agencies have their own SOPs and training, there are decades of data, and there are signals of quality high and low that you can build benchmarks against. Still, it's only one input to decisions — historically many decision-makers looked at the same intelligence and made completely different decisions.

38:36 Bill by the hour and someone will report more hours
Garrett says the government buys a great deal on hourly rates by person and seniority, and this time and materials structure has a status quo bias. The logic is plain: if the incentive is for companies to report more hours, and there's no hard delivery requirement at the end of those hours, they will report more hours. He says there have been signs of change over the past 12 to 18 months, but looking at public spending data, there's been no large-scale shift — most spending is still time and materials. He also mentions that top companies spend 10% of their budget on tokens, while the US government is nowhere near that level.

item.title: Procrastination Isn't a Willpower Problem: You'll Fail With the Same Plan Next Time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.description: Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it's harmful, and about one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need different fixes, but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan and nothing about the result changes.
item.content:encoded:
Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it's harmful, and about one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need different fixes, but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan and nothing about the result changes.

It breaks procrastination into types you can treat, and hands you a concrete toolbox instead of another round of "just be disciplined" platitudes. Medium-to-high information density.

1:16 The definition of procrastination has reluctance buried inside it
Itamar's definition is: we delay something even though we don't intend to delay it, and we know it's bad for us. So "I deliberately decided to do it later and I feel fine about that" is not procrastination. The grey zone is: does it count when you think delaying is good for you but it's actually harmful? His test is "could you have anticipated that this would be better for you." About 20% of adults procrastinate chronically; among students it's 50%. He stresses that procrastination doesn't only happen to people who don't care — people high in conscientiousness, genuinely productive, who truly want to make an impact, procrastinate too.

3:27 Procrastination is several types, not one thing
Treating procrastination as a single phenomenon makes two mistakes at once: you fail to see that it happens to people other than students, and you can't deal with it in practice. Because the student who procrastinates from distraction, the executive who procrastinates from burnout, and the artist who procrastinates from perfectionism have different drivers and need different solutions. In his book Itamar distinguishes the anxious type, the pulled-away-by-external-temptation type, the burnout type, and a category he calls zigzaggers — closer to ADHD and impulsivity, switching back and forth between internal rather than external distractions.

5:00 Anxiety has two faces: fear of the task or fear of the consequences
The mechanism by which anxiety causes procrastination is: doing this thing hurts, the brain says I don't want to hurt, so you push it away. But anxiety also has an adaptive side — if what you're anxious about isn't the task itself but the consequences of not finishing it, a little anxiety actually pushes you to act. The key variables are intensity and self-efficacy: a little anxiety may motivate you, a lot of anxiety paralyses you no matter what it's aimed at; and if you also believe you're incapable of finishing, anxiety turns into paralysis more easily. Itamar adds one thing: even when anxiety does push you, it's a dangerous source of motivation, because it brings stress and a worse experience along with it.

9:25 The biggest mistake is believing you'll try harder next time
Itamar says the biggest mistake people make when tackling procrastination is falling into the self-control fallacy: believing that next time, if you just try harder and summon more willpower, you'll pull it off. The absurdity is that we watch it fail again and again, and believe it again and again. The reasons include the bias blind spot (being unable to spot your own biases) and the empathy gap (predicting, in a calm state, what you'll do when you're in a hot emotional state). The real harm of this belief is that it offers a superficially minimal silver bullet, which stops you from looking for what actually works. Spencer's addition: change nothing and nothing changes.

12:45 Design for your future self as if they were someone else
Spencer's approach: don't assume that the you of two weeks from now will get it done on willpower — instead ask "for someone a lot like me, what would help them get this done in two weeks?" Set reminders, make social commitments, add rewards. Itamar says this is exactly an illustration of his core claim: procrastination is not a time management problem, and even excellent time management can fail; what you should be doing is distance management. Addressing yourself in the second or third person, or using your name instead of "I", or asking "what advice would I give a friend", all create psychological distance and help you enter wise reasoning, seeing through the situation and routing around your biases.

16:13 The anxious type: decatastrophize, or do it anxious
For the anxious procrastinator, Itamar's first choice is to decatastrophize: catastrophizing is overestimating both the probability that something bad happens and the harm it does to you. For example, "there's a typo in my proposal, so the agent will blacklist me, and tell everyone else to blacklist me too." The method is to press on: how likely is this to happen? If it did happen, how bad would the impact be? If it happened, how would I carry on? Spencer offers an almost opposite strategy: notice that this task makes me anxious, sit inside that feeling, feel it, and then do it anyway — he calls it metacognitive awareness. Itamar files it under the umbrella of mindfulness and self-compassion.

21:39 Procrastination is short-term emotional repair, and it reinforces itself
Spencer points out that anxiety generates anxiety: the moment you say "I'm not doing this now", the anxiety usually drops immediately, and you're learning that procrastinating makes you feel better — a reinforcement loop. Doing the opposite can undo it: doing it while anxious functions like an exposure. Itamar says procrastination here is a defence mechanism: because you feel pressure or anxiety about what you should be doing, you push it away to avoid the painful emotion. It makes you feel better in the short term and worse in the long term, because you haven't solved the problem — you've only arranged to face it again and again later, or to face worse consequences.

26:39 The burnout fix is to do less
Itamar admits this is the last thing burnt-out people want to hear: if you're burnt out because you're doing too much, or doing things that drain you, you probably need to do less and take more deliberate care of yourself — concretely, deciding more deliberately what to do and, more importantly, what not to do. He describes a loop: you're used to performing well, burnout makes your performance drop, so you work harder, then you burn out more, and it gets worse and worse. He calls this "borrowing health and productivity from your future self." He also notes that burnout doesn't only come from hours: reasonable hours with high-pressure, meaningless, or otherwise draining tasks will burn you out just the same.

item.title: The cost of RLHF is mode dropping, not alignment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.description: RLHF forces the model to be extremely conservative to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.
item.content:encoded:
RLHF forces the model to be extremely conservative to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.

High information density: Diogo goes into the trade-offs of RLHF, RLVR, and RLCD in detail, suited to anyone who needs to make judgments about model training routes.

6:03 The cost of RLHF is mode dropping
Diogo thinks nobody notices RLHF's downsides, especially mode dropping. The mechanism: to generate very long strings without errors, the model must be extremely conservative, because errors are immediately visible, while places that look correct but are subtly wrong are hard to spot; this calibration is "total poison" for the probability distribution over strings. He uses this to explain why Yann LeCun's chart that "LLMs necessarily make mistakes as sequences get longer" is mathematically obvious but empirically false — when you cover the distribution you are not over-penalized by outliers; mode drop is what loses the minority classes.

11:12 Refusing to answer is a type error, not a safety issue
Diogo distinguishes safety alignment from capability alignment: the latter is "doing what the user wants," the former is "following someone else's instructions," like OpenAI and Anthropic. He thinks safety alignment is reasonable for products like ChatGPT and Claude, but in an API it is "nuts," "completely unacceptable" — if a dependency runs in the background, having software randomly crash because a user sent a strange message is insanity. He opposes adding restrictions at the technical layer, on the grounds that every overfit fractures intelligence a bit more, and today's models are already fractured enough.

18:15 Public benchmarks are a substitute for trust
Diogo says he is extremely anti-public benchmarks, because they are extremely gameable: in the early days every lab had a team dedicated to collecting data like MMLU to boost scores, essentially "benchmarking with extra steps." He admits intelligence has a je ne sais quoi (good model smell), so people need benchmarks to build trust, but in the long run you can only rely on vibes and trust, until you put the model into a concrete workflow and evaluate it there. He also says that if they wanted to make Jev dumb, they could have shipped it a year and a half ago.

27:34 RLCD is a new North Star, not a new algorithm
Diogo says the term RLHF has been conflated: the original work was Paul Christiano teaching a robot to do a backflip, then it was learning to summarize, and only later instruction following. What he actually calls RLHF is "instruction following as the North Star," unrelated to the PPO algorithm — just as DPO and its descendants don't use that paper's algorithm but still count as RLHF. RLCD is the same: a new task direction, programs in the loop, taking the human out of the loop.

40:38 Reliability is a catchall; the North Star is robustness
Diogo defines reliability as a catchall: if AI can't automate something, in the end it's some kind of reliability problem — it might be type safety, it might be determinism, or it might just be that the model is too jagged. He explicitly opposes treating determinism (same input, same output) as the North Star, thinking it is only slightly valuable for unit tests; what really matters is robustness — similar inputs get similar outputs. The test is to stuff nonces like UUIDs into the prompt and see whether semantically identical questions get similar answers. He says when people get burned by AI decisions, that happens at the robustness layer.

1:17:12 Reliability is more underrated than speed and cost
Diogo thinks the industry is focusing on the wrong place: "people focus too much on speed and cost and not enough on reliability." His judgment is that reliability is what makes people happy and what makes them dare to trust. He ties this to TFP growth — he expects TFP growth above 3% within five years, and says that is the mark of an economic revolution, and also what the OpenAI charter originally meant to express. He estimates that all current models are still roughly at zero, maybe not even 1%, on valuable work in the world economy.

1:44:10 The optimal dose of RLVR is zero
Diogo says directly that for a model of TypeSafe's shape, the optimal amount of RLVR is zero. His argument is not "RLVR is useless," but that the discussion of "pacing the frontier" swaps out the premise: it assumes everyone must do more RLVR, and RLVR looks dangerous because it lets the model "do anything they want" in the middle of training — the less you restrict it, the stronger the model is on the outside. So the danger is not a side effect, it is the design goal. He calls this a "disillusion of responsibility": treating "we must do more RLVR" as an axiom, then deriving the conclusion "we are heading toward a dangerous world."

2:09:13 The KV cache is a tyranny over coding agents
Diogo wants to explore coding agents "free from the tyranny of the KV cache." The KV cache locks you into one model, and for efficiency you must keep appending, so you can't do state management, abstraction, decomposition — normal software practices. From this he explains several phenomena: why routing is hard, why sub-agents seem not to work, why compaction is a hard problem — because passing state requires intelligence that is much cheaper than reading state. Directions he envisions include: explicitly annotating state for subtasks, searching for relevant context in a tree of subtasks, parallel sub-agents reading each other's state, and coordinating with smart locks rather than basic-ass locks.

item.title: AI will hit an energy wall within three years, and the fix is to build a computer that isn't a computer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.description: Google alone burns 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month; at 10 joules per token that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.
item.content:encoded:
Google alone burns 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month; at 10 joules per token that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.

The first half is the energy math; the second half is his first public prototype of a physical dynamics computer and its measured efficiency numbers, which is rare hard information. The biology analogy in the middle can be fast-forwarded.

4:45 Energy isn't a cost line, it's the ticket to entry
Naveen's math: Google crosses 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month, and at 10 joules per token — a low estimate — that's 12 gigawatts. The US today puts about 40 gigawatts into data centers; the world, under 100 gigawatts. So one company's AI service eats more than a tenth of global data center energy. His call is that we hit the energy ceiling in about three years. More important, the ranking of scarce resources in a data center has changed: it used to be floor space, racks, networking gear, GPUs; today it's energy — get the power contract first, then figure out how to fill it. And energy is 50% of the cost of serving a token; only the rest is hardware capex and site.

7:04 What a squirrel does on 8 milliwatts takes a GPU watts
A human brain is about 20 watts. Scale linearly by neuron count down to a monkey brain and you get one watt, exactly your phone in your pocket. Further down, rats and bats are in the milliwatt range. A squirrel leaping between branches lands it a thousand times out of a thousand on an 8-milliwatt brain. So your phone's battery could run a hundred-plus squirrel brains. Naveen's conclusion is that biology has already built a physical substrate suited to intelligence, while synthetic systems went another way: the human cortex moves only about 16 billion bits per second, while a high-end GPU moves close to 30 trillion bits per second in and out of memory, and inside the chip it's another 10 to 100 times higher. The energy goes almost entirely into moving information, not computing on it.

10:06 Moore's Law stopped, and the abstraction layers still charge rent
Transistor counts are still rising, but frequency stopped scaling long ago, single-thread performance stopped, and now even efficiency no longer improves as process nodes shrink — Naveen says flatly that Moore's Law is basically over. His diagnosis is the abstraction layers: digital itself is an abstraction of the physical world, and transistors actually have intermediate states that get engineered into 0s and 1s. Every layer of abstraction is lossy and ignores the complexity beneath it. So their approach is to wire the physics of the semiconductor directly to the neural network, skipping the layers in between. His intuition pump is flocks of birds and ant colonies: individuals do something extremely simple, and complex behavior emerges from the whole — the field is called dynamical systems theory.

12:07 Metronomes on a board sync up on their own
Put several metronomes on a rigid board that can roll back and forth, and they synchronize to exactly the same phase, simply because each one gives the board a tiny push. That's a purely physical dynamical system. Their question was whether such a system can compute. The answer is yes — they open-sourced an image generation model called UNO built on a set of such oscillators, and it trains and produces images. Define the system state as the phases of all the oscillators, condition on the output, and generating planes, cars or birds follows different state space trajectories. It's the first demonstration that this class of system can be trained at scale and produce useful results.

14:08 Throwing away connections makes the system easier to train
Full connectivity is n squared: 10 elements and 100 connections is fine, 1,000 elements is a million connections and simply doesn't scale. Their sparsity is deliberately discarding some connections and then seeing whether the overall behavior can be rescued. The result isn't just that you can throw them away — after throwing them away the system behaves better and is more trainable, and that holds both in simulation and in real physical systems. Naveen calls this the rare case where more efficient, more scalable and better performing all hold at once, a holy grail nobody had cracked for a long time, provided you frame the problem correctly first.

15:09 The first physical dynamics computer has already generated images
This is Naveen's first public disclosure: they built the first physical dynamics computer. The company only formally started in January of this year, with no team at the time; on June 1 they sent the design to tape-out, and the chip is back in the lab with results — the first images generated by this kind of computer. On efficiency, generating an image takes about 500 nanojoules, versus millijoules for an ordinary GPU; a nanojoule is 10 to the minus 9, several orders of magnitude apart. The reason is that it doesn't move information at all. Architecturally it differs from both CPUs and GPUs: those are von Neumann architectures with memory and compute separated and data shuttled back and forth; in this machine compute and storage are the same thing, there is no memory interface, and every compute unit is itself the memory.

17:09 4D computing: three spatial dimensions plus one of time
They call the whole thing 4D computing: physically, die stacking uses all three dimensions vertically and in plane, and the fourth dimension is time in the dynamics. The objective function is intelligence per watt. There is a thermodynamic limit that can never be crossed; animal brains are only one to two orders of magnitude from it, while today's computing systems are about 10 billion times away. Their plan is to hit the limit of 2D lithography within three and a half years, and the company's overall goal is to beat biology. Naveen expects the result to be a change in form factor: from gigawatt-scale mega data centers to small data centers scattered everywhere, more local, more adaptive, and supporting billions of robots that dynamically combine to solve problems.

19:12 A thousand times cheaper means a thousand times more consumption
Naveen closes with the Jevons paradox: when the underlying cost of an asset falls, consumption grows by more than the price drop. Halve the price and consumption more than doubles; cut the price to a thousandth and consumption grows more than a thousandfold. So he doesn't think efficiency gains shrink the market — they create the largest market in human history. Chamath then presses on the ecosystem — tape-out, packaging and so on need a whole set of people to line up. Naveen's answer is a complete product within two years, in the form of an entire rack, sold as a new data center product: tokens in, tokens out over the network, but internally structured completely differently from existing computers.

item.title: Strategic Reserves Are Nearly Drained — the Oil Price Crisis Is Only Now Beginning
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.description: For the past six months oil prices didn't spiral out of control thanks to three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. Now all three are being drained, and the real shock is only about to hit diesel and consumer prices.
item.content:encoded:
For the past six months oil prices didn't spiral out of control thanks to three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. Now all three are being drained, and the real shock is only about to hit diesel and consumer prices.

Medium information density, but breaking down "why oil prices didn't rise" into three buffers and the pace at which they're being exhausted is more useful than reading headlines.

2:03 Close Hormuz and a fifth of the world's oil is gone
The moment the war began, Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, cutting off roughly 20% of global oil supply. This was the move everyone treated as the "nuclear option" — nobody wanted to see it, because it's too bad for every side. Once the strait closed, oil shot from around $70 a barrel to well over $100. But the market didn't spiral out of control from there; it found several buffers that held prices down. The real question isn't "why did it rise" but "why didn't it rise more."

3:09 Three buffers, each less usable than the last
The first is the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve — backup crude stored in salt caverns along the Gulf Coast after the 1970s Arab oil embargo — plus the commercial inventories held by refiners, which were at high levels before the conflict. The second is sanctioned oil: a large volume of "dark fleet" crude from Iran and Russia floating at sea, which in March the US temporarily allowed other countries to buy. The third is China — the world's largest oil importer, normally buying about 12 million barrels a day, roughly 10% of global supply, which earlier this year bought about 3 million barrels a day less, effectively giving that oil to others. Together, these three held oil below $100 and the national average gasoline price just under $5.

6:12 Ceasefire talks slapped every analyst in the face
In June the US and Iran began talks and reached a ceasefire, and market sentiment flipped 180 degrees: from "extreme crude shortage" to "crude surplus," with analysts predicting oil would fall to $70 or even $60 a barrel. But the peace deal collapsed weeks later, Iran closed the strait again, and Trump declared the ceasefire over. So it was back to the state at the start of the conflict. This episode shows one thing: this price contains a large bet on "the war ends soon," and that bet has repeatedly failed.

8:15 Six months of draining the buffers, and they're nearly dry
Commercial inventories have been drawn down, strategic reserves released — and reserves can't be released in unlimited quantity; the government only authorized a specific amount. The US has taken more than 130 million barrels out of the strategic reserve, leaving about 280 million, which sounds like a lot but is approaching the authorized ceiling. Worse, this time there's an added refinery crisis: Middle Eastern refineries were struck in the war, and Ukraine, in self-defense, knocked out a large chunk of Russia's refining capacity — and Russia is the world's second-largest diesel exporter. Once a refinery is destroyed, it takes months to restore. So the problem now isn't whether there's crude; it's that there isn't enough refining capacity to produce the fuel the world needs.

9:16 Venezuela can't put out a fire next door
The Trump administration holds Venezuela up as the solution, and its reserves may be the world's largest. But reserves being there doesn't mean production capacity is there: to actually raise output you have to invest money, move rigs, hire people, drill, and then ship the barrels out — that's a matter of years and billions of dollars of investment. As for other "miracle solutions," Benoit says there basically aren't any; you can only hope for "small miracles" — like China deciding to raise diesel output, or refinery repairs finishing early. But none of these take effect tomorrow.

10:17 Gas stations haven't blown up yet — diesel blew up first
US consumers haven't yet seen prices spike at the pump; what's really rising is diesel — the fuel that drives the heavy trucks moving consumer goods from one end of the country to the other. So the question becomes: will companies cut back on deliveries? When do they pass costs on to consumers? Once diesel rises, every kind of business has to factor it into its pricing. This is the real channel through which this shock transmits from energy markets to the real economy, and why "gas prices are okay" is a misleading comfort.

12:23 Two paths: absorb it, or pass it on
Businesses have only two choices. One is to absorb it without raising prices: Jim Barber, a third-generation Pennsylvania farmer, has raised his beef price only once in five years, and even with the cost of hauling in hay up 15% to 20%, he eats it himself, because he values his relationship with customers and believes the conflict will end soon and that holding out will be rewarded. A farmer's fuel exposure is triple-layered — fertilizer, hauling in hay, and shipping his own goods out — so energy costs can be paid three times over or more. The other is to pass it on: Ambix, which makes plastic parts, uses resin, and resin comes from oil; some costs rose 30%, 40%, 50%. At first it resisted raising prices, but as the war dragged on it began passing the 60 cents its suppliers raised straight to customers.

15:36 Six-dollar diesel in August, and the shock starts embedding in the economy
When energy prices eased this summer, many businesses had a spell of optimism, thinking maybe they were coming out of the woods. Then in August tensions heated up again, fuel prices rose again, and recently six-dollar-a-gallon diesel appeared. Owen thinks this is the moment some businesses and economists began to realize "the price shock is truly embedding in the economy." Meanwhile, JPMorgan commodity analysts said in their latest forecast that they no longer know how to model it — there's no baseline, because they can't see around the corner. On paper many economic indicators are healthy, but consumers feel terrible about prices, and no one — oil executives, politicians, or CEOs — can say clearly how long this will last.

item.title: AI Safety Language Is Destroying the Regulatory Debate: It's a Bug, Not a Demon
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-a16z-ai-安全语言正在毁掉监管讨论-那是-bug-不是恶魔/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-a16z-ai-安全语言正在毁掉监管讨论-那是-bug-不是恶魔/
item.description: Calling AI failures ‘misalignment’ gives software intent and moral judgment, making it impossible for Congress and the public to understand what actually happened — it should be debugged, reported and fixed like a bug.
item.content:encoded:
Calling AI failures ‘misalignment’ gives software intent and moral judgment, making it impossible for Congress and the public to understand what actually happened — it should be debugged, reported and fixed like a bug.

Medium information density, but Sinofsky uses three personal histories — the 1983 hacker arrests, the 1998 virus, and Y2K — to pull ‘AI safety’ back into the context of software engineering. Useful for people doing product and policy communication.

0:00 ‘Misalignment’ just means the software has a bug
Sinofsky's core claim: when AI does something we didn't expect, that isn't ‘misaligned’ — it's software not running as intended, i.e. a bug. He says that back when Word ate files and deleted all the content, nobody thought a demon had possessed Word and made it act against people's will; and when a spreadsheet miscalculated, nobody circled up to pray to the alignment gods. Calling an AI failure ‘misalignment’ attributes to it properties that don't exist — that it's ‘trying to do something’, that it ‘made a moral judgment’, that it ‘has rules and principles’. And if it's just making decisions based on statistics, that doesn't change the standard that ‘it should do what you want it to do’ — a statistical error is still a bug in the product.

7:07 Full self-driving running a red light is also a bug
Sinofsky uses autonomous driving as an example: if full self-driving runs a red light because it recognized a stop sign as a Christmas tree, we wouldn't say it ‘failed to align with the December holiday and road sign philosophy’ — we'd say it's a bug, and a dangerous one, because that stop sign has meaning. He points out that both Tesla and Waymo have built in a huge amount of telemetry, diagnostics and extra cameras — things you wouldn't put in a spreadsheet, but would put in life-critical software. And AI models are still at the research-project stage, lacking the tools and telemetry that important software should have.

8:07 Once telemetry went live, there were more bugs than could ever be fixed
Sinofsky recalls that the software industry spent twenty years with no idea why programs crashed, and could only list crash locations and fix the top ten. Until someone said: why not write a program that, when it crashes, tells us through this new thing called the internet? Then suddenly there was telemetry, and suddenly there were far more bugs than anyone imagined — going from ‘we have no bugs, we can ship’ to ‘if we stopped all work, we could fix bugs forever’. From this he argues that when talking about an AI pause, labs should of course slow down: stop adding new things, and go fill in telemetry, tooling, logging and step-by-step debugging. He read the bug report OpenAI had just published, and the conclusion was clear: they just don't know.

9:08 Excel wrote ‘send dogs’ to disk
The first version of Windows Excel in 1987 had a bug: it would write the letters ‘send dogs’ into some Windows settings file on disk. Nobody knew where the phrase came from, and everyone combed through the Excel source code without finding it. Finally a tester wrote a script that continuously generated charts and printed them on an old dot-matrix printer for days, and found that after about two days it would write send dogs into that location — it depended on how much memory there was, how long it had been running, and what printer and device drivers were used. Sinofsky says we could easily have concluded that ‘Excel's brain decided to print send dogs’, but we didn't — we actually debugged it, and then added telemetry.

13:10 PC software once claimed it was different from mainframes
Sinofsky recalls that back then IBM people looked at them and said their software was terrible, that Windows was garbage compared to the mainframe software running banks, airlines and power plants. For a long time their response was ‘you don't get it, we're different, this is new and cool, we run in 64K not 1MB, we sell for $5,000 not $5 million’. But in the end they found the only thing they had to do was grow up: when people started using Excel to decide how planes fly, Word to submit briefs to the Supreme Court, and PowerPoint to present the Challenger space shuttle disaster, the standard changed. His conclusion: once your tools are used in those settings, you no longer get to use ‘we're new’ as an excuse.

14:10 The virus that caused $12 billion in losses in a day
In March 1998, a virus spread across the internet as a worm. Sinofsky got a call in the morning from a reporter gasping ‘I love you, I love you, I love you’. The next day's headline was: $12 billion in damage to the US economy in a single day. He says nobody had previously imagined a bug could cause $12 billion in losses in 12 hours, but it happened. So they held a meeting and decided to pause Outlook development until they understood the matter. His attitude: the more people use a system, the more damage it can do when something goes wrong, but that's the price of admission, it's what you signed up for — ‘we're too popular to handle it’ is not an excuse.

16:10 Alignment is a Google-scale problem with extra difficulty
Sinofsky points out a concrete problem with alignment: to achieve it, you must have a huge set of rules defining what alignment is — what may be done, what may not, what is safe, what is unfair. And software engineering has long understood that adding too many constraints to a system makes it stop working, and produces endless unexpected side effects. You set one rule, and someone asks ‘what about this case’, so you add another rule. He says this starts to look like Google's job of deciding how to present search results — they spent 20 years and thousands of full-time people on it, and it's very, very hard. And AI labs have signed up for an upgraded version of that problem: they aren't just retrieving results, they're synthesizing them, so they also have to invent a whole lot of things themselves, and no law is going to invent them for them.

17:10 Y2K didn't happen because people did things
Asked whether AI alignment is like Y2K, Sinofsky stresses there's a causal chain here: professionals worried a lot, then professionals took on a lot of responsibility, and then nothing happened — that's a direct causal chain. They rented generators and RVs, moved computers into secure bunkers, and that's what caused nothing to happen. And there was almost no legislation — there were some odd regulations about Y2K compliance, but most of the rules were drafted by the industry itself, by cross-industry coalitions of banks, insurers and others.
