He thinks OpenAI needs to sit down with all the frontier model players and labs and build a much better reporting mechanism; yesterday's report is a good start, but far short of what a third party needs to understand what happened.

item.title: Optimism Is Not a Personality Trait, It's an Explanatory Style You Can Train
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.description: Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.
item.content:encoded:
Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.

Seligman himself walks through the full chain from learned helplessness to learned optimism, and in the back half treats agency as a civilizational variable and tries to quantify it — a rare angle.

9:36 The dog doesn't run, and it isn't because it never learned to run
In Solomon's lab, on day one the dog was strapped into a hammock and given Pavlovian shocks it could not escape no matter what it did; on day two it was put in a shuttle box where running to the other side would shut off the shock, and the dog just lay there. Seligman's judgment was that what the animal actually learned was not "the tone predicts the shock" but "nothing I do matters." That reading collided head-on with behaviorism at the time, because it required the animal to be a cognitive subject capable of thinking and of integrating experience across time.

13:50 People can be taught to give up by noise, too
Hiroto moved the same design onto humans: on day one, headphones playing an unpleasant noise, with one group unable to turn it off no matter what they pressed and another group able to stop it with a button. On day two they got a four-foot "human shuttle box" — hand on one side, the noise sounds; move it to the other side, it stops. People who had been through uncontrollable noise the day before left their hand sitting in the box. Seligman stresses that the variable doing the work is not the trauma itself but whether there was control over the trauma — and they ran control experiments on exactly this point.

19:00 Helplessness became the model for depression
In 1970 depression was not yet a diagnostic category; there was only "manic-depressive illness." By 1975 the American Psychiatric Association's DSM had for the first time split out "unipolar depression," listing nine symptoms: passivity, cognitive difficulty, sadness, anxiety, sleep problems, food losing its taste, numbness, loss of pleasure, thoughts of death. Seligman compared the nine symptoms against the learned-helplessness literature that had accumulated by then and found that eight of them could be reproduced in the lab; the only one missing was thoughts of death — presumably because the experiments used noise rather than something more severe. That model went on to become the dominant model of depression, and the drugs that could break helplessness in the lab became the mainstream antidepressants.

22:19 Five out of eight give up, and a third never do
Across the whole helplessness literature the effect is statistical: on average five out of eight people or eight rats become helpless, and about a third do not. From the 1970s on, Seligman kept asking what was different about that third, and it became the turning point of his career. The answer landed on explanatory style: people who explain bad events as permanent ("I'm stupid"), pervasive ("I'm unlovable"), and their own fault become helpless; people who explain them as temporary, local, and not their fault recover quickly.

26:50 West Point's first week already predicts who drops out
The first six weeks after entering West Point are called Beast Barracks: woken at four in the morning to run ten miles, systematically put through the wringer, with the stated purpose being to "break them," and roughly a third of candidates quit. Seligman's team measured explanatory style on day one, and the ones who dropped out were the pessimists. The same pattern shows up in college grades (optimists outperform their talent, pessimists underperform it) and in insurance sales: MetLife lost 50% of new hires within a year and 90% within four years; they hired 140 "special forces" whose optimism-scale scores were off the charts, and this cohort outsold the whole company and still had 75% on the job after four years, while the ordinary group was down to 10%.

34:17 Agency breaks apart into three beliefs
Seligman defines agency as the opposite of learned helplessness, made up of three parts: efficacy, the belief that you can accomplish a specific goal right here and now; optimism, the belief that you can accomplish it not only now but in the future and the further future; and imagination, the range of possible goals you can picture — the wider the range, the stronger the agency. Full agency is: I can do it now, I can do it in the future, and I can innovate across many different situations.

36:22 The Axial Age's answer may have been "I can do it"
Between 1000 and 500 BC, Greece, the Hebrew world, China, India, and Persia all underwent upheaval: the Buddha, Confucius, and Socrates appeared, and technology, medicine, art, literature, and the first political freedoms all erupted together. Seligman's hypothesis is that over those five centuries humanity discovered the concept of agency. The evidence is vocabulary: in the Iliad, Achilles does not decide to act on his own — Athena tells him to act; a hundred years later, in the Odyssey, Odysseus is already a wily, resourceful man who makes his own decisions, and the gods begin to exit the stage. By 500 BC, every culture had produced a large vocabulary of human agency.

38:30 In the Old Testament, the verbs God commands with are dwindling
Seligman took the entire Old Testament and counted agency verbs: broadly, in the Pentateuch God commands and people obey, with only a few exceptions like "choose life"; the further you go, into the Prophets and the Writings, the more words of human agency appear and the fewer words of divine agency. You can now have AI score each book for agency volume by book, and plotted against time it comes out linear — from the Pentateuch to the Babylonian exile around 300 BC, agency increases, and it correlates linearly with human innovation, population, living standards, political freedom, and technology.

item.title: He Never Won Elected Office, Yet He Reshaped All of New York
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-stuffmissed-他从未当选任何公职-却重塑了整座纽约/

item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Robert Moses stacked appointed positions to accumulate power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Moses stacked appointed positions to accumulate power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.

This episode is medium-density on information, but how Moses accumulated power through unelected positions, and the exact words from his 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, are valuable for understanding urban governance and how power operates.

1:01 Never elected, yet he held enormous power
Robert Moses was never elected to any public office in his life, yet he accumulated enormous power through appointment to various government positions. According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, his work includes 35 highways, 12 bridges, numerous parks, Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, Shea Stadium, many housing projects, two hydroelectric plants, and the 1964 New York World's Fair. He has been dead 45 years and remains a divisive figure, and his legacy may be argued over for another century or more.

6:10 His mentor taught him not to anger voters
Moses became chief of staff of the New York State Reconstruction Commission in 1919 and learned a great deal from Belle Moskovitz. Moskovitz understood deeply how to maneuver within government to achieve goals without antagonizing those in power. One example: in an early draft of a report, Moses suggested cutting part of the workforce, and Moskovitz reminded him that every one of those people was a voter, that they could not be angered, and that a way had to be found to cut costs without cutting that many people. This ‘don't anger the voters’ thinking ran through his later government work.

11:11 Parks were the means, highways were the end
When Moses took over the parks commission, most green-space plans merely preserved natural wilderness, but he envisioned adding more manicured landscaping and dedicated recreation areas. More importantly, every time he built a new park, he made sure the project included roads connecting the park to highways — that is where the parkway came from. From the start he planned a large state park system for Long Island, all linked by new roads. In just four years in the job, he added 13 parks to Long Island, totaling about 9,700 acres, where previously there had been only one park.

13:14 His mother lent him $20,000 to save Jones Beach
Jones Beach was originally just a sandbar on the southern edge of Long Island, almost completely submerged at high tide. Moses wanted to turn it into a great park, and most of the government and the press considered it impractical. He first used large-scale dredging to dig about 40 million cubic yards of sand from the seabed, raising the sandbar from two feet above sea level to twelve feet. But the project nearly died when the money ran out, and Moses did something highly unusual: he borrowed $20,000 from his mother, Bella, to continue the work. He later confirmed that if his mother had not put up the money, the contractor would not have brought the equipment back to finish. Jones Beach finally opened on August 4, 1925, in a dust storm, and an estimated 1.5 million people visited in its first year.

22:31 His only campaign, and he lost badly
Moses ran for public office only once in his life. In 1934 he ran for governor of New York and was thoroughly defeated by the incumbent Democratic governor, Herbert H. Lehman. Lehman received more than 2.2 million popular votes; Moses got fewer than 1.4 million. The New York Times, reporting Lehman's victory, wrote: ‘Meanwhile his formidable and pugnacious opponent, Robert Moses, will be free to continue his work as the great parks commissioner.’ After this defeat he never tried to run again, and instead continued to expand his power through appointed positions.

23:33 235 new playgrounds, only one in Harlem
Beginning in the 1930s, Moses greatly expanded the city's playgrounds, building 235 new ones. But a pattern began to emerge: he ignored the needs of districts with predominantly non-white populations. Of the 235 playgrounds, only one was in Harlem. In the summer of 1936 he opened 11 new swimming pools: 4 in Manhattan (including one in Harlem and one in West Harlem), 4 in Brooklyn, and 1 each in the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island. These pools had new filtration and chlorination systems, heating and underwater lighting, and were considered advanced, but they were also designed to be drained in the cooler months and used for other activities, from shuffleboard to roller skating.

24:35 ‘Clear the slums, just build a road’
In a 1945 article in The Atlantic Monthly, Moses opened by describing how slums form: existing buildings become overcrowded, speculators add tenants, and people are packed into tenements like chickens. But the ‘cure’ he offered was this: clearing slums in most cities is done indirectly — not for public, semi-public, or private housing, but for parks, playgrounds, parkways, highways, boulevards, and other public improvements. He boasted that his ‘demolition-and-construction demon squad’ had torn down more old slums than all the housing experts combined, and that ‘we built nothing but broad highways lined with landscaping and recreational facilities.’

33:43 Eminent domain is the only salvation
In the article Moses explicitly endorsed the use of eminent domain to acquire land. He wrote that buying large tracts of land at a reasonable price had become impossible, and that in such a situation, ‘eminent domain is the only salvation.’ Eminent domain must be exercised by the city, state, or federal government for private limited-dividend or redevelopment companies. He also criticized unions as ‘a serious obstacle to financing slum clearance,’ accusing them of insisting on retaining hourly-wage rights, striking, and ‘resisting invention and improvement in the building field.’ He said this attitude was ‘unreasonable’ and would not change until a better-educated new generation of union officials appeared.

item.title: Blame Is Not Revenge: A Philosopher Argues We Should Blame Less
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.description: Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to truly grasp the moral significance of what they did, and reaching shared moral understanding.
item.content:encoded:
Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to truly grasp the moral significance of what they did, and reaching shared moral understanding.

In 23 minutes it lays out a workable moral framework: distinguishing retributive from communicative blame, and explaining why blaming less does not mean giving up on responsibility.

0:04 There is no single definition of blame
Fricker points out that the philosophical literature holds a great many different views of blame: some say it is a hostile emotion, some a reactive attitude, some merely a judgment, some a rupture in a relationship, and some a form of protest. She suspects these views are not even talking about the same thing. She holds that the object of blame can be any agent — an individual, an institution, or even a collective as large as a nation — so long as it has done something wrong, it is a fitting object of blame.

2:05 Retributive blame has no logic to it
Fricker defines retributive blame as: you wronged me, I am at a disadvantage, so I am entitled to even the score by making you hurt a little too — "getting even" is its most apt metaphor. She says she does not believe this logic in interpersonal morality, and does not find it useful. She concedes she does not want to say anything specific about criminal punishment, but admits she is strongly inclined to think the retributive idea there is rather distasteful. She believes genuinely useful alternatives exist.

3:08 Communicative blame wants shared understanding
Fricker holds that the morally most valuable model of blame is the one aimed at getting the other person to fully appreciate the moral significance of their conduct. If you blame me for wronging you, perhaps I did not fully understand the moral weight of what I did; you put it into the conversation, and I either come to understand what I did or push back that it was "not that serious," and in the end the two of us reach shared moral understanding of what happened between us. She admits this is an ideal, but one worth pursuing, and calls it "communicative blame."

5:11 Blame is at bottom a judgment of moral wrongdoing
After the functional analysis, Fricker gives her own definition of blame: blame is a judgment of moral wrongdoing, and that judgment is in some sense activated or motivated by a disposition suited to holding someone responsible. She stresses that this is the context of moral blame. The definition is minimalist, and she thinks its virtue is that it transplants across domains — when she studies epistemic blame, for instance, she need not assume the blamer harbors hostile feelings toward the blamed, only that there is an epistemic fault and that the judgment issues from a responsibility-holding stance rather than passive observation.

6:11 An apology must be made to the right person
Fricker points to a key difference between apology and blame: communicative blame can be broadcast anywhere, and conveying blame's meaning to a third party can be derived from conveying it to the person concerned, both promoting shared moral understanding; but apologizing to someone you did not wrong is not an apology at all. Apology is essentially second-personal moral address, and must be done to the right person. She also notes that apology's reparative power is tied to an ongoing relationship — wronged at random by a stranger in the street, there is no need to chase an apology, and we all have to learn to let things go.

9:12 Sincerity is not all-or-nothing
Fricker rejects treating sincerity as all-or-nothing. She holds that in most apology practices a person need only be "sincere enough" to count as apologizing, and sincere enough in the right way to be accepted by the particular person being apologized to. She cites the philosopher Jeffrey Helmich's notion of the "apology stance": an apology is a speech act that not only expresses but "enacts" the appropriate sorry inner state. She adds that an over-elaborate apology is merely irritating, and that apology is a social performance that must fall within the bandwidth of aptness to be accepted.

12:15 Responsibility is a social construction, not metaphysics
Facing the minority view that genes and environment determine everything and no one is ever responsible, Fricker argues that this line of thought sets the threshold for responsibility in a metaphysical rather than a natural place. She understands responsibility as something that grows out of the practice of human living together, for the sake of social coordination and harmony, constructing shared moral consciousness. She borrows Peter Strawson's approach: whatever the metaphysics, in everyday life we simply cannot help praising and blaming. She holds that separating metaphysics from the practice of responsibility is itself what leads people astray.

19:20 Blaming less is a trainable choice
Fricker says that if blame is a judgment of fault, and the judgment issues from a responsibility-holding moral stance, then we can choose how much of human behavior to bring into this "fault-finding" construction. She gives the example of lateness: some people are highly moralistic about others being late, others are not offended at all. She admits she prefers a world in which everyone is a bit more relaxed about lateness of up to 15 minutes, where it need not be constructed as a matter of respect — it is just "you were a little late," and that is all.

item.description: Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation only explains a one-to-two-month gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation only explains a one-to-two-month gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.

This is a state-of-open-models briefing written for Congress: dense with data, clear in its judgments, and suited to anyone who wants to grasp the US-China open-model landscape quickly.

0:00 Open weights is not the same thing as open source
An open-weight model releases only the weights and a license; an open-source model also releases the training code and data. America's genuinely open-source models are led by nonprofits, such as the Allen Institute for AI's Olmo, OpenAthena's Marin, and EleutherAI's Pythia. Nvidia's Nemotron is more open than most open-weight models, having released a large amount of training data, but because it has not released all of it, it still does not count as fully open source. The distinction matters: when people discuss "open source," what they are actually talking about is mostly open weights.

0:00 Chinese models have crossed the agentic capability threshold
GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 delivered a step change in commercial viability, crossing an agentic capability threshold similar to the one Anthropic's Claude Code crossed in December 2025. Chinese open-weight models overtook the US in these two key areas roughly 18 months ago. On Hugging Face downloads, China took the lead in July 2025, driven mainly by Alibaba's Qwen. Data from the ATOM project, which the author maintains, shows China's download lead has grown to about 1.6 billion out of a total of 3.2 billion, twice that of the US.

0:00 The benchmark score gap is stark
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, as of September 14, 2026, the top three are Chinese models: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash score 45 and 42, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scores 44. The US leaders are Thinking Machines' Inkling and Inkling Small, both scoring 26, and Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. The top US models were released in June and July 2026, with a lower update cadence than their Chinese counterparts. Chinese labs are closest on tasks with well-defined demand such as agentic coding, and lag further behind on open-ended scientific tasks such as physics and biology.

0:00 Distillation only explains a one-to-two-month gap
Distillation is a technique Chinese labs use commonly, training their own models on the outputs of stronger models, but the author estimates that even if distillation were blocked entirely, for instance by deploying KYC tools at Anthropic and OpenAI, the gap between the strongest US models and Chinese open-weight models would widen by only 1-2 months. Distillation matters most in new domains, and it cannot easily produce a comprehensively strong final model. Chinese labs ship faster and have a narrower task distribution, which slightly inflates scores on public benchmarks, because all labs keep improving and later-released models naturally score higher.

0:00 US companies are already building products on Chinese models
Harvey, Cursor and DoorDash use Kimi, Airbnb uses Qwen, and Perplexity uses DeepSeek. A large number of young Silicon Valley startups use Chinese models to get a low-cost, flexible option. US startups sign enterprise agreements with Chinese model labs to license products for use, a new form of cross-border technology cooperation the author has not seen in his career. On OpenRouter, the Chinese model share has grown from about 70% to more than 80%, and weekly processed tokens have grown from about 1 trillion in September 2025 to about 80 trillion today. On OpenCode, Chinese models account for about 95% or more of inference volume.

0:00 Academia has been taken over by Qwen
The author scanned papers in the five most popular ML categories on arXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.LG, stat.ML). In January 2023, papers mentioning any open model were 2%; by September 2026 the figure reached 50%. In April-May 2023, of about 12,000 new papers, 2,600 mentioned at least one open-model family, 5.5% mentioned Llama and 1% mentioned Chinese models. At Llama's peak in fall 2024, 23% mentioned Llama and 7.5% mentioned Qwen. Today Llama is still mentioned by about 21% of papers, while Qwen has risen to 30%. Any Chinese open-weight model is mentioned by more than 40% of papers, versus 30% for the US.

0:00 US models get higher adoption at equal capability
Research shows that US models see disproportionately high adoption when capability and scale are comparable. OpenAI's gpt-oss, its first open-weight models after ChatGPT, became one of the most widely adopted open-weight models ever. Google's Gemma 4 is one of the few models whose adoption approaches Qwen's most popular small models. Nvidia's Nemotron, despite being more capable at the same scale, has seen middling adoption. This shows US models have brand and ecosystem advantages, but not enough to reverse the overall trend.

0:00 Open-model risk requires ecosystem-level preparation
The structural challenge of open-weight models is that there is almost no effective way to stop pieces of open-source software from falling into the wrong hands. If access to China's strongest open-weight models were restricted because of risk, the ones hurt would be US companies. HuggingFace once used a Chinese open-weight model to understand a cyberattack, because closed models refused the request. Managing open-weight model risk tends to come down to ecosystem preparation. Open models are becoming an essential tool for AI diffusion, and continuing to invest in US open models is the best path to staying ahead of these risks.

item.title: Poetry Is Not Democracy's Ornament but Its Pillar
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.description: Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free expression just as surely as censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape entirely through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.
item.content:encoded:
Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free expression just as surely as censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape entirely through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.

Not a literature class: a working poet who also heads the largest humanities funder in the country explains why close reading, naming and literacy are political capacities; the second half is harder than the opening.

5:32 The poet went to the scene instead of writing reflections
Rukeyser was not a poet who stayed in her study. At 19, while studying at Vassar, she felt she had to go south to sit in on the Scottsboro trial — staying at school simply wasn't an option; in 1936 she went to Spain to see the anti-Olympics mounted against the Berlin Games, and arrived just as the Spanish Civil War broke out; she also went to West Virginia to write about the Hawks Nest mine disaster — Union Carbide dug tunnels without wet drilling and without giving workers protective gear, the workers were mostly African American, and nearly all of them died of silicosis, which Alexander says may be the largest corporate industrial accident in American history. The conclusion: writing let more people know what happened, and connected people of different identities on shared human experience.

13:50 Art is democracy's pillar, not its illustration
She breaks democracy down into a question of language: who a collective is, what it values, which voices it contains — all of it takes shape through language, so without language there is no collective. When we talk about free speech we always fixate on journalism, but artists being censored, books being banned, teachers being told what they may teach — that moves the same foundation. Her wording is hard: art is not democracy's explanatory diagram, art is itself part of democracy — one of its pillars. And poetry doesn't just wave a flag for values; it is the thing itself. You can judge whether a democracy is healthy by whether art can still live in an unfettered space.

33:37 Close reading is critical thinking, and it can be taught
She describes close reading very plainly: a method, a practice, anyone can learn it, and its other name is critical thinking. Its uses aren't limited to poetry — you use it reading the newspaper, reading the propaganda around you, whether that propaganda comes from above or from advertising and very, very powerful culture. Figuring out how someone is working on you is a good thing. And in America many people are nervous about poetry, feeling they ‘aren't supposed to understand it’; her method is concrete: drop your shoulders, read it again, don't just read it on the page, read it aloud, then you read it to me — the same poem in a different person's voice, and you hear something different every time.

42:37 Misnaming people is an anti-democratic weapon
She says one of the most powerful weapons against democracy is misnaming people — calling people by the wrong name. In America there's a saying, calling people out of their names, which means flattening people, using insulting labels, even smearing the behavior of an entire people as a whole — this is abuse of language, its purpose is to wound and divide, and it is coming from the highest levels of government. She stresses one thing in particular: it has real consequences. Conversely, naming things precisely, saying what you mean, saying who you are, and receiving what others say — that itself is the capacity democracy requires.

47:58 Grief has to be put into language before you can hold it
Her husband Fikre died 14 years ago. She wrote a memoir shortly after his death, which surprised even her — she had never imagined writing one or showing it to anyone; it was more a way of landing, of knowing what she was going through: too overwhelming, too unprecedented, and turning some of it into language helped her name the feeling. Writing about him years later was different in kind, became a responsibility: this person was her ‘my person’, who lived a brave, extraordinary, beautiful life and left hundreds of paintings, now shown in museums and galleries. She is wary of herself too: she hopes she isn't wringing this experience dry.

57:30 Writing poetry means throwing away far more than you keep
She doesn't start a poem from ‘I want to write a poem about X’ but from a word, an image, a phrase that is ringing there, and she can't say why, so she writes it down again and again. She has a day job — almost all poets do — so the real question is: while you're busy with something else, where do you put the thought down. Fragments accumulate, and when she has time to sit down she asks which piece is still vibrating, still alive. How much do you write versus throw away? Her answer is one word: Most. A serious writer throws away many times what they keep, and it takes a little courage to keep writing when it's wrong. What really excites her is the editing stage, because ‘the beast is there’ — the shape is already visible.

1:02:17 The cost of college is a problem; learning is not
She pushes back directly on the claim that the humanities have no prospects: critical thinking, close reading, extracting meaning from complex texts, communicating persuasively, imagining other people's lives, understanding multiple cultures — these are capacities useful in any career. She doesn't deny that the cost of higher education is a real problem that really needs solving, but she puts her emphasis elsewhere: what's more worrying is the attack on the university itself, interference in its mission, and the loud repetition of the claim that ‘the university is not a valuable thing.’ Her last line is sharp: manufacturing an undereducated populace serves another purpose.

1:07:22 Those who cannot read are the easiest to control
‘free people read freely’ is a line from the poet and librarian Tracie D. Hall, and Alexander says she borrows it all day long. She reads those five words out of the African American tradition: under slavery, it was a crime for Black people to learn to read and write, and a crime for a free white person to teach them — what was being controlled was not the text but the people. So the line holds two halves: free people read freely, and, free people are meant to read. If a person cannot read, cannot access a great deal of information, they cannot understand their own life, and so lose the capacity to act on an understanding of how outside forces work on them. Where literacy is taken away, there is only one logic: this is how you are easier to control.

item.title: Literacy Once Democratised Europe; Now It Is Retreating
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.description: Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward a pre-literate age.
item.content:encoded:
Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward a pre-literate age.

Medium information density, but two mechanisms are worth hearing: "writing cools discourse" and "bad ideas are easier to whitewash on film"; the later section on pop music and reading is looser.

8:13 Literacy is historically extremely recent and fragile
Marriott stresses that we are so used to literacy that we forget how anomalous it is. By one estimate, in a certain ancient Mesopotamian city-state there may have been only 20 living people who could read and write; literacy in ancient Rome was around 10%. For thousands of years, reading and writing was not a cultural phenomenon but an esoteric code circulating within a wealthy scribal elite — some rulers were literate, some were not. The real turning point was printing: books could be reproduced in quantity, more people could read, and books became more practical; Protestantism then placed enormous emphasis on the written word, pushing more people to become literate in order to read the Bible. These factors fed each other until the "Reading Revolution" historians identify in the mid-to-late 18th century.

11:19 The Reading Revolution really did change the shape of politics
Roberts pushes back: if literacy exploded, why doesn't the world look turned upside down? Marriott's answer is that the spread of literacy has a democratising effect — the more people who can access information and ideas, the more people participate in politics and criticise power. Early 18th-century Europe was ruled by absolute monarchs, and political affairs were essentially court secrets discussed among a small elite; by the late 18th and early 19th centuries, newspapers appeared, the standing of absolute monarchs declined sharply, France became a republic, the authority of the British monarch was far weaker than at the start of the century, parliamentary debates were reported, and public affairs were no longer discussed only in court. He calls this the great age of democratic revolution and democratic reform, and ties it directly to the spread of literacy.

16:32 Writing forces bad ideas into logical form
Marriott concedes books are imperfect, but argues that the way a book organises information is more rational and more coherent than conversation, video or TikTok. Writing forces you to polish an idea repeatedly, externalising part of your mind onto the page and then testing it; a reader faces a fixed text and can reread and critically analyse it. More crucially, the book limits the means of non-logical persuasion — you cannot bypass argument with charisma, shouting or tears. He uses the Nazis as a counterexample: Hitler's Mein Kampf was unreadable even to senior Nazis, because Nazism simply does not hold together once it is required to be presented coherently as a written text; Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will, meanwhile, is treated as an artistic masterpiece, screened in film classes, and regarded as an extremely powerful argument for fascism. Bad ideas are easier to whitewash on a screen than in a book.

25:05 The Republic of Letters filtered out trolls through writing
The 17th- and 18th-century European "Republic of Letters" was a community of thinkers, philosophers and scientists who wrote to each other and ran journals. The economic historian Joel Mokyr rates it extraordinarily highly, saying it is the single cultural fact that explains the Industrial Revolution. Marriott's mechanism is this: if a clever person sits alone in a village, his ideas can only be told to his neighbours, and scientific innovation struggles to accumulate; the spread of literacy let ideas travel further, more and more people joined the conversation, ideas flowed into one central pool, and thought grew more complex. Roberts adds that the key difference is not public versus private but who the participants are — in conversation with Adam Smith, David Hume and Newton, the standard is naturally high; it is a kind of "submission to that which cannot be enforced". Marriott concedes that the literacy barrier itself carries a benign elitism: you cannot burst in and shout like a troll on X, because nobody will pay attention to you.

34:49 The novel gives us a passage into other minds
Marriott believes there is a truth about life reachable only through prose fiction: it lets us see the inside of another person's mind. Reading is an active rather than passive process — you build images in your head out of the words on the page, which is why it feels immersive, why it feels like having lived another life. Film cannot do this, because it gives you the external world and cannot enter another mind directly; and writing is precisely the medium we use to express what is in our minds, a communication of mind to mind. He also notes that oral poetry takes little interest in the subtle differences between human consciousnesses, and that this capacity to "inhabit another mind" appears only in prose fiction. Roberts does not fully agree, arguing that great films can get close through dialogue, but concedes that film almost never captures the inner activity that is conveyed by more than dialogue.

47:59 The post-literate commentator is more like Homer
Marriott writes that the post-literate commentator does not explain and analyse the world like the print-era public intellectual, but is more like an oral storyteller, weaving strange and unforgettable tales for a spellbound audience. Roberts calls this the deepest insight in the whole piece: faced with the mass of absurd, untenable claims online, people habitually interrogate them by the author's standard — "that isn't logical", "where's the evidence?" — but these people are not in that business at all. Their job is to entertain the audience; truth does not matter, what matters is a story that keeps the audience spellbound. Marriott goes further: presenting an argument logically, supplying evidence, driving to a rational conclusion — these are not in fact natural to human communication; in an oral culture, the more effective way to persuade someone is to entertain him, move him, get angry at him. Writing imposes an impersonal, more rational form of communication, and it is not a necessary product of human communication.

53:59 The richness of pop music also feeds off reading
Roberts gives an example from The History of Rock and Roll in 500 Songs: the opening of Jagger's "Sympathy for the Devil" is taken directly from Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita — the novel opens with two Russian intellectuals mocking God and faith, after which a suave gentleman appears, they take him for mad, and finally realise he is Satan. Marriott calls this an "annoyingly good" example and regrets not having put it in the book. He concedes it cannot be pushed too far — it is not that you have to move Penguin Classics into the British Library to join a boy band — but Bob Dylan and Paul McCartney are both obviously heavy readers. He cites research showing that over the past 20 years pop songs have become less complex in both lyrics and melody, partly because the environment favours the simple and the immediate: to go viral on TikTok, a song has to grab you within three or four seconds.

58:17 The future of reading will be deliberate, like fitness
Marriott stresses this is not a new phenomenon: statistics on the decline of serious reading go back to the 1950s and 1960s, television was the beginning of the screen age, and the remote control was the first scroll. Roberts quotes what his father said at the time — books have existed for centuries, television has been a mass medium for only 20 years, let's see if it lasts — and concedes his father should have worried more. Marriott's consolation comes from the analogy with junk food and fitness: McDonald's arrived, many people got fat, but some people realised that health could no longer be absorbed naturally from the environment and required deliberate effort, so they started running and going to the gym. He guesses cognitive health will follow the same path: if reading has a future, it will become more deliberate, less "I'm bored at the airport, I'll pick up a book" and more "I value this experience, so I sit down for half an hour to an hour every night". He admits this makes him a little sad, because reading will become more artificial, no longer the unavoidable part of life it once was.

item.title: A Glass of Water Has No Final Truth: Quantum Mechanics Forces Us to Abandon the Single Perspective
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.description: Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is multiple perspectives that enrich one another but never converge.
item.content:encoded:
Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is multiple perspectives that enrich one another but never converge.

A four-person roundtable crossing physics, poetry, drama and economics; high density of quotable lines but the argument is loose. Worth listening if you want a few perspectives that can change your judgment; skip it if you want hard information.

2:06 A glass of water has no final version
Rovelli opens with a glass of water the BBC provided: you look from one side, I look from the other, you wear glasses, I see a different colour. This glass of water can be a physical object (mass, velocity, position), it can be temperature and pressure, it can be the chemistry of H2O plus floating bits, it can be the global economy of being bottled in Italy and shipped to England, or it can simply be "we want to drink it." His claim is that these perspectives are all real, none exhausts another, none contradicts another, and there is no "ultimate glass of water." This is anti-Platonic — he does not accept a distinction between a "level of appearances" and a "fundamental level."

6:13 We have not yet digested quantum mechanics
Rovelli says what he is describing is not borrowed from philosophy but grown from inside physics. Physicists ran into quantum phenomena; quantum mechanics is an enormous revolution, but "we have not yet digested quantum mechanics" — the newspaper stories about experiments that "confirm what I learned in a textbook in the 1970s" show precisely that we do not yet truly believe it. Take quantum mechanics seriously and what it says is this: the Enlightenment dream of "a complete, determinate, clear description of reality independent of the observer" does not hold. The observer here need not be a human; anything that interacts with something counts.

8:19 The deepest level of reality is not more objective
Rovelli turns it around: the most basic level of reality physics can reach is not essentially different from the reality Lavinia deals with in poetry, or the characters in James's play deal with in economics — both are realities that allow different views, not a reality that is "absolutely objective underneath." So quantum physics is not that hard; it has simply not been digested. The concrete physical phenomena are of course very complex, but poetry is complex and economics is complex too.

10:25 Scientists have always used metaphors
Rovelli says the words Lavinia uses could be lifted line by line into his book. What is an electron? "It is a grain, a grain of sand, but it is not really a grain of sand." Why is an electric field called a field? Because it is "a bit like a field in the countryside." We think through metaphors, by taking old concepts apart and assembling a new concept from a piece of each. The goal is not to arrive at a final, perfect description of reality — a century ago we thought we could, but it does not work — but to gain a better understanding, a better way of navigating reality. He adds a crucial qualification: admitting that everything has a perspective does not mean all perspectives are equivalent, nor that there is no better and worse; it is only that the hope of "arriving at the final correct story about reality" is empty — not unreachable, but meaningless.

12:27 Seeking an ultimate morality is itself the error
Rovelli turns from "complexity" to "value": if you ask "what is the ultimate definition of good and evil, what is universal ethics," he thinks this is itself a morally and ethically mistaken approach. Our morals and values are powerful, important and indispensable not because they are outside us, but because they are inside us, and therefore equally perspectival. This passage connects directly to James Graham's play — whose first line is "what is a good life."

15:30 Do not be afraid to learn a jargon
Lavinia Greenlaw argues for embracing jargon: not everyone has to learn it, but if you are genuinely interested in something, do not be afraid to learn its language — a mechanic has to learn the names of parts, a surgeon has to learn the names of parts, and a poet has to as well. It lets you see more clearly, and it lets you see where something has gone wrong. She admits jargon can be exclusionary, but "that depends on the context in which you use it," and "you can perform difficulty, poets and poems are probably very good at that, but that is not what difficulty means." She gives the example of poems on the subway: before everyone looked at their phones, people would read a poem first and only then realise they were reading a poem, and that engagement was far more direct and confident than sitting down and being told "now you are going to read a poem."

22:55 Friction is treated as a problem to be solved
James Graham says modern culture has fetishised "efficiency" and stripped out every layer of difficulty as friction. He gives a concrete image: emailing himself a script to save it, a prompt pops up — "this is a long document, shall I summarise it for you?" — and his reaction is "how rude, I want you to sit inside it and read." He connects this back to Bloomsbury and Keynes: meaning is discovered precisely in the friction, in the difficulty, in the process. He also says the collapse of reading is despairing, because reading demands personal investment, and today that investment is treated as a problem to be solved rather than something to be celebrated.

26:05 War refuses to acknowledge complexity
Rovelli uses the International Day of Peace on 21 September and the statements of the UN Secretary-General and the Pope to connect the perspectival argument to war: war is to a large extent driven by greed and power games, but it always wraps itself in a hypocritical narrative — there is only one truth, only one good, we are the good ones, they are the bad ones, we tell the truth, they tell lies and propaganda. So war is built on a total refusal to be prepared to accept complexity, perspectives, and worldviews different from our own. The host Adam Rutherford raises a counterexample on the spot: we also always need to pursue simplicity; if you embrace difficulty and act the scholar all day, you may end up achieving nothing and enjoying nothing. Lavinia's response pulls the topic back to rhetoric: language therefore matters more than ever, and poetry and poetics can teach people how to argue.

item.title: Apple has no frontier model of its own, but wants to win again with a foldable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.description: Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event introduced no new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.
item.content:encoded:
Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event introduced no new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.

Mark Gurman is the most accurate reporter on Apple, and this episode strings executive turnover, the AI roadmap, the privacy controversy and foldable predictions into one line, with high information density.

5:09 The biggest difference between Ternus and Cook is willingness to make the call
Gurman says the event was almost interchangeable with the Cook era, with the only difference being that Ternus opened by laying out a view on AI. The mechanism he gives is management style: you bring an idea to Cook and he keeps probing with questions, in many cases not making a single decision — it's collective decision-making; you bring it to Ternus and he gives you a decision, gives you an opinion, you may hate the opinion, but he has a position. Gurman stresses this is exactly the biggest difference between the two men from talking to insiders, and it explains why Ternus talked about AI first thing on stage.

8:20 The 2026 event had not a single new AI feature
Gurman points out that Apple held a big product event in September 2026 yet launched no notable new AI feature, and the roughly 15-minute opening just retold the past two years of Apple Intelligence. His explanation: Apple has gone as far on AI as it can and can only tell the best story with the cards it holds; and Apple has no AI-centric device at all, so it has to prop up the iPhone as its AI device until a killer device appears and it can switch narratives.

13:29 Under Cook, Apple became an institution
Gurman draws a distinction between the Cook era and the Jobs era: in the Cook era people's relationship with Apple is a relationship with an institution — global, enormous, like IBM; the Jobs era was one new product after another redefining categories. He also corrects the host's read on Vision Pro — every time he writes that Vision Pro is on life support, he gets dozens of reactions close to death-threat level, because some people have built businesses around spatial computing and some consumers paid four thousand dollars for it.

20:45 Apple swapped out the old guard one by one over five years
Gurman reconstructs the rhythm of the handover: in 2023 Cook began saying at every executive meeting that succession had to be taken seriously; at the time the top ranks either had five hundred million in the bank or were billionaires, and were close in age. So they lined up an order and went one by one — at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, replaced by Kevin Parekh; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, succeeded by his deputy; in 2026 the general counsel changed, with Jennifer Newstead poached from Meta; and only at the end of 2026 did Cook hand off to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy Hotel California: you never want to leave.

28:07 The chip chief was kept with a title invented on the spot
Gurman says the second most important person at Apple now is the hardware head, who built Apple Silicon, Apple's key differentiator. In late summer or early autumn last year he went to tell Cook he was quitting, right in the middle of preparations for Ternus's succession. Cook had him stay to take part in the transition and promised him the title of chief hardware officer, which Apple had never had, letting him keep his existing team and also take over Ternus's side of the business. Gurman judges this is not a long-term arrangement and that the man already wants to leave again — he conquered the Mac, shed Intel and Qualcomm, and Apple has no next goal, so he may leave within a year or two, at which point the hardware engineering team will have to be split up again, because no successor carries his industry weight.

33:15 Willing to spend tens of billions on a modem, yet says it needn't own AI
Gurman finds the most absurd thing to be executives saying in interviews over the past year that "we never owned search, we don't need to own AI." He counters: these are two completely different things, and Apple spent tens of billions to own an already commoditized cellular modem, acquiring and fixing Intel's modem business — willing to do that for a modem but unwilling to own AI is ridiculous. The internal idea was originally to partner with Google as a stopgap until it could build its own models, but Gurman says he has seen no evidence that Apple is restarting its own model effort, making big AI acquisitions, or paying AI researchers top salaries.

48:53 All-day transcription on the watch stepped on the privacy landmine
Gurman's reaction to the Apple Watch's all-day listening feature was "I can't believe they did it." The feature only transcribes, doesn't record or store, and a double tap shows you the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their consent. He says Apple knows the next-generation interface needs some degree of always-on capture, but the societal privacy problem is unsolved: technical white papers, private cloud compute and encryption can't hold back the social backlash. He thinks Apple could have put audio and visual intelligence together next year and told one coherent privacy story; as it is, it's boiling the frog slowly.

57:05 Foldables will become the new normal within a decade
Gurman offers a bold prediction: foldables will become the new normal within a decade. He draws an analogy with smartphone penetration — at the end of 2006 smartphones were about 6% of the market, now 85%, crossing the halfway mark five or six years later; the iPhone itself wasn't that source, but it pulled everyone into the smartphone game, and he thinks the iPhone Duo will do the same for the phone market. He also mentions the iPhone's number migration feature, hinting the future may be a combination of a foldable for work and a smaller, lighter phone for weekends with family.

item.title: The Real Bottleneck in the Treasury Market: Not Size, but Not Enough Intermediaries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-macromusings-美债市场真正的瓶颈-不是规模-是中间商不够用了/
