item.description: Primary dealer balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers gave way to high-frequency traders — but those traders retreated en masse in March 2020. That is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.
item.content:encoded:
Primary dealer balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers gave way to high-frequency traders — but those traders retreated en masse in March 2020. That is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.

A frontline New York Fed operator explains Treasury market structure, with empirical data from two 2025 papers and the latest TBAC developments. High information density.

11:26 The Treasury market is so big it has to attract new buyers
Golay gives the scale: CBO counts $30 trillion in outstanding Treasuries at the end of 2025, and projects another $26 to $27 trillion over the next decade. The market splits into two parts — the cash market (buying and selling Treasuries directly, partly through electronic inter-dealer broker trading and partly dealer-to-client) and the repo market (borrowing against Treasuries as collateral, intermediated mainly by dealers). A market this large and growing necessarily has to attract different types of investors, including high-frequency traders and hedge funds that are more sensitive to price.

14:31 High-frequency traders went from zero to the main force in electronic markets
Golay calls these firms principal trading firms (PTFs), which mostly use high-frequency strategies and trade on electronic platforms. Twenty years ago they were not in the Treasury market at all; today they may account for the majority of trading in the electronic cash market. The turning point was the 2014 flash rally — yields moved sharply and no one could explain why, and the official sector began to truly understand the growth of PTFs in electronic markets, which also sparked the IAWG's work to study market structure and obtain better data.

16:33 Primary dealer balance sheets have not kept up with the growth in outstanding Treasuries
Golay cites a chart from a Darrell Duffie paper: the size of primary dealer balance sheets devoted to intermediating Treasuries has completely failed to keep pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Part of the reason is post-2008 reforms, and part is simply that the stock itself has grown too fast. The result is that the market has had to attract more price-sensitive types of investors. She also corrects a common impression: it is not that PTFs always retreat during volatility — in other volatile periods the official sector has observed PTFs increasing their activity; but in March 2020, everyone retreated.

19:42 The essence of all-to-all is bypassing dealer matching
All-to-all trading is literally that: any participant in the Treasury market can trade with any other participant. This is nothing new in the equity market, but the Treasury market is largely over-the-counter and dealer-intermediated, so it is not. Golay points out that entering the March 2020 crisis, dealers already had a lot of Treasuries piled up on their balance sheets, and when the wave of selling hit there was no intermediation capacity left. If counterparties could be matched without going through a dealer, that might ease things. But she says plainly that at the time most people were selling, and it is hard to imagine all-to-all perfectly solving that situation — it is just that every incremental improvement helps.

22:51 All-to-all is stuck on the absence of counterparty matching
One of the paper's core findings: in the off-the-run market, if you look at a 15-minute window, almost no one wants to buy the same off-the-run security you want to sell. Stretch the window to a day and the match rate rises to 60% to 70%. Golay mentions possible directions for innovation, such as an end-of-day batch auction, and some institutions already have this capability. But to date, no case in this area has actually gotten off the ground successfully. She also notes that expanding central clearing could push the transition to all-to-all, because you would not need to establish bilateral clearing arrangements with every counterparty — only to connect to a central counterparty.

29:06 Off-the-run is 97% of the stock but a liquidity backwater
Off-the-run refers to older Treasuries, ranging from those issued three months ago to 29- and 30-year ones, and they make up about 97% of outstanding Treasuries. The selling in the March 2020 dash for cash was mainly off-the-run, and the off-the-run market is dealer-intermediated, with no all-to-all. Golay and colleagues at the Board of Governors and the New York Fed did empirical work using TRACE data collected by FINRA, in which transaction-level data is visible only to the official sector. The conclusion: the older the Treasury, the worse its liquidity — larger price impact, lower volume, wider bid-ask spreads.

31:15 The cheapest to deliver can revive liquidity
Another finding of the paper: when an off-the-run Treasury becomes the cheapest to deliver into a Treasury futures contract, its liquidity becomes better than that of comparable off-the-run securities. This suggests the off-the-run problem is partly about trading activity itself — with trading activity, liquidity improves; without it, liquidity deteriorates. On policy implications, Golay mentions that Treasury buybacks can create trading activity around off-the-run securities and improve liquidity; central clearing makes clearing smoother; and as for reducing the number of issuance dates and making individual issues larger, the paper reaches no conclusion, because investors also like the finer granularity of monthly issuance.

36:33 TBAC put the brakes on expanding transparency
At a recent TBAC meeting, a member suggested expanding transparency of Treasury trading data: there is already market-wide aggregate statistics, as well as transaction-level data for on-the-run securities; the suggestion was to consider publishing transaction-level data for Treasury bills, and more frequent on-the-run data. But TBAC expressed caution about expanding transparency in other areas, including the off-the-run and TIPS markets. Golay says this is interesting, because data transparency has been a focus of the IAWG's work in recent years and was listed as a priority in 2021. She personally thinks small incremental transparency is beneficial, but understands that in less liquid markets, releasing too much information can make intermediation very difficult.

item.title: Stanford Has a Secret Course That Teaches 12 People How to Extract Value From Others
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-grayarea-斯坦福有一门秘密课程-教12个人如何从他人身上提取价值/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-grayarea-斯坦福有一门秘密课程-教12个人如何从他人身上提取价值/
item.category: The Gray Area with Sean Illing
item.description: The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO about extracting value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has long rewarded.
item.content:encoded:
The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO about extracting value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has long rewarded.

Not a vague critique of Silicon Valley but a specific investigation with course names, dollar figures and people's names; if you care about early-stage investing and talent pipelines, the detail density is high.

5:12 You can take hundreds of thousands of dollars before you have a company
Pre-idea funding was the newest layer of the game when Theo arrived on campus: give an 18-year-old who just got there hundreds of thousands, even millions, of dollars, sign a one-page SAFE check, agree that "if you start a company later, come back to us" — otherwise the money never has to be repaid. For a VC it's pocket change; they don't really believe in these hyped-up teenagers, and they don't need you personally to succeed — one overnight sensation is enough. Meanwhile students are encouraged to make enormous promises and then discover again and again that no one follows up: lie, and there are no consequences.

13:22 The secret course teaches extracting value
Stanford has a course that isn't in the catalog, called How to Rule the World, taught by a Silicon Valley CEO who styles himself a professor, admitting only 12 students a year — merely knowing it exists is a status symbol. Its central assignment is extracting value from people, with a strong whiff of the ends justifying the means. One woman Theo interviewed said the course taught her how to lie to VCs to raise money — she later raised millions, dropped out of Stanford, despite having already been caught cheating in a computer science class; months later she put out a glossy launch video for a technology that didn't exist, and Silicon Valley cheered her on anyway, she moved into a mansion, and was invited back to Stanford to speak.

26:46 Ethics isn't a premise; getting caught is what counts
During ethics week in the intro computer science course, the professor discussed a software defect that killed four people on a radiation therapy machine, and the TA asked who in the room cared about ethics — Theo was the only one who raised his hand. Weeks later a classmate told him he was taking a business ethics course, and "we're all just there to figure out how they got caught." He didn't sense these people needed to pretend to care; when Sam Bankman-Fried was under house arrest in the house on the Stanford campus where he grew up, students made pilgrimages, threw parties themed around him, and said they wanted to replicate his success minus the final fall. A colleague's summary of the money that mysteriously vanished at Tree Hacks: it's all just a little bit of fraud.

38:01 The real reason the president fell wasn't the data
Board members who ousted Marc Tessier-Lavigne later told Theo that one of the heaviest reasons they gave was his posture — a highly aggressive public stance when challenged, deny, deny, deny, plus the threatening letters sent by the lawyer he hired, Steve Neal, which embarrassed the university. Theo found no evidence he personally falsified data: the problem was in the lab he oversaw, where subordinates fabricated data in papers he co-authored, including the 2009 paper claiming to have found the cause of Alzheimer's, while internal company results before publication showed its core finding was "at best unreliable." He was asked to retract and refused, dragging it out for a decade. What drove him out was image management, not the data.

39:01 Four days after being ousted, the mansion closed
Four days after the board unanimously removed him, Tessier-Lavigne closed on a 7,600-square-foot mansion in "America's most expensive zip code," valued at over $10 million; eight months later he announced he had raised $1 billion for a new company doing AI biotech. Of the two VCs that led the round, an investor at one messaged Theo two months later to rib him, followed by a winking emoji; an investor at the other offered him money to start a company. Theo says it's the most Silicon Valley thing you can imagine: everything can be monetized, even taking down a university president turns into an invitation.

45:44 Duck syndrome: paddling furiously under the surface
Duck syndrome is a word Stanford coined itself: students glide elegantly across the surface like ducks, seeming to do everything effortlessly, while underneath their legs paddle furiously just to stay afloat. Katie Meyer was its best illustration — women's soccer captain, led the team to an NCAA title, headed to law school, didn't drink, didn't smoke, didn't speed. Months before graduation, late on a Friday night, after every student support office had closed, she received a letter: because six months earlier she had spilled coffee on a football player (she said it was an accident, he said it was deliberate), her degree was suspended. That night she took her own life. Afterwards 12 schools paid tribute to her; Stanford was not among them; the women's soccer team she had just captained held a mental health night and didn't mention her name.

52:01 A legendary professor's fraud case, and the school says it never heard of it
Stan Cohen was the first geneticist to transplant a gene from one living organism into another; his 1970s recombinant DNA technique gave rise to the model of universities making money from patents; in its last valid year, that patent contributed 62% of all Stanford patent revenue. In his freshman year, Theo found that Cohen had been found by a court to have committed fraud: he promised investors a drug target that might cure Huntington's disease, and said the drug was already approved to treat another disease, without telling them it had been permanently banned by the FDA in 1976 because it was lethal. He was ultimately ordered to pay $29 million and paid it. Theo asked the university, and the university replied it had never heard of the case and had no involvement at all — even though Stanford owned the relevant intellectual property and had been subpoenaed by the court.

55:04 Raising money is easier than getting an internship, and that itself is a signal
The saying circulating in Stanford's inner circles is that raising money for a startup is easier than landing an internship — Theo says that's absurd, it shouldn't be that way, but that's the status quo. He describes the moment as a game of AI musical chairs: everyone is waiting to see who's still standing when the music stops and who's left holding the bag. He isn't worried about cash-flow-positive companies like Meta and Google; he's worried about the companies clinging to the AI narrative that have no technology of their own, no revenue, and no ability to generate revenue — they can't hold on, and they will collapse. But he also cautions that Silicon Valley hasn't held power for long, that it's a very immature power system that hasn't grown guardrails, transparency or accountability, and that one collapse doesn't necessarily mean a reckoning.

item.title: America's Manufacturing Hollowing-Out Is Not a Capability Problem, It's a Financial Return Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.description: Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statements, while China manages it like national security; tariffs are just an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is to stop American consumers from subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statements, while China manages it like national security; tariffs are just an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is to stop American consumers from subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.

Two frontline hardware founders explain the real bottlenecks of American reindustrialization: not technology, but trust, cost, and supply chain definitions. High information density, with the second half's breakdown of tariffs and subsidies being the most valuable.

2:02 The reserve currency is the first step of decline
Chris Power gave a four-step cycle: great powers first have a generative population and the best industrial capacity, then win or prevent a war, then become extremely lazy, and finally outsource the things that made them successful. He says this cycle repeats roughly every 150 years: the Netherlands gave way to Britain, Britain gave way to America, and each time industrial power was re-traded for financial power, the world's reserve currency changed. This judgment was the starting point for him founding Hadrian: you think you're Mike Tyson at his peak, but your opponent thinks you're the Mike Tyson before Buster Douglas knocked him out.

9:10 90% of the factory floor is a software problem
Chris Power says the biggest misconception about advanced manufacturing is that seeing people moving things in a factory means it's a humanoid robot problem. In reality, 90% of advanced manufacturing is smart people sitting at computers doing digital engineering, or operating a very dumb computer on the shop floor. Welders or machinists have to stand in front of machines because the system isn't closed-loop; they do trigonometry in their heads to judge whether the tool is about to break. So Hadrian positions itself as a software company, doing the work of breaking physical tasks into high-judgment setups, then handing them off to robots, CNC, or welding systems for execution.

14:14 Software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in Los Angeles
Tom Mueller says the aerospace talent ecosystem in Southern California is recovering; three or four years after SpaceX was founded in 2002, the aerospace employment curve in the South Bay started to rise. He lists what this area is simultaneously doing: nuclear energy companies, drone companies, defense companies, 3D printing companies, and Anduril in Orange County. The two companies poach from each other and compete for talent; Northrop Grumman is right across the street from Impulse. Tom's summary: software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in Los Angeles.

15:17 Vertical integration is to learn the problem, not to save money
Tom Mueller explains the real logic of SpaceX-style vertical integration: the first development engine or spacecraft must be built in-house, because you need to learn all the assembly and machining problems during the prototype phase. If you hand it to a machine shop from the start, and the drawings have problems or the parts don't fit when made, you learn nothing. Once the design converges, then you outsource. Chris Power adds that every company should keep 10% to 15% of in-house capacity, because there's always a "hot pan" moment when you need a genius to make something within an hour to meet a flight milestone, but scale must happen externally.

16:18 Outsourcing decisions are about trust, not finance
Chris Power says what's bought and sold in manufacturing is trust. Hadrian's vertical integration strategy is to outsource as much as possible to every reindustrialization startup and small business, because there are too many projects to run. But they will vertically integrate the links where they "don't believe you can deliver on time." This isn't a financial trade-off; they'd rather spend an extra two million dollars on equipment and hire a team than bet the risk on a traditional foundry that has been late on every submarine project for the past thirty years. His exact words: most of America is incompetent when it comes to trust and scheduling.

19:20 In WWII, America was China
Chris Power uses WWII as an analogy: German engineers crushed America in engineering, but America wore them down with McDonald's-style mass production and better logistics. He says America played the role in WWII that China plays today—not by having the best engineering, but by producing the most. Now the situation is reversed: U.S. missile stockpiles run out in seven days in war games, China built 2,600 ships while America built six. His conclusion: you can have the best Raytheon missiles, but if you can't mass-produce them, you have no options.

21:23 The robot bottleneck is training data velocity
Chris Power says the robot competition ultimately depends on software, and software, especially AI, now depends on the velocity of training data, which in turn depends on physical-world deployment—that is, mass manufacturing. So this isn't a friendly competition between American companies over "whether Tesla sells more Optimus units or Google wins"; it's a civilization-level confrontation. Tom Mueller adds from the space perspective: building on the Moon and Mars requires robot legions rather than humans, because the environment is too dangerous and too expensive; good robots need three things—dexterous hands, vision which is basically solved, and an AI brain.

29:40 Tariffs are an imperfect corrective tool
Chris Power says manufacturing has four inputs: energy, labor, cost of capital, and export tariffs. He has done the math: even if Hadrian's labor costs and energy costs were both zero, importing components from China would still be three times cheaper than buying raw materials in America and making them yourself. He believes China has operated industrial policy as national security since 1985, subsidizing energy, labor, capital, and export tariffs, while America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement returns. The problem with tariffs is enforcement: banning only China and not Singapore means Chinese companies route through Singapore; differences in definitions of raw materials and assembly also inadvertently hurt American companies importing components from Mexico.

item.title: He Cooked the Chickpea Pasta Into Mush, Then Survived by Telling People to Steep It Like Tea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.description: Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board: 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said "steep it like tea" and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.
item.content:encoded:
Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board: 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said "steep it like tea" and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.

The founder's oral account is dense with failure detail: three scrapped production batches, a kidney stone, being thrown out of the factory, a 30% week-over-week decline. Worth hearing for anyone who wants to know how you survive a near-death moment.

5:14 The starting point wasn't a business insight, it was a case of rhinitis
In college, Brian's fridge held nothing but hummus, eating was just "fuel" to him, and he cycled between antibiotics and steroids for so long he was nearly facing surgery. It was his father, an orthodontist, who got him to try an elimination diet, and that's how he found that wheat-based foods triggered his sinus inflammation — one beer and the next day he couldn't breathe. The ENT told him: I don't know what you're talking about, but if it works, keep doing it. That private problem later became the product definition: high-protein, high-fiber, gluten-free pasta, doing what Chobani did for yogurt.

10:26 The first recipe had chia in it and was too sticky to look at
He bought Bob's Red Mill chickpea flour on Amazon and followed blogs for combinations. The first version was chickpeas plus eggs plus chia — the chia was too sticky and the result was ugly. With no rolling pin he used a wine bottle; with no pasta cutter he used a knife, dusting flour on the table as he cut to keep it from sticking. The second version dropped the chia, leaving just chickpeas and eggs, and was clearly better, but to make it usable for more people he added back tapioca starch and xanthan gum and stuck to a vegan route. His first capital expenditure was an Atlas Mercado hand-crank pasta machine, about $30 on Amazon. He got up at 5 a.m. every day to make pasta, put on country music, and his roommates thought he was insane.

20:49 Going from 200 pounds an hour to 1,000 magnified every mistake
They first found a tiny gluten-free factory in Michigan that could only do 150 to 200 pounds an hour — wildly inefficient, but they could learn as they went. To get into 190 Meijer stores and 2 Eataly locations, that capacity wasn't enough, so they found what was then the largest gluten-free pasta factory in the country, outside Los Angeles. The problem: that plant had only ever run rice and corn pasta, never legumes. After scaling to roughly 1,000 pounds an hour, the pasta coming out looked fine but turned into total mush the moment it was boiled. Each trial run was 8,000 to 10,000 pounds, and a failure meant the mold costs and ingredient costs were all gone, while they had only a little over $100,000 on hand.

26:02 He got thrown out of the factory for asking the line operator
After several failed trial runs, Brian ignored the other side's objections and went straight to the operator on the production line to ask what was actually going wrong. The worker said, "This corn smells weird," and he answered: that's not corn, we're not making corn pasta today, it's chickpeas. He realized on the spot that communication had broken down completely, and right after that he was escorted out of the plant. At the same time, the distributor was threatening him: if you don't fulfill this purchase order, you'll never work with this retailer again. He later estimated this shipment would cost nearly every dollar they had.

28:07 The solution was don't boil it — steep it like tea
With nowhere left to turn, they started testing: boil one minute, two minutes, three minutes, then skip boiling entirely — bring water to a boil, turn off the heat, and let the pasta sit in the hot water. What came out of steeping was better than what came out of boiling, or at least it didn't fall apart. Brian says he wasn't proud of the product, and it even hurt to sell it under his own brand, but he knew it was a life-or-death question. The packaging was already printed, so they could only make extra stickers reading "Banza is easier to cook than regular pasta — steep it like tea," then find people to hand-apply them to 20,000 boxes. Once that shipment went out, they immediately pulled back from the big factory and returned to the small one in Michigan.

35:18 The box is orange because every other pasta box is blue
They noticed that nearly every pasta package on the shelf at the time was blue — Brian put it as "you'd think they'd colluded." Orange contrasts most strongly with blue, and orange was also the color he loved growing up watching Nickelodeon, so it became the brand color. The packaging copy involved trade-offs too: putting "chickpeas" in the most prominent spot would scare off a lot of people, and so would gluten-free, so the gluten-free certification was moved to the side while the front led with high protein and high fiber — making consumers feel this was "a product for me," not "a product that isn't for me."

41:31 The glyphosate report knocked weekly sales down by a third
Moms Across America published a report saying glyphosate residue had been detected in Banza products. Brian saw the Google alert during a one-on-one meeting; he says his heart sank and his mind jumped twenty steps ahead. He wanted to verify first, so he only issued a statement saying "we are investigating" — which was nowhere near enough for the most panicked people. The lab results were delayed again and again, dragging on for three weeks. The final published result was 98% lower than the allegation, but not zero — still a very low level, and below the EWG's risk benchmark. He decided to make the supply chain 100% traceable and joined the Detox Project's certification system.

52:15 The natural channel recovered far more slowly than ordinary channels
Sales recovery was a mixed bag: some channels came back better than before, but the natural channel recovered much more slowly — and that was precisely the customer base with the best repeat purchase rates and the highest sales per store. Brian says this actually makes sense, because natural-channel consumers are the most susceptible to this kind of information. What he does now: keep alerts on for anywhere Banza and glyphosate are mentioned, personally go on Reddit to reply and add context, with the goal of making it impossible for the story to be seen without its context. He also admits he should have acknowledged what was happening faster and more visibly at the time.

item.title: AI Won't Replace People — What Replaces Them Is Work That Was Never Written Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.description: Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that map of work is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company training its own model.
item.content:encoded:
Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that map of work is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company training its own model.

Daniel Dines breaks down the real bottleneck of AI inside the enterprise from UiPath's front line, with a high density of counter-consensus claims — for anyone trying to judge the pace of enterprise AI adoption.

6:17 AI does not change its own weights on the job
Daniel argues the biggest difference between AI and humans is not reasoning ability, but that AI does not change its own weights on the job. A human is changed by a job; AI just writes things into a notebook. He gives the example of two chefs: one who has cooked Japanese cuisine for 20 years, one who has cooked Italian for 20 years. Give them the same recipe and what they produce is completely different. This is not something you can replicate by writing the company down on paper, because human judgment comes from years of being reshaped by the work. So on the claim that there are "millions of Einsteins in the data center," Daniel thinks what Dario meant is millions of entities with partial reasoning ability — not Einsteins who can learn on the job the way a person does.

16:29 Probabilistic tech shouldn't do work that demands precision
Daniel raises another limit on AI: precision. Every step AI takes is probabilistic — even if each step is 99% correct, after 100 steps the overall success rate may be only 60%. So if you have AI do long multiplication over and over, it will eventually get it wrong. His conclusion: just because a tool can do something doesn't mean you should use it for that thing. ChatGPT looks like it is doing arithmetic, but behind the scenes it is calling a computer tool — the precision is not coming from ChatGPT. Extend that logic to the enterprise: all work that demands precision should run on precise technology, and there is no reason for it to run on probabilistic technology.

18:34 Deploying AI hasn't gotten easier; deploying automation has
Daniel points to an asymmetry inside the enterprise: deploying AI agents is no easier than it was two years ago, but deploying automation has become much easier, because you can use coding agents to generate the automation. He lists ChatGPT, chain of thoughts and coding agents as the three main milestones. Coding agents work at "design time": people use them to build automations that run precisely every time at "execution time"; and when an automation breaks because an upstream system changed, AI can come back and fix it. The result is that AI is generating the software that runs the company, and that software cannot change its behavior in real time — it can be audited, tested and read by people. This is the pattern he sees taking shape in the enterprise right now.

23:46 Blind layoffs cut the people AI most needs
In his book Daniel introduces the concept of the "credentialed middle": companies used to hire for deep domain credentials in some field, and that is exactly the kind of expertise AI helps with most. His judgment is counterintuitive — you will be inclined to cut the people who are not the biggest experts in the domain, but those are precisely the people you will need to supplement expert work with AI. He gives the example of a law firm: it used to hire 25 interns a year, this year it hired only 4. He agrees most roles will need fewer people, but the key question is "which people." His criterion: keep the ones with the most initiative, who can maintain client relationships, who can mentor newcomers, who carry the company culture — because AI cannot show initiative in the human sense.

25:51 What decides whether AI can take over is how clear the framework is
Harry argues that work like finance and accounting is highly verifiable, and therefore easy for AI to replace. Daniel disagrees outright: it is not a question of verifiability, but of whether the work is framed by a framework someone else has already defined. He says finance is precisely an area where the framework is unclear — when an invoice or an order comes in, there can be different ways to handle it, such as whether Nvidia would ship to OpenAI first, and that kind of rule may never have been written down at all. If the rules are not captured by a framework, AI cannot learn them. So a company must first hand AI the "map of work": all workflows, all exceptions, all processes, all systems. This is also what he keeps stressing: models are interchangeable — the map of work and the processes built around it are where the real value is.

29:01 Use agents to interview employees and draw work as a map
UiPath has launched a technology called cartography, as a discipline to help companies surface how work actually gets done. Concretely, it uses a product called a cartographer agent to interview real business experts and have them record what they are doing, with the agent following up in real time: why did you change how you handled this invoice because the zip code was different? Why did you take the other path? That is how exceptions get dug out one by one. Then it aggregates data across multiple people to generate a real-time process map. With that "map of work" in hand, you then use coding agents to design how the process should be transformed, and ultimately, through "printing software," move the process from purely manual point A toward a state with fewer people operating systems and more automation and agentic AI operating systems.

34:15 Vibe coding is easy for prototypes, hard for production
Daniel admits UiPath tried vibe coding, and at first it looked astonishing, but pushing it into production hit a wall: connectors, permissions, auditing, security — all of it has to be maintained. He gives his own example of writing a procurement tool: it was initially written entirely by AI, but the database schema was completely wrong and someone had to rebuild the structure. His conclusion is that going from prototype to production is where the real work is, not writing the code itself. In the end you will very likely spend as much as, or more than, the tool you replaced — while also consuming the bandwidth of your best people. So he does not think systems of record like Salesforce will be replaced by vibe coding.

45:34 The opportunity in legal AI is in the process, not the model call
Harry does the math: the US legal industry is a $300 billion market, and if 30% of the labor can be replaced, that is $90 billion in revenue. Daniel counters that the $90 billion will not convert into token revenue — maybe only 10%, so a $10 billion token opportunity. His judgment: for producing a legal opinion, both open-source and frontier models are good enough; what is actually valuable is the custom workflow built around the legal process. If Harvey and Lagora just call a model once for you to get a legal opinion, that is not a hundred-billion-dollar market; but if they really draw the work as a map, build the workflows, and create a legal department for you, the value is far greater.

item.title: Even Legal-Cannabis States Can't Escape: A Federal Ban Is About to Empty the THC Shelves

item.description: A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even legal-cannabis states will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.
item.content:encoded:
A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even legal-cannabis states will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.

Eight minutes that explain how a regulatory loophole grew into an industry and how it gets cut off in one stroke — for anyone watching policy risk and regulatory arbitrage.

0:00 Legal-cannabis states can't escape a federal ban either
Recreational cannabis is legal in half of US states, but the reason THC drinks, vapes and gummies can be sold openly in states that ban cannabis is a loophole left by the 2018 farm bill: it allows low-concentration THC from hemp. After lab processing, that low concentration is enough to mimic a cannabis high, which is how you get Delta 8, Delta 9 — and, as the show jokes, by now Delta 11. Congress now wants to close the loophole, and it's using a stricter ban to do it. The key point is that this is a federal ban, so even if your state has legal cannabis, you get hit.

1:00 What's being banned is a $28 billion industry
The show puts the size at $28 billion and says the industry could disappear before the end of this year. Tennessee has already gone first: since July it has banned most THC hemp products, and a local reporter describes herself as already living in a ‘post-hemp world’. State legislators even beat Congress to it, banning full-spectrum CBD and smokable flower first. For retailers, farmers and processors, this isn't a policy debate — it's a choice that has to be made before year-end.

3:07 Farmers are going back from hemp to blackberries and corn
Tennessee farmer Lee Crabtree's farm used to grow mostly CBD-variety hemp, and the new state law makes selling those products illegal, so he's gone back to traditional seasonal crops like blackberries and corn. The family still has the industrial kitchen from its CBD food days, and now his wife Stacy uses that big stainless-steel counter to cut grapes for chicken salad to sell at the roadside farmers market. Lee says income is down, and if the traditional crops don't sell, he'll have to go find a job. This is what the ban looks like landing on one specific household.

5:08 The regulator's reason: consumers don't know what they're drinking
Tennessee Republican Representative William Lamberth uses a drinks analogy: someone buying a Sprite expects a Sprite, not a beer; someone buying a beer expects a beer, not a tequila; someone buying a tequila expects not to get a Sprite. He says the goal is for consumers to know exactly what they're buying. But even farmers who agree with the logic worry the law overcorrects. The show also gives the other side: big companies are laying people off, and some are simply moving across state lines — for example Emily Schaeferich's company Burning Acre moved from Columbia, Tennessee, to North Carolina to keep growing, and she admits ripping up an entire retail, manufacturing and wholesale supply chain ‘definitely costs a lot of money’.

6:10 Moving to another state may be a wasted move
Hemp economist Beau Whitney calls the nationwide ban taking effect in December an ‘extinction-level event’. His mechanism: cannabis can only be grown in certain states, while hemp can be grown and shipped anywhere, so hemp businesses can build supersized capacity, push costs down and ship nationwide; cannabis, by contrast, needs a separate supply chain per state and can't get hemp's economies of scale. The result is that hemp-derived foods are far cheaper than their cannabis equivalents. So even in states where recreational cannabis is legal, consumers will feel the squeeze when they lose the cheap alternative.

7:13 The ban takes away state tax revenue
The show singles out economies of scale to explain: the more of the same good you produce, the lower the unit cost, and the savings can be passed on to consumers. That also explains why hemp-derived foods are cheaper than cannabis products. But consumers aren't the only ones affected. For many state budgets, losing the hemp industry means losing a sizable source of tax revenue — in Tennessee alone, a $54 million budget hole. Beau Whitney also says this could put hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk.

7:13 The delay just moves it from November to December
The White House has urged Congress to delay or amend the ban, the Senate currently supports it, and the House voted earlier this month to delay it too. But these moves only push the effective date from November to December — a one-month delay. For companies that have already moved across state lines and rebuilt supply chains, a month changes nothing — they may have just moved the whole business only to find the industry destroyed in December.

8:14 Those staying behind switch to fiber hemp
Tennessee farmer Bill Corbin, in Springfield, is preparing the first fiber hemp crop for the French company Hemp-It; this kind of hemp is used for rope, packaging and auto parts. He says there isn't a single person in the industry who didn't know this day was coming, that he thinks the industry was unsustainable to begin with, and he agrees with legislators' efforts to suppress recreational use of hemp derivatives. But he worries about medical consumers: he himself is older and has arthritis, relies heavily on full-spectrum CBD, and the products left after the ban may not be strong enough for older people or those trying to avoid opioid painkillers.

item.description: The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.
item.content:encoded:
The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.

The second half of episode 400, and listenable on its own. The first half is about theories of consciousness; the second half unexpectedly slides into animal ethics, and the four of them never do settle their disagreement.

1:07 A bat having an inner world is not the same as being conscious
Christopher summarises Dennett's response: he flatly denies Nagel — we can talk about what it's like to be a bat in all sorts of ways (by first ruling out the things bats don't do, for instance), and with enough information we eventually get there, because so-called "what it's like to be a bat" just is the discriminative, dispositional states the bat has. Dylan supplies the step Dennett actually rejects: drawing on von Uexküll's Umwelt and Innenwelt (surrounding world and inner world), Dennett grants that the bat has an inner world, which is not crazy; what he won't accept is going straight from "has an inner world" to "therefore consciousness exists," and that latter step is exactly the one Nagel uses to prove consciousness exists. Our mode of access is heterophenomenology: treat the bat's behaviour and physiology as a text in need of interpretation.

5:37 Consciousness is not an all-or-nothing property
Christopher reads out a passage from Dennett: are language-less animals not conscious at all? Dennett says the question shouldn't be taken as a matter of course, because it presupposes something "we've had a hard time getting rid of" — that consciousness is an all-or-nothing property, splitting the universe into two utterly different categories: things that have it and things that don't. That dichotomy is what Dennett wants to dismantle; what he wants is consciousness in degrees. Christopher then offers his own version: he doesn't want to accept property dualism, he wants to deny the hard problem, because subjectivity can perfectly well have a biological and evolutionary explanation — agency and subjectivity co-evolved; a physical process organising itself from the inside into "what it's like" is a real biological phenomenon.

12:57 The bat doesn't know what it's like to be a bat either
Seth pushes the argument to its extreme: it isn't "we don't know what it's like to be a bat," it's that there is no "what it's like to be a bat as seen from the bat's side" at all; the bat itself doesn't know either, because it lacks the machinery to string experiences into a narrative and give them names. Dylan immediately marks the cost of this inference: if anything with dynamic activity has its own experience, then atoms count too, and that's panpsychism. Christopher says you don't have to go as far as atoms, but concedes the direction really does sound like panpsychism — he'd rather use a threshold: you need a feedback loop of sensing and acting before you can talk about a new way of being.

14:35 Even plants have a perspective in some sense
Mark digs up a line from Dennett's book: the perspective of a conscious observer is a refined descendant of the primitive perspective of the first replicators, which "divided the world into good and bad" — on that account even plants have a perspective in this sense, and "perspective" thereby becomes a metaphor. Christopher then offers gradualism: from sponges to mantis shrimp to humans, subjectivity accumulates layer by layer and gets thicker and thicker, with a fuzzy threshold in between. Dylan wants to nail the threshold down harder: you can't use "complex" as the criterion, since weather is also a complex self-maintaining system; the difference is that living things can replicate themselves and have a wholeness, so the only thing the Earth lacks is its own replication.

19:47 You are a bunch of things, not a soul
Mark finds Dennett's 1994 reply collection Get Real, which uses snakes as an example: a snake has no central representation of "mouse," it just responds to prey separately through three sensory systems. Dennett's point is that the perceptual system we take to be a single whole is really a pile of little homunculi each making its own discriminations; you are not an Aristotelian form, a soul, an organisation that runs you — we are all a bunch of things. Christopher objects: failure to integrate information processing doesn't mean there's no self — the two hemispheres of a split-brain patient are also separate, and we don't conclude from that that he has no self; the snake may still have a more ancient, minimal sense of boundary and evaluative experience.

27:39 Reducing experience to discrimination looks a lot like behaviourism
Christopher says he agrees with Dennett 99%, and is stuck on the 1%: when Dennett wants to reduce a person to dispositional states, saying that experiencing red is nothing over and above being able to discriminate red from non-red and being in that discriminative state, it sounds like behaviourism. Seth offers a defence: even if the substrate is just discriminative states, subjective experience, the self, is a composite stitched together out of memory, imagination, representation and symbolic language — it weaves scattered discriminative states into a story with descriptions, meanings and colour, and that story is me. Christopher agrees about the narrative self, but points out that the bat lacks the metacognitive capacity to construct such a self.

38:54 You can club iguanas, but not rabbits
Mark says "everyone is a world" is a good moral fiction, but he doesn't know how to apply it to animals: there are too many iguanas in Florida, and he encourages people to go out and club them, which he says is completely fine and humane; swap in a rabbit and he won't accept it. Seth offers an evolutionary explanation: we already feel differently about animals domesticated over tens of thousands of years, wild animals, and reptiles, and this doesn't conflict with "the self is a narrative centre of gravity." Christopher anchors it in valence: animals are not reflex machines, they are situated perspectives that evaluate, and that is the reason they enter moral consideration — he says that after reading Lars Chittka's The Mind of a Bee, the way he deals with bees changed.

46:10 Take away caring and nothing is left of pain
Mark turns to where Dennett talks specifically about pain: what is the functional relation of pain? If you take away "caring about it, wanting to get away from it," take away everything else, and leave only the sensation of pain, then nothing is left — your not liking pain is itself part of the pain. Mark says this is exactly Dennett's attitude to philosophical zombies: imagine a being biologically, behaviourally, even internally related to you in exactly the same way, but the light of consciousness never came on — Dennett thinks this is so absurd that it's hard even to explain to scientists.
